stem_md: Let the continuous functions  $ f_n(x), \; n\equal{}1,2,3,...,$  be defined on the interval  $ [a,b]$  such that every point of  $ [a,b]$  is a root of  $ f_n(x)\equal{}f_m(x)$  for some  $ n \not\equal{} m$ . Prove that there exists a subinterval of  $ [a,b]$  on which two of the functions are equal.
solution_md:
The sets  $ \{ X: m,n \in \mathbb{N} \mbox{ and } f_m \equal{} f_n \equal{} 0 \mbox{ on } X\}$  form a countable set of closed subsets of  $ [a,b]$ .
So, according to Baire, one of these sets contains an (open) interval, because  $ [a,b]$  is complete.

stem_md: Let  $ f$  be a continuous, nonconstant, real function, and assume the existence of an  $ F$  such that  $ f(x\plus{}y)\equal{}F[f(x),f(y)]$  for all real  $ x$  and  $ y$ . Prove that  $ f$  is strictly monotone.
solution_md:
Since the link above isn't working (at least for me), I'll go ahead and post a solution.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $f$  is not strictly monotone. 
That means that  $f$  has a local extrema, which is attained at some real number, call it  $n_0$ .

For arbitrarily small  $\epsilon > 0$  we can find  $x_1,$   $x_2 \in (n_0-\epsilon,n_o+\epsilon)$  such that  $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ .
Now, see that   $$ f(x+x_2-x_1) = F[f(x-x_1), f(x_2)] = F[f(x-x_1), f(x_1)] = f(x) $$  for any  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ .

It follows that  $f$  is a continuous function that has arbitrarily small periods, therefore  $f$  is constant, contrary to the hypothesis.

stem_md: A gambler plays the following coin-tossing game. He can bet an arbitrary positive amount of money. Then a fair coin is tossed, and the gambler wins or loses the amount he bet depending on the outcome. Our gambler, who starts playing with   $ x$  forints, where  $ 0<x<2C$ , uses the following strategy: if at a given time his capital is  $ y<C$ , he risks all of it; and if he has  $ y>C$ , he only bets  $ 2C\minus{}y$ . If he has exactly  $ 2C$  forints, he stops playing. Let  $ f(x)$  be the probability that he reaches  $ 2C$  (before going bankrupt). Determine the value of  $ f(x)$ .
solution_md:
Fair game, should be <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$ f(x)\equal{}\frac{x}{2C}$</details>

Formal proof: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Fortune,  $ F_{t}$  is a martingale, winning (or loosing) time  $ T$  satisfies optionall stopping time theorem, so  $ F_{0}\equal{}E(F_{T})\equal{}p2C\plus{}(1\minus{}p)0$ , so  $ p\equal{}\frac{F_{0}}{2C}$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $ f(n)$  denote the maximum possible number of right triangles determined by  $ n$  coplanar points. Show that \[ \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \frac{f(n)}{n^2}\equal{}\infty \;\textrm{and}\  \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{f(n)}{n^3}\equal{}0 .\] 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
At first it's easy to see that  $f(n)$  won't decrease.
Let's prove  $$ \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{f(n)}{n^3}=0 $$  at first. Assume it is wrong, then there will be  $\varepsilon>0$ , so that for  $\forall N>0$ , there are  $n>N$ ,  $f(n)\geq\varepsilon n^3$ . Assume that there is a graph  $G$  which can reach the upper bound. We use  $e_{ij}$ ,  $1\leq i<j\leq n$  to denote the edge construct by point  $i$  and  $j$ . For  $e_{ij}$ , we use  $m_{ij}$  to denote the number of points that can form right triangle with  $e_{ij}$ . We have  $$ \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}m_{ij}=2f(n)\geq2\varepsilon n^3 $$  So there must be some  $i$  and  $j$ , so that  $m_{ij}\geq\frac{2\varepsilon n^3}{{n \choose 2}}=\frac{4\varepsilon n^2}{n-1}>4\varepsilon n$ . We can see that there must be at least  $2\varepsilon n$  points on the same line which is vertical to  $e_{ij}$ . We call this line  $l$ , and the number of point on  $l$  is  $m_{l}$ . We first count the number of right triangles which have points on  $l$ , We consider two case:

1. Assume the triangle has two points on  $l$ , and one point out of  $l$ . In this case, for every point  $p$  not on  $l$ , there are at most  $l-1$  edge which can form right triangles with  $p$ , so in this case the total number is less than  $n^2$ 2. Assume the triangle has only one points on  $l$ . In this case, for any pair  $i, j$  not on  $l$ , there will be at most  $2$  points on  $l$ , which can form right triangle with  $i,j$ ( $e_{pi}$  vertical to  $e_{ij}$  or  $e_{pi}$  vertical to  $e_{ij}$ ). So in this case the total number is less than  $2{n\choose 2}<n^2$ Now, if we remove  $\lceil 2\varepsilon n\rceil$  points on  $l$  from  $G$ , there should be more than  $f(n)-2n^2$  right triangle in the rest graph. So we have  $f(n-\lceil 2\varepsilon n\rceil)>f(n)-2n^2\geq\varepsilon n^3-2n^2$ . Now choose  $N_1=\lceil\frac{1-2\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^2}\rceil$ , we for any  $n>N_1$ ,  $\varepsilon \left(\frac{n}{1-2\varepsilon}\right)^3-2\left(\frac{n}{1-2\varepsilon}\right)^2>\left(\frac{1}{1-2\varepsilon}\right)^2 \varepsilon n^3$ .

Now let  $M$  be a large number so that  $(\frac{1}{1-2\varepsilon})^{2M}>\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ . We can construct a sequence  $n_0, n_1, n_2, \cdots, n_{M}$ , so that all  $n_i>N_1$ ,  $n_{i+1}-\lceil 2\varepsilon n_{i+1}\rceil=n_i$ , and  $f(n_0)\geq\varepsilon n_0^3$ . (The construction is possible when we choose a very large  $n_0$ ). Then we can prove by mathematical induction that  $f(n_k)>\varepsilon(\frac{1}{1-2\varepsilon})^{2k}n_k$ . So  $f(n_M)>n^3>{n_M \choose 3}$ . It's a contradictory.

Now we prove  $$ \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{f(n)}{n^2}=\infty $$  First assume that  $n=(2m+1)^2, m\in \mathbb{N}$ , since  $f(n)$  won decrease, it's not difficult to extend the proof to other case. Assuming that all points form a grid  $G=\{(i, j)|i,j\in \mathbb{Z}\ and\  |i|, |j|\leq m \}$ . For all odd prime number  $p<\frac{m}{100}$ , we consider sub-grid  $G_{p,a,x,y}=\{(ip-ja+x, ia+pj+y)|i,j\in \mathbb{Z}\ and\  |i|, |j|\leq \frac{m-p}{a+p} \}$ , here  $x, y, a\in \mathbb{Z}$ ,  $0 < a\leq \frac{p-1}{2}$ ,   $0\leq x, y \leq \frac{q-1}{2}$ . We can see that each sub-grid has  $4{ 2\lfloor \frac{m-p}{a+p} \rfloor \choose 2}^2$  right triangle which has an edge with a slope of  $\frac{a}{p}$ . We can see right triangles in different sub-grid can't be the same right triangle.  And   $$ 4{ 2\lfloor \frac{m-p}{a+p} \rfloor \choose 2}^2 \geq(2\lfloor \frac{m-p}{2p} \rfloor-1)^4\geq (\frac{m-p}{2p})^4>(\frac{m}{3p})^4 $$  So in  $G$ , we have at least  $\sum_{p\in \mathbb{P}, 2<p<\frac{m}{100}}(\frac{m}{3p})^4 (\frac{p-1}{2})^3$  different right triangles. And we have  $$ f(n)\geq \sum_{p\in \mathbb{P}, 2<p<\frac{m}{100}}(\frac{m}{3p})^4 (\frac{p-1}{2})^3>\sum_{p\in \mathbb{P}, 2<p<\frac{m}{100}}(\frac{2m+1}{12p})^4 (\frac{p}{3})^3=\frac{n^2}{3^3*12^4}\sum_{p\in \mathbb{P}, 2<p<\frac{m}{100}}\frac{1}{p} $$   $\sum_{p\in \mathbb{P}, 2<p<\frac{m}{100}}\frac{1}{p}$  diverge as   $m$  grows. So we have   $$ \lim_{m\rightarrow \infty}\frac{f((2m+1)^2)}{(2m+1)^4}=\infty $$  Since  $f(n)$  won't decrease, we can use squeeze theorem to get  $$ \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{f(n)}{n^2}=\infty $$

stem_md:
Let  $ I$  be an ideal of the ring  $\mathbb{Z}\left[x\right]$  of all polynomials with integer coefficients such that 

a) the elements of  $ I$  do not have a common divisor of degree greater than  $ 0$ , and 

b)  $ I$  contains of a polynomial with constant term  $ 1$ . 

Prove that  $ I$  contains the polynomial  $ 1 + x + x^2 + ... + x^{r-1}$  for some natural number  $ r$ .

*Gy. Szekeres*
solution_md:
This problem can be solved in very easy way.

Easy to see from  $(a)$  that  $n\in I$ . Let  $f=1+a_1x+...+a_kx^k\in I$ , then if we proved that  $x^r(1+x+x^2+...+x^j)\in (n,f)$ , then  $x^r(1+x+x^2+...+x^j) = ng+fh$  where all coefficients of  $h$  not divisible by  $n$ , so easy to see that  $h=x^rh'$ ,  $g=x^rg'$  and  $1+x+x^2+...+x^j=ng'+fh'\in I$ .

In case where  $\gcd(a_k,n)=1$ , easy to see that we can take mod  $Z_n$  and see that for some  $r_1< r_2$  polynoms  $1+x+x^2+...+x^{r_1}$ ,  $1+x+x^2+...+x^{r_2}$  will have same remains by  $f$  in  $Z_n$ .

Let polynom  $f^*=1+d_1x+...+d_ex^e$  in  $I$  with constant term  $1$  and minimal value  $a=d_e$  of highest term, easy to see that  $d_e$  divides every other highest term of any polynom in  $I$ . Let  $a\not=1$ .

Fixed number  $b$  and take polynom  $u=u_1+...+u_{l}x^{l}+u_tx^t$  in  $I$  with minimal  $\deg\not= 0$  in  $Z_n$  and where  $t-l=b$  and  $u_t=a$ . We can see that  $u_t=a|n$ . Take  $\frac{n}{u_t}u=\frac{n}{u_t}u_1+...+\frac{n}{u_t}u_{l}x^{l}+nx^t$  in  $Z_n$  his  $\deg$  is smaller, so it is  $0$  and so  $n|\frac{n}{u_t}u_{l}$  and  $u_t|u_{l}$ , so take  $x^{t-l}u-\frac{u_l}{u_t}u\in I$  with bigger value of  $t-l$  and highest term  $a$ .

So we can take polynom  $Q=q_1+...+q_gx^g+ax^w$ , where  $w-g>e$ . And from  $f^*$  construct polynom in  $I$  with smaller highest term. So  $a=1$ . done

 $ I$  has a primary decomposition as  $ I \equal{} \bigcap_i\frak q_i$ . Since  $ A$  injects into  $ \prod_i\left(\mathbb Z[x]/\frak q_i\right)$  and the  $ \frak q_i$  obviously satisfy conditions (a) and (b), it suffices to prove that a primary ideal  $ \frak q$  satisfying (a) and (b) has finite quotient  $ \mathbb Z[x]/\frak q$ . Finally, since  $ \mathbb Z[x]/\frak p^n$  can be written as successive extensions of  $ \frak p^k/\frak p^{k \plus{} 1},\ k \equal{} \overline{0,n \minus{} 1}$ , and these are finitely-generated modules over  $ A/\frak p$ , it suffices to show that given a *prime* ideal  $ \frak p$  with properties (a) and (b), the quotient ring  $ A \equal{} \mathbb Z[x]/\frak p$  is finite (in other words, the initial problem has been reduced to the case when  $ I$  is prime). This is easy: (a) implies that the ideal contains a positive integer, so, being a prime ideal, it must contain some prime number  $ p$ . But now (b) shows that  $ x\in A$  is algebraic over the field  $ \mathbb F_p$  with  $ p$  elements, so  $ A$  is a finite-dimensional vector space over  $ \mathbb F_p$  (since  $ A \equal{} \mathbb F_p[x]$ ).

A "letter  $ T$ " erected at point  $ A$  of the  $ x$ -axis in the  $ xy$ -plane is the union of a segment  $ AB$  in the upper half-plane perpendicular to the  $ x$ -axis and a segment  $ CD$  containing  $ B$  in its interior and parallel to the  $ x$ -axis. Show that it is impossible to erect a letter  $ T$  at every point of the  $ x$ -axis so that the union of those erected at rational points is disjoint from the union of those erected at irrational points. 

*A.Csaszar*
solution_md:
We have to prove that $ (\cup \{T_i : i \in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}\}) \cap (\cup \{T_i : i \in \mathbb{Q}\}) \ne \emptyset$ .
For a point  $ D$ , the projection on the x-axis is  $ D_x$ .
A letter  $ T$  gives rise to two areas (the left and right rectangle),  $ L = C_xABC$  and  $ R = AD_xDB$ .

We create a sequence  $ T_{i_1}, T_{i_2},\cdots$ .
Choose  $ i_1 \in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}$ .
For the even terms  $ T_{i_{2k}}$ :
Choose  $ A_{i_{2k}}$  with  $ i_{2k} \in \mathbb{Q}$  and  $ R_{i_{2k}} \subset L_{i_{2k - 1}}$ 
and distance  $ A_{i_{2k}}A_{i_{2k - 1}}$  less than  $ \frac12 (CB)_{i_{2k - 1}}$ 

For the odd terms  $ T_{i_{2k + 1}}$ :
Choose  $ A_{i_{2k + 1}}$  with  $ i_{2k + 1} \in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}$  and  $ L_{i_{2k + 1}} \subset R_{i_{2k}}$ 
and distance  $ A_{i_{2k}}A_{i_{2k + 1}}$  less than  $ \frac12 (BD)_{i_{2k}}$ 

Say, the sequence  $ i_k$  converges to  $ z$ .
The sequence of  $ y$ -values  $ (B_{i_k})_y$  is positive and decreasing.
Therefore  $ (B_{i_k})$  converges to a point  $ (z,u)$ .
Let wlog  $ z \in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Q}$ .
For letter  $ T_z$  we must have  $ B_z \le u$ , because otherwise it crosses  $ (CD)__{2k}$  for infinite many  $ k$ . $ (CD)_z$  now crosses infinite many  $ (AB)_{2k}$  which proves the statement.

stem_md:
Does there exist a function  $ f(x,y)$  of two real variables that takes natural numbers as its values and for which  $ f(x,y)\equal{}f(y,z)$  implies  $ x\equal{}y\equal{}z?$  

*A. Hajnal*
solution_md:
The answer is yes. We proceed to construct such a function. Let  $\mathbb{N}=\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ , and for a set  $S$  and number  $k$ , let  $S+k = \{s+k:s\in S\}$ .

It is well know that  $\mathbb{R}$  is in bijection with  $2^{\mathbb{N}}$  (power set). For a real number  $x$ , let  $S_x$  denote the subset of  $\mathbb{N}$  associated to it. Let
\[A_x = \{2s : s\in S_x\}\cup\{2s+1 : s\not\in S_x\}.\]
Note that  $A_x\subseteq\mathbb{N}$  and furthermore, if  $x\ne y$ , then  $A_x\not\subseteq A_y$ . Indeed, if  $A_x\subseteq A_y$ , then looking separately at the even and odd elements would imply that  $S_x\subseteq S_y$  and  $\mathbb{N}\setminus S_x\subseteq \mathbb{N}\setminus S_y$ , which implies  $S_x=S_y$ , which implies  $x=y$ .

Thus, to each real number  $x$ , we have an associated subset  $A_x\subseteq\mathbb{N}$  such that  $A_x\not\subseteq A_y$  for any two distinct reals  $x$  and  $y$ . Now, construct the function  $f$  in the following way. Let  $f(x,x)=1$ , and for  $x\ne y$ , let  $f(x,y)$  be some element of
\[1+A_x\cap(\mathbb{N}\setminus A_y),\]
which is nonempty since  $A_x\not\subseteq A_y$ . Note that this step requires the axiom of choice.

Let's now show that this works. Suppose  $f(x,y)=f(y,z)=k$  and  $x\ne y$  and  $y\ne z$ . Then,
\[k-1\in [A_x\cap(\mathbb{N}\setminus A_y)]\cap[A_y\cap(\mathbb{N}\setminus A_z)],\]
which is clearly empty, so we have a contradiction. Thus,  $x=y$  or  $y=z$ , and WLOG  $x=y$  (the other case is similar). Then,  $f(x,y)=1$ , and  $f(a,b)=1$  if and only if  $a=b$  (as the other  $f$  values are at least  $2$ ), so we also have  $y=z$ , so  $x=y=z$ , as desired. This completes the construction and thus the proof.

stem_md:
For a real number  $ x$  in the interval  $ (0,1)$  with decimal representation 

\[ 0.a_1(x)a_2(x)...a_n(x)...,\] 

denote by  $ n(x)$  the smallest nonnegative integer such that 

\[ \overline{a_{n(x)\plus{}1}a_{n(x)\plus{}2}a_{n(x)\plus{}3}a_{n(x)\plus{}4}}\equal{}1966 .\] 

Determine  $ \int_0^1n(x)dx$ . ( $ \overline{abcd}$  denotes the decimal number with digits  $ a,b,c,d .$ ) 

*A. Renyi*
solution_md: This is actually a standard exercise, hardly disguised. Indeed, we are asked to compute  $\mathbb{E}[n(X)]$  where  $X$  is uniformly distributed on the interval  $(0,1)$ . But since  $X$  can also be represented as  $X = \sum_{k \geq 1} U_k \, {10}^{-k}$  where  $\{U_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$  is an i.i.d sequence of discrete random variables uniformly distributed on  $\{0,1, \ldots, 9\}$ , the problems only ask how long we are expected to wait before observing  $(U_{t},U_{t+1},U_{t+2},U_{t+3})=(1,9,6,6)$ . A similar exercise might even have already been discussed on this forum. This can for example be solved by the usual [first step](http://goo.gl/evja8) analysis.

Let \[ f(x)\equal{}a_0\plus{}a_1x\plus{}a_2x^2\plus{}a_{10}x^{10}\plus{}a_{11}x^{11}\plus{}a_{12}x^{12}\plus{}a_{13}x^{13} \; (a_{13} \not\equal{}0) \] and \[ g(x)\equal{}b_0\plus{}b_1x\plus{}b_2x^2\plus{}b_{3}x^{3}\plus{}b_{11}x^{11}\plus{}b_{12}x^{12}\plus{}b_{13}x^{13} \; (b_{3} \not\equal{}0) \] 
be polynomials over the same field. Prove that the degree of their greatest common divisor is at least  $ 6$ .


*L. Redei*
solution_md:
Euclidean algorithm, basically the notation  $(f_1;g_1)$  keeps track of which coefficients may not be zero when we subtract a multiple of one of the polynomials from the other. stem_md:
Let  $ a_1,a_2,...,a_N$  be positive real numbers whose sum equals  $ 1$ . For a natural number  $ i$ , let  $ n_i$  denote the number
of  $ a_k$  for which  $ 2^{1-i} \geq a_k \geq 2^{-i}$  holds. Prove that 
\[  \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{n_i2^{-i}} \leq 4+\sqrt{\log_2 N}.\] 

*L. Leinder*
solution_md:
We have  $ \sum_{i=1}^N a_i= 1 $  and  $ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} n_i = N $ Observe that  $ 1 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i \geq \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left( \mbox{ Number of } a_k \mbox{ such that } 2^{1-i} \leq a_k \leq 2^{-i} \right) \cdot 2^{-i} $  $ \Rightarrow 1 = \sum_{i=1}^N a_i \geq \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} n_i 2^{-i} $ Now  $ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{ n_i 2^{-i} } = \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor } \sqrt{ n_i2^{-i} } + \sum_{i= \lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor + 1}^{\infty} \sqrt{n_i 2^{-i} } $  
By Cauchy Schwarz Inequality we have  $$  \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{ n_i 2^{-i} } \leq \left( \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor } 1 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \left( \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor } n_i2^{-i} \right)^{\frac{1}{2} } + \left( \sum_{i= \lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor + 1}^{\infty}  n_i \right)^{\frac{1}{2} } \left( \sum_{i= \lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor + 1}^{\infty}  2^{-i} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}  $$    $$  \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{ n_i 2^{-i} } \leq \sqrt{ \lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor} \left( \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} n_i 2^{-i} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} + \left( \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} n_i \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \left( 2^{ -\frac{ \lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor }{2} } \right)   $$    $$  \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{ n_i 2^{-i} } \leq \sqrt{ \log_2{N} } \cdot 1 + \sqrt{N} \left( 2^{ - \frac{ \lfloor \log_2{N} \rfloor }{2} } \right)  $$    $$  \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{ n_i 2^{-i} } \leq \sqrt{ \log_2{N} } + \sqrt{N} \left( 2^{ - \frac{ \log_2{N} - 1 }{2} } \right)  $$    $$  \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sqrt{ n_i 2^{-i} } \leq \sqrt{ \log_2{N} } + \sqrt{2} < \sqrt{ \log_2{N} } + 4  $$

stem_md:
Let  $ A$  be a family of proper closed subspaces of the Hilbert space  $ H\equal{}l^2$  totally ordered with respect to inclusion (that is
, if  $ L_1,L_2 \in A$ , then either  $ L_1\subset L_2$  or  $ L_2\subset L_1$ ). Prove that there exists a vector  $ x \in H$  not contaied in any of the subspaces  $ L$  belonging to  $ A$ . 

*B. Szokefalvi Nagy*
solution_md:
Suppose (for a contradiction) that  $ \bigcup_{L\in A}L \equal{} H$ . Let  $ \{e_n\}_{n \equal{} 1}^\infty$  be an orthonormal basis for  $ H$ . Inductively, construct an increasing sequence  $ (L_n)\subset A$  such that  $ e_n\in L_n$  for all  $ n$ . For each  $ n$  choose a unit vector  $ x_n\in L_{n \plus{} 1}\ominus L_n$  and let  $ x \equal{} \sum_{k \equal{} 1}^\infty2^{ \minus{} k}x_k$ .

By supposition,  $ x\in L$  for some  $ L\in A$ . If  $ L\subset L_n$  then  $ \sum_{k \equal{} n}^\infty2^{ \minus{} k}x_k\in L_n\cap L_n^{\perp} \equal{} \{0\}$ , which is not possible. Therefore  $ L_n\subset L$ . But if that holds for all  $ n$  then  $ L\supset\bigcup L_n$ , which is dense in H (because it contains all the vectors in an orthonormal basis). Since  $ L$  is closed, that means that  $ L \equal{} H$ , contradicting the fact that  $ L$  is a proper subspace.

stem_md:
Let  $ U$  be an  $ n \times n$  orthogonal matrix. Prove that for any  $ n \times n$  matrix  $ A$ , the matrices \[ A_m=\frac{1}{m+1}  \sum_{j=0}^m U^{-j}AU^j\] converge entrywise as  $ m \rightarrow \infty.$  

*L. Kovacs*
solution_md:
if  $ \mu$  is the usual probability measure on the unit sphere  $ S^{n\minus{}1}$  of  $ \mathbb{R}^n$ , then it also induces a probability measure on  $ X\equal{}S^{n\minus{}1} \times S^{n\minus{}1}$ . Moreover,  $ \phi: X \mapsto X$  defined by  $ \phi(x,y) \equal{} (Ux, Uy)$  is a measure preserving transformation. So if  $ f: X\to \mathbb{R}$  is defined by  $ f(x,y) \equal{} x^tAy$ , the ergodic theorem says that
\[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{1}{m\plus{}1} \sum_{j\equal{}0}^m f( \phi^{j})\]
converges almost everywhere.

stem_md:
Let  $ n$  and  $ k$  be given natural numbers, and let  $ A$  be a set such that \[ |A| \leq \frac{n(n+1)}{k+1}.\] For  $ i=1,2,...,n+1$ , let  $ A_i$  be sets of size  $ n$  such that \[ |A_i \cap A_j| \leq k \;(i \not=j)\ ,\] \[ A=  \bigcup_{i=1}^{n+1} A_i.\] Determine the cardinality of  $ A$ . 

*K. Corradi*
solution_md:
Let's assume  $ A\equal{}\{1,2,\dots,m\}$ .
Let  $ b_i$  ( $ i\equal{}1,2,...,m$ ) denote the number of occurrences of  $ i$  among all the sets  $ A_j$  ( $ j\equal{}1,2,...,n\plus{}1$ )
we have  $ k\binom{n\plus{}1}{2}\geq \sum_{i>j}\left|A_i\cap A_j\right|\equal{}\sum_{i\equal{}1}^m \binom{b_i}{2}$ 

So,  $ kn(n\plus{}1)\geq \sum_{i\equal{}1}^m (b_i\minus{}\frac12)^2\minus{}\frac{m}{4}\geq \frac{1}{m}(\sum_{i\equal{}1}^m(b_i\minus{}\frac12))^2\minus{}\frac{m}4$ 
As,  $ \sum_{i\equal{}1}^m b_i\equal{}n(n\plus{}1)$ 
we get  $ kn(n\plus{}1)\geq \frac{1}{4m}\left((2n^2\plus{}2n\minus{}m)^2\minus{}m^2\right)\equal{}\frac{n(n\plus{}1)(n^2\plus{}n\minus{}m)}{m}$  $ \Rightarrow mk\geq n(n\plus{}1)\minus{}m$ 
or  $ m\geq \frac{n(n\plus{}1)}{k\plus{}1}$ 
so we conclude that  $ |A|\equal{}\frac{n(n\plus{}1)}{k\plus{}1}$

Let  $ f(x)$  be a real function such that 
\[ \lim_{x \rightarrow \plus{}\infty} \frac{f(x)}{e^x}\equal{}1\] 
and  $ |f''(x)|\leq c|f'(x)|$  for all sufficiently large  $ x$ . Prove that \[ \lim_{x \rightarrow \plus{}\infty} \frac{f'(x)}{e^x}\equal{}1.\] 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
Let $ f(x)$ be a real function such that \[ \lim_{x \rightarrow \plus{}\infty} \frac{f(x)}{e^x}\equal{}1\] and $ |f''(x)|\leq c|f'(x)|$ for all sufficiently large $ x$ . Prove that \[ \lim_{x \rightarrow \plus{}\infty} \frac{f'(x)}{e^x}\equal{}1.\] *P. Erdos*
There is an $x_0$ such that $f'(x_0)>0$ . Then $e^{cx}f'(x)$ is non-decreasing and $e^{-cx}f'(x)$ is non-increasing. Thus $f'(x)>0$ and $e^{-cy}f'(x)\leq f'(x+y)\leq e^{cy}f'(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},y\geq0$ . Thus \begin{align*} f'(x)\cdot\frac{e^{cy}-1}{c}=\int_0^ye^{ct}f'(t)\;\mathrm{d}t\geq f(x+y)-f(x)\geq\int_0^ye^{-ct}f'(t)=f'(x)\cdot\frac{1-e^{-cy}}{c} \frac{f'(x)}{e^{x}}\cdot\frac{e^{cy}-1}{cy}\geq\frac{e^y\frac{f(x+y)}{e^{x+y}}-\frac{f(x)}{e^x}}{y}\geq\frac{f'(x)}{e^{x}}\cdot\frac{1-e^{-cy}}{cy} \end{align*} Assume there is an $\varepsilon>0$ such that there is a sequence $x_1,x_2,\cdots$ with $\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=+\infty$ and $\frac{f(x_n)}{e^{x_n}}>1+\varepsilon$ for all $n$ . Choose $y>0$ sufficiently small such that $\frac{1-e^{-cy}}{cy}\geq(1+\varepsilon)^{-1/3}$ and $\frac{e^y-1}{y}\leq(1+\varepsilon)^{1/3}$ . Then choose $n$ large enough such that $\frac{e^y\frac{f(x_n+y)}{e^{x_n+y}}-\frac{f(x_n)}{e^{x_n}}}{y}\leq(1+\varepsilon)^{2/3}$ . We get the contradiction $$ (1+\varepsilon)^{2/3}\geq\frac{e^y\frac{f(x_n+y)}{e^{x_n+y}}-\frac{f(x_n)}{e^{x_n}}}{y}\geq\frac{f'(x_n)}{e^{x_n}}\cdot\frac{1-e^{-cy}}{cy}>(1+\varepsilon)^{2/3}. $$ So we must have $\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{f'(x)}{e^x}\leq1$ . Similarly, we get $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{f'(x)}{e^x}\geq1$ . Thus $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f'(x)}{e^x}=1$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ A_1,...,A_n$  be arbitrary events in a probability field. Denote by  $ C_k$  the event that at least  $ k$  of  $ A_1,...,A_n$  occur. Prove that \[  \prod_{k=1}^n P(C_k) \leq  \prod_{k=1}^n P(A_k).\] 

*A. Renyi*
solution_md:
Let $ A_1,...,A_n$ be arbitrary events in a probability field. Denote by $ C_k$ the event that at least $ k$ of $ A_1,...,A_n$ occur. Prove that \[ \prod_{k=1}^n P(C_k) \leq \prod_{k=1}^n P(A_k).\] *A. Renyi*
If one of the $P(A_k)$ -s is $0$ , we have $P(C_n)=0$ and equality. If the left hand side is $0$ , the inequality holds. So it suffices to check the case that both sides are not equal to $0$ . We can further assume $P(A_1)\geq P(A_2)\geq\cdots\geq P(A_n)$ . We claim that $P(C_1),P(C_2),\ldots,P(C_n)$ majorizes $P(A_1),P(A_2),\ldots,P(A_n)$ . Then the inequality follows directly from applying Karamata's inequality with the concave function $\ln x$ . To check the claim note that each of the $2^n$ events of the form $B_1\cap B_2\cap\cdots\cap B_n$ with $B_k\in\{A_k,\overline{A_k}\}$ appears at least as often in $C_1,C_2,\ldots,C_j$ as in $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_j$ for every $1\leq j\leq n$ with equality for $j=n$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ G$  be an infinite group generated by nilpotent normal subgroups. Prove that every maximal Abelian normal subgroup of  $ G$  is infinite. (We call an Abelian normal subgroup maximal if it is not contained in another Abelian normal subgroup.) 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
Solution:

Lemma 1: $\forall \{e\}\not= H\triangleleft G$ ,  $H\cap Z(G)\not= \{e\}$ .

See it here: http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/blog/95197

Lemma 2:

Let  $H\triangleleft G: |H|<\infty$ , then  $Z_G(H)\triangleleft G$ ,  $[G:Z_G(H)]<\infty$ Let's use this, let  $A$  is maximal Abelian normal subgroup of  $G$ ,  $\{G_i\}_{i=1}^n$  are nilpotent normal generators of  $G$ ,  $|A|<\infty$ , so from Lemma 2 we get that  $A\subset Z_G(A)$ ,  $[G:Z_G(A)]<\infty$ , so  $A\not= Z_G(A)$  denote  $\pi_A : G\to G/A$ ,  $\pi(Z_G(A))\triangleleft \pi_A(G)$ , easy to see that  $\{\pi_A(G_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$  are nilpotent normal generators of  $\pi_A(G)$ , so from Lemma 1  $\pi(Z_G(A))\cap Z(\pi_A(G))\not= \{e\}$ , take  $\alpha \in \pi(Z_G(A))\cap Z(\pi_A(G)) : \alpha \not=e$ ,  $<\alpha>\subset Z(\pi_A(G))$ , so  $<\alpha>\triangleleft \pi_A(G)$ , so  $A^*= \pi_A^{-1}(<\alpha>)\triangleleft G$ ,  $A\subset A^*$ ,  $\pi_A(A^*)\subset \pi(Z_G(A))$ , so  $A\subset Z(A^*)$ ,  $A^*/A=<\alpha>$  is cyclic, so  $A^*/Z(A^*)$  is cyclic, so  $A^*$  is Abelian  $A^*\triangleleft G$ , so  $|A|=\infty$ . done

stem_md:
Find all continuous real functions  $ f,g$  and  $ h$  defined on the set of positive real numbers and satisfying the relation \[ f(x\plus{}y)\plus{}g(xy)\equal{}h(x)\plus{}h(y)\] for all  $ x>0$  and  $ y>0$ . 

*Z. Daroczy*
solution_md:
$ f(x + y) + g(xy) = h(x) + h(y)$  (Eq.  $ I$ )

Integrate between  $ \epsilon$  and 1: $ \int_{y+\epsilon}^{y+1}f(u)\,du + \frac{1}{y}\int_{\epsilon y}^{y}g(u)\,du = \int_{\epsilon}^1 h(u)\, du + (1-\epsilon) h(y)$ 
which tells us that  $ h$  is continuous differentiable.
In the same way, we may substitute  $ y = u - x$  in  $ I$  and integrate from  $ x = \epsilon$  to  $ \frac{u}{2}$  and conclude that  $ f$  is continuous differentiable.
And so  $ g$  has also this property. $ f'(x+y) + xg'(xy) = h'(y)$ 
Integration between  $ x=\epsilon$  and  $ x=1$  shows that  $ h$  is twice differentiable.
 $ g(x^2-\epsilon^2) - g(x^2) = h(x+\epsilon) + h(x-\epsilon) - 2h(x)$ 
Divide this equation by  $ \epsilon^2$  and take the limit for  $ \epsilon \to 0$ .
Then  $ -g'(x^2) = h''(x)$ .

Write  $ I$  in the following form: $ f(u) + g(v) = h(x) + h(y)$ , with  $ x,y = \frac12(u \pm \sqrt{v^2-4u})$ ,  $ (x \ge y > 0)$ .
Differentiate both sides by  $ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial u \partial v}$ .
Then $ 0 = h''(x)\frac{dx}{du}\frac{dx}{dv} + h'(x)\frac{d^2x}{du dv} + h''(y)\frac{dy}{du}\frac{dy}{dv} + h'(y)\frac{d^2y}{du dv}$ .
Then $ (h''(x)-h''(y))(x-y)^2 +  (h''(x) + h''(y))(x^2-y^2) = 2(x+y)(h'(x)-h'(y))$ .
If  $ y=c$  (a constant) and  $ h' = j$ , then  $ j'(x)x(x-c) - j(x)(x+c) = px+q$  for certain constants  $ p$  and  $ q$ .
The general solution of this differential equation is  $ j(x) = r + sx + \frac{t}{x}$ , where  $ r,s,t$  are constants.
Then  $ h(x) = a + bx + cx^2 + d\ln(x)$  ( $ a,b,c,d$  are constants). $ g'(x) = -h''(\sqrt{x})$ , so $ g(x) = \alpha -2cx + d\ln(x)$  $ f(x) = -g(\frac{x^2}{4})+2\h(\frac{x}{2}) = -\alpha+2a +bx +cx^2$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ f$  and  $ g$  be continuous positive functions defined on the interval  $ [0, +\infty)$ , and let  $ E \subset[0,+\infty)$  be a set of positive measure. Prove that the range of the function defined on  $ E \times E$  by the relation \[ F(x,y)= %Error. "dispalymath" is a bad command.
\int_0^xf(t)dt+ %Error. "dispalymath" is a bad command.
\int_0^y g(t)dt\] has a nonvoid interior. 

*L. Losonczi*
solution_md:
Let  $A = \{ t >0 \colon t = \int_0^x f(s)ds \text{ for some } x \in E\},$  and define  $B$  analogously with  $g$  in place of  $f.$  It suffices to show that  $|A|, |B| > 0,$  and then classical methods with convolutions imply that  $A+B$  contains an interval -- and hence the range of  $F$  has nonempty interior.

Let  $\tilde{f}(x) = \int_0^x f(s)ds.$  Then  $\tilde{f}$  is strictly monotone on  $[0,+\infty).$  Moreover, since  $f>0$  is continuous, we have, for any compact set  $K \subset [0,+\infty),$  that  $\tilde{f}$  is bi-Lipschitz over  $K$ . That is,  $\tilde{f}$  is invertible, and, letting its inverse be  $\tilde{f}^{-1},$  then  $|\tilde{f}'|,|(\tilde{f}^{-1})'| \le C$  for some constant  $C.$  

It is not hard to show that this condition implies that, for any set  $S \subset K,$  we have  $|S|/C \le |\tilde{f}(S)| \le C |S|,$  where  $|\cdot|$  denotes Lebesgue measure. The claim then follows by approximating  $E$  by a such interval, and using the analysis conducted above for both  $f$  and  $g.$

We have  $ 2n\plus{}1$  elements in the commutative ring  $ R$ : \[ \alpha,\alpha_1,...,\alpha_n,\varrho_1,...,\varrho_n .\] Let us define the elements \[ \sigma_k\equal{}k\alpha \plus{} \sum_{i\equal{}1}^n \alpha_i\varrho_i^k .\] Prove that the ideal  $ (\sigma_0,\sigma_1,...,\sigma_k,...)$  can be finitely generated.


*L. Redei*
solution_md: In fact, the sequence  $ [\sigma_k]$  satisfies a difference equation  $ (S\minus{}1)^2 \prod_i (S\minus{}\varrho_i) [\sigma_k] \equal{} 0$ , where  $ S$  is the successor operator  $ S [a_k] \equal{} [a_{k\plus{}1}]$ .  It follows that each  $ \sigma_k$  is a linear combination of  $ \sigma_0,\ldots \sigma_{n\plus{}1}$ .

stem_md:
Let a neighborhood basis of a point  $ x$  of the real line consist of all Lebesgue-measurable sets containing  $ x$  whose density at  $ x$  equals  $ 1$ . Show that this requirement defines a topology that is regular but not normal. 

*A. Csaszar*
solution_md:
In other words, the open sets are those measurable sets which have density  $ 1$  at all their points. 

Regular:

Let  $ F$  be a set closed in the given topology, and which does not contain the origin  $ 0$  of the real line. Let  $ (x_n)_n$  be a sequence of positive reals converging to  $ 0$  such that the measure of  $ F\cap( \minus{} t,t)$  is at most  $ \frac 1n$  times the measure of  $ ( \minus{} t,t)$  for all  $ 0 < t\le x_n$ ; it's obviously possible to find such a sequence because the complement  $ \mathbb R\setminus F$  has density  $ 1$  around  $ 0$ . Also assume that  $ 2x_{n \plus{} 1} < x_n,\ \forall n$  (the factor  $ 2$  is not important here). It follows from these conditions that it's possible to cover  $ F\cap(( \minus{} x_n,x_n)\setminus( \minus{} x_{n \plus{} 1},x_{n \plus{} 1}))$  with an open set  $ D_n$  of measure  $ \le\frac 2n$  times the measure of  $ ( \minus{} x_n,x_n)\setminus( \minus{} x_{n \plus{} 1},x_{n \plus{} 1})$ . The union  $ D$  of all  $ D_n$  is an open set containing  $ F$  but not  $ 0$ , and its complement  $ U$  has density  $ 1$  at  $ 0$ . By the Lebesgue Density Theorem we can eliminate a set of measure zero from  $ U$  so that the remainder has density  $ 1$  at all its points, and we have the disjoint open sets containing  $ x$  and  $ F$  that we were looking for.

Not normal:

Let  $ A$  and  $ B$  be disjoint dense  $ G_\delta$  sets of measure zero (constructing such sets should be easy enough).  $ A$  and  $ B$  are disjoint closed sets in our topology; I claim that there they cannot have disjoint neighborhoods. Assume otherwise, and let  $ U\supset A$  and  $ V\supset B$  be disjoint open sets. For each positive integer  $ n$ , let  $ A_n$  ( $ B_n$ ) be the subset of  $ A$  ( $ B$ ) consisting of those points  $ x$  with the property that the measure of  $ (x \minus{} t,x \plus{} t)\cap U$  (resp.  $ (x \minus{} t,x \plus{} t)\cap V$ ) is at least  $ \frac 23$  times the measure of  $ ( \minus{} t,t)$  for all  $ 0 < t\le\frac 1n$ .  $ A_n$  are closed subsets of  $ A$ , and  $ A \equal{} \bigcup A_n$  (similarly for  $ B$ ). Because  $ G_\delta$ 's in Polish spaces are Polish, we can apply Baire's Theorem to conclude (using also the density of  $ A$  and  $ B$ ) that we can find an  $ n$  and an interval of the real line in which both  $ A_n, B_n$  are dense. But this is absurd: we would be able to find two intervals of length  $ \frac 2n$ , arbitrarily close (i.e. their centers are arbitrarily close), such that  $ U$  has density  $ \ge\frac 23$  in one of them, while  $ V$ , which is disjoint from  $ U$ , has density  $ \ge\frac 23$  in the other one.

stem_md:
Let  $ 0<a_k<1$  for  $ k=1,2,... .$  Give a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence, for every  $ 0<x<1$ , of a permutation  $ \pi_x$  of the positive integers such that \[ x= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{a_{\pi_x}(k)}{2^k}.\] 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
It is obvious that  $\inf a_k = 0$  and  $\sup a_k = 1$  are necessary conditions.

We will show that the these two conditions are also sufficient. That is, if  $(a_k)_{k \geq 1}$  is a sequence such that  $0 < a_k < 1$  and  $\inf a_k = 0$  and  $\sup a_k = 1$ , then for any  $x \in (0, 1)$  there exists a bijection  $\pi: \Bbb Z_{\geq 1} \rightarrow \Bbb Z_{\geq 1}$  such that  $x = \sum_{k = 1}^\infty \frac{a_{\pi(k)}}{2^k}$ .
-----
Given any  $x \in (0, 1)$ , we will construct the map  $\pi$  inductively.
We define  $i_0 = 0$  and  $s_0 = 0$ . For  $t \geq 0$ , assume that we have defined  $\pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)$  in such a way that  $x_t = 2^{s_t}\left(x - \sum_{k = 1}^{s_t} \frac{a_{\pi(k)}}{2^k}\right)$  lies in the interval  $(0, 1)$ .
We define  $i_{t + 1}$  as the smallest positive integer that doesn't belong to  $\{\pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)\}$  and write  $a$  for  $a_{i_{t + 1}}$ .

There are two cases:  $x_t \leq \frac 1 2$  or  $x_t > \frac 1 2$ .
We first treat the case  $x_t \leq \frac 1 2$ .
In this case, we may choose  $r \in \Bbb Z_{\geq 0}$  such that  $\frac a 2 < 2^r x_t < \frac{a + 1}2$ . In fact, if  $x_t > \frac a 2$ , then taking  $r = 0$  suffices; otherwise, we can take  $r$  to be the smallest integer such that  $2^r x_t > \frac a 2$ , so that  $2^{r - 1}x_t \leq \frac a 2$  and hence  $2^r x_t \leq a < \frac{a + 1}2$ .
We choose  $b_1, \dots, b_r$  such that all  $b_j$  are different, none of the  $b_j$  appears in  $\{i_{t + 1}, \pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)\}$ , and that  $\sum_{j = 1}^r 2^{r - j}a_{b_j} < 2^rx_t - \frac a 2$ . This is possible, thanks to the assumption  $\inf a_k = 0$ . It follows that  $\frac a 2 < 2^r x_t - \sum_{j = 1}^r2^{r - j}a_{b_j} < \frac{a + 1}2$ .
We define  $\pi(s_t + j) = b_j$  for  $1 \leq j \leq r$ ,  $\pi(s_t + r + 1) = i_{t + 1}$ , and  $s_{t + 1} = s_t + r + 1$ .

Let us verify that  $x_{t + 1} = 2^{s_{t + 1}}\left(x - \sum_{k = 1}^{s_{t + 1}}\frac{a_{\pi(k)}}{2^k}\right)$  lies in the interval  $(0, 1)$ .
From the definitions, we compute  $x_{t + 1} = 2\left(2^r x_t - \sum_{j = 1}^r 2^{r - j}a_{b_j}\right) - a$ , which lies in the interval  $(0, 1)$ .

The case  $x_t > \frac 1 2$  is treated similarly. For convenience, we write  $\overline z = 1 - z$  for any  $z \in (0, 1)$ .
In this case, we have  $\overline{x_t} < \frac 1 2$ , thus we may choose  $r \in \Bbb Z_{\geq 0}$  such that  $\frac{\overline a}2 < 2^r \overline{x_t} < \frac{\overline a + 1}2$ .
We choose  $b_1, \dots, b_r$  such that all  $b_j$  are different, none of the  $b_j$  appears in  $\{i_{t + 1}, \pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)\}$ , and that  $\sum_{j = 1}^r 2^{r - j}\overline{a_{b_j}} < 2^r \overline{x_t} - \frac{\overline a}2$ , which is possible because  $\sup a_k = 0$ . This implies  $\frac{\overline a}2 < 2^r\overline{x_t} - \sum_{j = 1}^r2^{r - j}\overline{a_{b_j}} < \frac{\overline a + 1}2$ , which is equivalent to  $\frac a2 < 2^rx_t - \sum_{j = 1}^r2^{r - j}a_{b_j} < \frac{a + 1}2$ .
We define as before  $\pi(s_t + j) = b_j$  for  $1 \leq j \leq r$ ,  $\pi(s_t + r + 1) = i_{t + 1}$ , and  $s_{t + 1} = s_t + r + 1$ .

It is then verified in the same way that  $x_{t + 1}$  lies in the interval  $(0, 1)$ .

This finishes the inductive construction of the map  $\pi$ . It remains to prove that  $\pi$  is bijective and that  $x = \sum_{k \geq 1}\frac{a_{\pi(k)}}{2^k}$ .

The injectivity of  $\pi$  is clear from the definition. To see that  $\pi$  is surjective, we show that any integer  $t \geq 1$  appears in  $\{\pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)\}$  by induction on  $t$ .
Suppose this is true for  $\leq t$  and we want to prove it for  $t + 1$ .
If  $t + 1$  appears in  $\{\pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)\}$ , then it is already OK.
Otherwise, we must have  $i_{t + 1} = t + 1$ , because  $1, \dots, t$  all appear in  $\{\pi(1), \dots, \pi(s_t)\}$  by induction hypothesis. Thus  $\pi(s_{t + 1}) = i_{t + 1} = t + 1$ .

Finally, we know that  $x_t = 2^{s_t}\left(x - \sum_{k = 1}^{s_t}\frac{a_{\pi(k)}}{2^k}\right)$  lies in the interval  $(0, 1)$  for every  $t$ . This clearly implies that  $x = \sum_{k = 1}^\infty\frac{a_{\pi(k)}}{2^k}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ n \geq 2$  be an integer, let  $ S$  be a set of  $ n$  elements, and let  $ A_i , \; 1\leq i \leq m$ , be distinct subsets of  $ S$  of size at least  $ 2$  such that \[ A_i \cap A_j 
ot\equal{} \emptyset, A_i \cap A_k 
ot\equal{} \emptyset, A_j \cap A_k 
ot\equal{} \emptyset, \;	extrm{imply}\ \;A_i \cap A_j \cap A_k 
ot\equal{} \emptyset \ .\] Show that  $ m \leq 2^{n\minus{}1}\minus{}1$ . 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
Let $ n \geq 2$ be an integer, let $ S$ be a set of $ n$ elements, and let $ A_i , \; 1\leq i \leq m$ , be distinct subsets of $ S$ of size at least $ 2$ such that \[ A_i \cap A_j \not\equal{} \emptyset, A_i \cap A_k \not\equal{} \emptyset, A_j \cap A_k \not\equal{} \emptyset, \;\textrm{imply}\ \;A_i \cap A_j \cap A_k \not\equal{} \emptyset \ .\] Show that $ m \leq 2^{n\minus{}1}\minus{}1$ . *P. Erdos*
Let $\mathcal{F}=\{A_1,\cdots,A_m\}$ . Induction on $n$ . For $n=1$ , the family $\mathcal{F}$ must be empty. And for $n=2$ , there can be at most one element of $\mathcal{F}$ , the set $A_1=S$ . So the claim holds for $n=2$ . Let $A$ be an inclusion-maximal set from $\mathcal{F}\setminus\{S\}$ . Then $S$ is the only potential proper superset of $A$ in $\mathcal{F}$ . By the induction hypothesis there are at most $2^{|A|-1}-1$ subsets of $A$ and at most $2^{n-|A|-1}-1$ subsets of $S\setminus A$ in $\mathcal{F}$ . All the other sets in $\mathcal{F}$ have elements in both $A$ and $S\setminus A$ . For every one of the $2^{n-|A|}-1$ choices of subsets of $\emptyset\neq B\subseteq S\setminus A$ we can not have both $B\cup C$ and $B\cup A\setminus C$ in $\mathcal{F}$ for $C\subseteq A$ . The sets $B$ and $B\cup A$ are already counted. So we have at most $2^{|A|-1}-1$ additional choices for subsets of $A$ each. So $\mathcal{F}$ contains at most $1+\left(2^{|A|-1}-1\right)+\left(2^{n-|A|-1}-1\right)+\left(2^{n-|A|}-1\right)\left(2^{|A|-1}-1\right)=2^{n-1}-2^{n-|A|-1}\leq2^{n-1}-1$ sets.

stem_md:
Let  $ G$  be a solvable torsion group in which every Abelian subgroup is finitely generated. Prove that  $ G$  is finite. 

*J. Pelikan*
solution_md:
Though perhaps the solution is somewhat more confusing then it needs to be. All one needs to say is--take a maximal abelian subgroup $ A\subset{G}$ . This exists by the hypotheses given.
Actually, a maximal abelian subgroup exists without any hypotheses. Of course, you do need the hypothesis of finite generation for your next step (to observe that $ A$ is finite), but not here.
Furthermore, we see at once that $ A$ is finite. Then notice that $ A$ must be self-centralizing, because if $ x$ is in $ C_G(A)$ but not $ A$ , then $ (A,x)$ is still abelian and strictly larger than $ A$ . But then the map $ G\to\operatorname{Aut}(A)$ is an injection.
How do you get a map $ G \to \mbox{Aut}(A)$ ? You don't know that $ A$ is a normal subgroup (or, at least, you never showed that it is).

\sigma(x,y)\plus{}\sigma(y,z) \;(x,y,z \in E) \ ,\] and, for any  $ p \in E$ , the sets \[ V_1(p,\varepsilon)\equal{}\{ x : \;\sigma(x,p)< \varepsilon \  \}  \;(\varepsilon >0) \] form a neighborhood base of  $ p$  with respect to  $ \mathcal{T}_1$ , and the sets \[ V_2(p,\varepsilon)\equal{}\{ x : \;\sigma(p,x)< \varepsilon \  \} \;(\varepsilon >0) \] form a neighborhood base of  $ p$  with respect to  $ \mathcal{T}_2$ . We throw  $ N$  balls into  $ n$  urns, one by one, independently and uniformly. Let  $ X_i\equal{}X_i(N,n)$  be the total number of balls in
the  $ i$ th urn. Consider the random variable \[ y(N,n)\equal{}\min_{1 \leq i \leq n}|X_i\minus{}\frac Nn|.\] Verify the following three statements:

(a) If  $ n \rightarrow \infty$  and  $ N/n^3 \rightarrow \infty$ , then \[ P \left(\frac{y(N,n)}{\frac 1n \sqrt{\frac Nn}}<x \right)
\rightarrow 1\minus{}e^{\minus{}x\sqrt{2/ \pi}} \;\textrm{for all}\ \; x>0 \ .\] 

(b) If  $ n\rightarrow \infty$  and  $ N/n^3 \leq K$  ( $ K$  constant), then for any  $ \varepsilon > 0$  there is an  $ A > 0$  such that \[ P(y(N,n) < A) > 1\minus{}\varepsilon .\] 

(c) If  $ n \rightarrow \infty$  and  $ N/n^3 \rightarrow 0$  then \[ P(y(N,n) < 1) \rightarrow 1.\]

stem_md:
We say that the rank of a group  $ G$  is at most  $ r$  if every subgroup of  $ G$  can be generated by at most  $ r$  elements. Prove
that here exists an integer  $ s$  such that for every finite group  $ G$  of rank  $ 2$  the commutator series of  $ G$  has length less than  $ s$ . 

*J. Erdos*
solution_md:
To prove this problem we need to prove problems  $A$  and  $B$ .

Problem  $A$ Prove that  $\exists s\in\mathbb{N}$ , such that for every finite solvable group  $G:rk G\leq 2$ , then  $G^{(s)} = \{e\}$ .

Problem  $B$ Prove that every finite group  $G:rk G\leq 2$  is solvable.

Let  $s\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every finite solvable group  $G:rk G\leq 2$ , we have that  $G^{(s)}=\{e\}$ .

Let  $s_1\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every finite Abelian group  $A: rk A\leq 2$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq Aut(A):rk G\leq 2$ , we have that  $G^{(s_1)}=\{e\}$ .

Let  $s_2\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every prime number  $p$ , finite Abelian  $p$  group  $A: rk A\leq 2$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq Aut(A):rk G\leq 2$ , we have that   $G^{(s_2)}=\{e\}$ .

Let  $s_3\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every number  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq GL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}) :rk G\leq 2$ , we have that  $G^{(s_3)}=\{e\}$ .

Let  $s_4\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every number  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}):rk G\leq 2$ , we have that  $G^{(s_4)}=\{e\}$ .

Denote for every  $n$  and prime number  $p$  subgroups  $X_i(p,n)=X_i:=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a+1 & d b &c+1\end{pmatrix}\in SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})|a,b,c,d\in p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\right\}\subset SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ . Easy to see that  $\{e\}=X_n<X_{n-1}<...<X_1<X_0=SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$  and  $X_i$  is  $p$  group.

Lemma  $A$ :

Prove that  $\forall n-2\geq i\geq 2, X_i\lhd X_2$ ,  $X_i/X_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}, \forall n-1\geq i\geq 2, X_{i+1}/X_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ .

Proof:

First we need to prove that  $\forall i>0, |X_i| = p^{3(n-i)}$ . It is true, because  $\forall (a,b,d)\in p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\times p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\times p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n},\exists c\equiv\frac{1-bd}{a+1}-1\pmod {p^n}$  easy to see that  $c\in p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}$ ,  $\begin{pmatrix}a+1 & d b &c+1\end{pmatrix}\in SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ , so  $\begin{pmatrix}a+1 & d b &c+1\end{pmatrix}\in X_i$ , so  $|X_i| = | p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\times p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\times p^i\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}| = p^{3(n-i)}$ . Easy to check that  $\forall i\geq 2, \forall A, A'\in X_i, [A,A']\in X_{i+2}$ , so  $X_i'\subseteq X_{i+2}$ . So we can prove that  $\forall n-2\geq i\geq 2, X_i\lhd X_2$ ,  $X_i/X_{i+2}$  is Abelian and  $\forall i\geq 2$ ,  $X_i/X_{i+1}$  is Abelian. Easy to see that  $\forall n-2\geq i\geq 2, \forall g\in X_i\setminus X_{i+1}, g^p\in X_{i+1}/X_{i+2}$ , so  $X_i/X_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$  and  $\forall n-1\geq i\geq 2, X_{i+1}/X_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ .  $\Box$ Sequence  $A$ :

Prove that  $\forall i<n,g\in X_i\setminus X_{i+1}$ , then we have that  $g^p\in X_{i+1}\setminus X_{i+2}$ .

Let  $s_5\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every number  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable  $p$  group  $G\subseteq X_2=X_2(p,n) :rk G\leq 2$ , we have that   $G^{(s_5)}=\{e\}$ .

Let  $s_6\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every prime number  $p$  and finite solvable  $p$  group  $G$ , such that  $\exists \{e\}<N_k<...<N_0=G: N_i\lhd G, \forall 0\leq i\leq k-2, N_i/N_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}, N_i/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$ , then we have that  $G^{(s_6)}=\{e\}$ .


Let  $s_7\in \mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}$  is minimal number such that for every numer  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable  $p$  group  $G$ , such that  $\exists \lambda, \tau\in \mathbb{Z}_{p^n} : G=\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \lambda &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau 0 &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\subset SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ , we have that  $G^{(s_7)}=\{e\}$ .

Lemma 1

Prove that  $s\leq s_1+2$ .

Proof to lemma 1:

Lemma:

Let given group  $G$  and  $N\triangleleft G$ . Prove that  $G/Z(N)\subseteq Aut(N)$ . (Where  $Z(N) = \{g\in G: \forall x\in N, gx=xg\}$ ).

Proof:

Denote homomorfism  $\pi: G\to Aut(N)$  where  $\forall g\in G, x\in N, \pi(g)(x) = gxg^{-1}$ . Easy to see that  $\ker\pi = Z(N)$ , so  $G/Z(N)\cong \pi(G)\subseteq Aut(N)$ .  $\Box$ Let given finite solvable group  $G:rkG\leq 2$ . Let  $\nu\in\mathbb(Z) : G^{(\nu)}\not= \{e\}$ ,  $G^{(\nu+1)} = \{e\}$ . If  $\nu<1$ , then  $G^{(s_1+2)} =\{e\}$ , so we can think that  $\nu\geq 1$ . Let homomorfism  $\pi: G\to G/G^{(\nu)}$ . From lemma we can get that  $G_1=G/Z(G^{(\nu)})\subseteq Aut(G^{(\nu)}), G_2=\pi(G)/Z(\pi(G^{(\nu-1)}))\subseteq Aut(\pi(G^{(\nu-1)})$ ,  $rk G_1, rkG_2\leq 2$ . From defenition of  $s_1$  we can get that  $G_1^{(s_1)}=G_2^{(s_1)}=\{e\}$ , so  $G^{(s_1)}\subseteq Z(G^{(\nu)})$ ,  $\pi(G^{(s_1)})=(\pi(G))^{(s_1)}\subseteq Z(\pi(G^{(\nu-1)}))$ . So  $\forall g\in G^{(s_1)}, x_1\in G^{(\nu)}, x_2\in G^{(\nu-1)}, [g,x_1]=\{e\}, [g,x_2]\in G^{(\nu)}$ , so  $\forall g_1, g_2\in G^{(s_1)}, x\in G^{(\nu-1)}, [[g_1,g_2],x]=\{e\}$ , so  $[G^{(s_1)},G^{(s_1)}]\subseteq Z(G^{(\nu-1)})$  and  $G^{(s_1+1)}\subseteq Z(G^{(\nu-1)})$ . Easy to see that  $G^{(\nu-1)}\nleq Z(G^{(\nu-1)})$ , so  $s_1+1\geq \nu$ ,  $\nu+1\leq s_1+2$  and it finish proof of lemma 1.  $\Box$ Lemma 2

Prove that  $s_1\leq s_2$ .

Proof of lemma 2:

Let given finite Abelian group  $A: rk A\leq 2$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq Aut(A):rk G\leq 2$ . Denote for every prime  $p||A|$  group  $A_p$  - Sylow  $p$  subgroup of  $A$ . Easy to see that  $\forall g\in G, g(A_p) = A_p$ . Denote for every prime  $p||A|$  homomorfisms  $\pi_p: G\to Aut(A_p)$ , where  $\forall a_p\in A_p, \pi_p(g)(a_p) = g(a_p)$ , let  $K_p = \ker\pi_p$ .  $\prod_p A_p = A$ , so  $\cap_p K_p = \{e\}$ . Easy to see that  $\forall p||A|, rk G/K_p, rk A_p\leq 2, G/K_p\cong \pi_p(G)\subseteq Aut(A_p)$ , so from defenition of  $s_2$ ,  $(G/K_p)^{(s_2)} = \{e\}$ , so  $G^{(s_2)}\subseteq \cap_p K_p = \{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 3

Prove that  $s_2\leq s_3+2$ .

Proof of lemma 3:

Let given prime number  $p$ , finite Abelian  $p$  group  $A: rk A\leq 2$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq Aut(A):rk G\leq 2$ . Let  $n\geq k\in\mathbb{N} : A\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$ . Denote  $A_0 = A^k = \{a^k|a\in A\}$ , easy to see that  $A_0\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^{n-k}}$ ,  $\forall g\in G, g(A_0) = A_0$ . Denote homomorfism  $\pi: G\to Aut(A_0)$ , where  $\forall g\in G, a_0\in A_0, \pi(g)(a_0) = g(a_0)$ , let  $K = \ker\pi$ .  $G/K\cong \pi(G)\subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{p^{n-k}} = Aut(\mathbb{Z}_{p^{n-k}}) = (\mathbb{Z}_{p^{n-k}})^{\times}$ , so  $G'\subseteq K$ . Easy to see that  $A/A_0\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$ , denote homomorfism  $\psi: G\to Aut(A/A_0)$ , where  $\forall g\in G, xA_0\in A/A_0, \psi(g)(xA_0) = g(x)A_0$ , let  $L=\ker\psi$ ,  $G/L\cong\psi(G)\subseteq A/A_0\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$ ,  $rk G/L\leq 2$ , so from defenition of  $s_3, (G/L)^{(s_3)} = \{e\}$ , so  $G^{(s_3)}\subseteq L$ . In addition  $G^{(s_3+1)}\subseteq K\cap L$ . Easy to check that  $K\cap L$  is Abelian, so  $G^{(s_3+2)} = \{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 4

Prove that  $s_3\leq s_4+1$ .

Proof of lemma 4:

Let given number  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq GL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}) :rk G\leq 2$ . Easy to see that  $G'\subseteq (GL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}))'\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ ,  $rk G'\leq 2$ , so from defenition of  $s_4, G^{(s_4+1)} = \{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 5

Prove that  $s_4\leq s_5+6$ .

Proof of lemma 5:

Let given number  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable group  $G\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}):rk G\leq 2$ .

Lemma  $(a)$  :

Prove that  $X_1\lhd X_0$ ,  $X_0/X_1\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb Z_p) = SL(2,p)$ .

Proof:

Denote homomorfism  $\pi: X_0\to SL(2,p)$ , where  $\forall x = \begin{pmatrix}a & d b &c\end{pmatrix}\in SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ ,  $\pi(x) = \begin{pmatrix}a_p & d_p b_p &c_p\end{pmatrix}\in SL(2,p)$ ,  $a_p,b_p,c_p,d_p\in \mathbb{Z}_p : a\equiv a_p\pmod p, b\equiv b_p\pmod p, c\equiv c_p\pmod p, d\equiv d_p\pmod p$ . Easy to see that  $X_1 = \ker\pi$ , so  $X_1\lhd X_0$ ,  $X_0/X_1\cong \pi(X_0) \subseteq SL(2,p)$ .  $\Box$ Lemma  $(b)$ :

Let given solvable group  $G: G\subseteq SL(2,p)/Z(SL(2,p)) = PSL(2,p)$ . Prove that  $G^{(4)} = \{e\}$ .

Proof:

It is easy sequense of Theorem  $1.1$  from http://www.academia.edu/1816978.  $\Box$ Sequence:

Let given solvable group  $G: G\subseteq SL(2,p)$ . Prove that  $G^{(5)} = \{e\}$ .

Denote homomolrfism  $\xi: X_0\to X_0/X_1$ , from lemma  $(a)$ ,  $X_0/X_1\subseteq SL(2,p)$ , so  $\xi(G)\subseteq SL(2,p)$ ,  $\xi(G)$  is solvable, so from lemma  $(b)$ ,  $(\xi(G))^{(4)}\subseteq Z(SL(2,p))$  and  $(\xi(G))^{(5)} = \{e\}$ , so  $G^{(5)}\subseteq X_1$ . Let's prove that  $X_1'\subseteq X_2$ .  $\forall x=\begin{pmatrix}a & d b &c\end{pmatrix}, x'=\begin{pmatrix}a' & d' b' &c'\end{pmatrix}\in X_1$ , easy to check that  $[x,x'] = \begin{pmatrix}a & d b &c\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a' & d' b' &c'\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c & -d -b &a\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c' & -d' -b' &a'\end{pmatrix}\in X_2$ , so  $[X_1,X_1]\subseteq X_2$ ,  $X_1'\subseteq X_2$ . So  $G^{(6)}\subseteq X_2$ ,  $rk G^{(6)}\leq 2$ , so from defenition of  $s_5$ ,  $G^{(6+s_5)}=\{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 6

Prove that  $s_5\leq s_6+1$ .

Proof of lemma 6:

Let given number  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable  $p$  group  $G\subseteq X_2=X_2(p,n) :rk G\leq 2$ . Denote groups  $N_i=X_i\cap G$ , from lemma  $A$ ,  $N_i\lhd G$ . Let  $j: G\subseteq X_j, G\nleq X_{j+1}$ , so  $N_j = G$ . From  $rk G\leq 2$ , lemma  $A$  and sequence  $A$  we get that  $\forall n-2\geq i\geq j$ ,  $N_i/N_{i+2}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\vee\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}\vee\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\vee\mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p},\forall n-1\geq i\geq j, N_{i}/N_{i+1}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}\vee\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ . From sequence  $A$  easy to see that if for some  $n-1\geq i\geq j+1, N_{i}/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ , then  $N_{i-1}/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$  and so  $N_{i-1}/N_{i}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ . So  $\exists k:\forall n>i\geq k, N_{i}/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}$  and  $\forall j\leq i< k, N_{i}/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ .  $rk N_k\leq 2$ , from sequence  $A$  we can get that  $\forall n-2\geq i\geq k, N_{i}/N_{i+2}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ , so from defenition of  $s_6$ ,  $(N_k)^{(s_6)} = \{e\}$ . From sequence  $A$  we can get that  $\forall l\in\mathbb{Z}, g\in G\setminus N_{j+1}, g^{p^l}\in N_{j+l}\setminus N_{j+l+1}$ , so  $G/N_k\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$ , so  $G'\subseteq N_k$  and  $G^{(s_6+1)} = \{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 7

Prove that  $s_6\leq s_7+6$ .

Proof of lemma 7:

Let given prime number  $p$  and finite solvable  $p$  group  $G$ , such that  $\exists \{e\}<N_k<...<N_0=G: N_i\lhd G, \forall 0\leq i\leq k-2, N_i/N_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}, \forall 0\leq i\leq k-1, N_i/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$ .

Lemma  $7.1$ :

Prove that for every subgroup  $F\subseteq G$ ,  $\exists i: N_i\subseteq F$ ,  $F/N_i$  is cyclic.

Proof:

Let  $i: N_i\subseteq F, N_{i-1}\nleq F$ . Define groups  $F_i = N_i\cap F$  let  $r: F\subseteq N_r, F\nleq N_{r-1}$  . Let's prove that  $\forall r\leq j<i, F_j/F_{j+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$ . Easy to see that enough to prove that if for some  $u, F_u/F_{u+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$ , then  $F_{u+1}/F_{u+2}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$  and this is true because  $F_u/F_{u+2}\subseteq N_u/N_{u+2}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}, F_{u+1}/F_{u+2}\subseteq N_{u+1}/N_{u+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$ . So  $\forall r\leq j<i, F_j/F_{j+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$ .  $\forall 0\leq i\leq k-2, N_i/N_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}, \forall 0\leq i\leq k-1, N_i/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$ , so  $\forall g\in F_r\setminus F_{r+1}, q\in\mathbb{N}, g^q\in F_{r+q}\setminus F_{r+q+1}$ , so  $F/N_i = F/F_i$  is cyclic.  $\Box$ Lemma  $7.2$ :

Prove that  $\exists a, b\in G\setminus N_1: G = <a><b>$  and  $\forall i, <a^{p^i}><b^{p^i}>=N_i=G^i:=<\{g^i|g\in G\}>$ .

Proof:

Take any  $a, b\in G: <a, b>N_1 = G$ . Easy to see that  $\forall i\leq k-2, x, y\in N_i\setminus N_{i+1} : <x, y>N_{i+1} = N_i$ , then  $<x^p, y^p>N_{i+2} = N_{i+1}$ , so  $N_k = <a^{p^k}, b^{p^k}>$ . So  $<a>\cap <b> = \{e\}$  and  $\#\{a^ib^j| i, j\in p^i\mathbb{Z}\} = p^{2(k-i+1)} = |N_i|$ . $\forall 0\leq i\leq k-2, N_i/N_{i+2}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}, \forall 0\leq i\leq k-1, N_i/N_{i+1}\cong\mathbb{Z}_p\oplus\mathbb{Z}_p$ , so  $\forall i,j\in\mathbb{N}, g\in N_i\setminus N_{i+1}, g^j\in N_{i+j}\setminus N_{i+j+1}$  and so  $<a^{p^i}><b^{p^i}>\subseteq G^i\subseteq N_i$ , so  $<a^{p^i}><b^{p^i}> = G^i = N_i$ .  $\Box$ Take  $\lambda\in\mathbb{N} : N_{\lambda}$  is Abelian, but  $N_{\lambda - 1}$  is not Abelian. Denote homomorfism  $\pi: G\to Aut(N_{\lambda})$ , where  $\forall g\in G, x\in N_{\lambda}, \pi(g)(x) = gxg^{-1}$ . Take  $a, b$  from lemma  $7.2$ ,  $N_{\lambda} = <a^{p^{\lambda}}><b^{p^{\lambda}}>$ .  $N_{\lambda}$  is Abelian, so  $N_{\lambda}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p^n}$ , where  $n=k+1- \lambda$ .  $\pi(G)\subseteq Aut(N_{\lambda})\cong GL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ , so  $\pi(G') = (\pi (G))'\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ . From lemma  $7.1$ ,  $\exists i: N_i\subseteq G'$ ,  $G'/N_i$  is cyclic. From defenition of  $a, b$ ,  $N_i = <a^{p^i}><b^{p^i}>$ ,  $a^{p^i}\in Z(a), b^{p^i}\in Z(b)$ , so in basis  $a, b$  of  $N_{\lambda}$  we get that  $\pi(N_i) = \left\langle\begin{pmatrix}k & 0u  &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & f 0 &v\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ ,  $\det\begin{pmatrix}1 & f 0 &v\end{pmatrix}\equiv\det\begin{pmatrix}k & 0u  &1\end{pmatrix}\equiv 1\pmod {p^n}$ , so  $v\equiv k\equiv 1\pmod {p^n}$ . So  $\pi(N_i) = \left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0u  &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & f 0 &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\subseteq SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$  and from defenition of  $s_7$ ,  $\pi(N_i^{(s_5)}) = (\pi(N_i))^{(s_7)} =\{e\}$ , so  $N_i^{(s_7)}\subseteq\ker\pi = Z(N_{\lambda})$ .  $G^{(2)}\subseteq N_i$ , so  $G^{(s_7+2)}\subseteq Z(N_{\lambda})$ . Let  $\tau = \lambda - 1$ . Denote homomorfism  $\xi:G\to Aut(N_{\tau}/N_{\lambda})$ , where  $\forall g\in G, xN_{\lambda}\in N_{\tau}/N_{\lambda}, \xi(g)(xN_{\lambda}) = g(x)N_{\lambda}$ . Easy to see that  $\xi(G^{(s_7+2)})\subseteq GL(2,p)$ ,  $\xi(G^{(s_7+2)})$  is  $p$  group,  $|GL(2,p)|=(p^2-1)(p^2-p)$ , so  $|\xi(G^{(s_7+2)})|\leq p$  and  $\xi(G^{(s_7+3)})=\{e\}$ , so  $G^{(s_7+3)}\subseteq \ker\xi$  and so  $\forall g\in G^{(s_7+3)}, xN_{\lambda}\in N_{\tau}/N_{\lambda}$  we have  $gxN_{\lambda} = xgN_{\lambda}$ . We know that  $G^{(s_7+3)}\subseteq G^{(s_7+2)}\subseteq Z(N_{\lambda})$ , so easy to check that  $G^{(s_5+4)}\subseteq Z(N_{\tau})$ . From defenition of  $\lambda$ ,  $N_{\tau}\nleq Z(N_{\tau})$ , so  $N_{\tau}\nleq G^{(s_7+4)}$ . From lemma  $7.1$ ,  $\exists d: N_d\subseteq G^{(s_7+4)}, G^{(s_7+4)}/N_d$  is cyclic.  $N_{\tau}\nleq G^{(s_7+4)}\Rightarrow\tau <d$ .  $N_d\subseteq N_{\tau}$ , so  $G^{(s_7+4)}/(N_{\tau}\cap G^{(s_7+4)})$  is cyclic and so  $G^{(s_7+5)}\subseteq Z(N_{\tau})\cap N_{\tau}$ , so  $G^{(s_7+6)} =\{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 7

Prove that  $s_7\leq 1$ .

Proof of lemma 7:

Let given numer  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ , prime number  $p$  and finite solvable  $p$  group  $G$ , such that  $\exists \lambda, \tau\in \mathbb{Z}_{p^n} : G=\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \lambda &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau 0 &1\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle\subset SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{p^n})$ . Easy to see that  $\forall\begin{pmatrix}a & d b &c\end{pmatrix}\in G, a\equiv 1\pmod {p^n}$  and  $\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau 0 &1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \lambda &1\end{pmatrix}\in G$ , so  $\lambda\tau + 1\equiv 1\pmod {p^n}$ ,  $p^n|\lambda\tau$ . So  $\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau 0 &1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \lambda &1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau \lambda &1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \lambda &1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau 0 &1\end{pmatrix}$  and  $G$  is Abelian,  $G' = \{e\}$ .  $\Box$ Solution to Problem  $A$ :

From lemmas 1,..., 7 we get that  $s\leq s_1+2\leq s_2+2\leq s_3+4\leq s_4+5\leq s_5 + 11\leq s_6+12\leq s_7+18\leq 19$ . done

stem_md:
Find a constant  $ c > 1$  with the property that, for arbitrary positive integers  $ n$  and  $ k$  such that  $ n>c^k$ , the number of distinct prime factors of  $ \binom{n}{k}$  is at least  $ k$ . 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
I think this is not enough by itself since we are considering  $A/k!$ , not just  $A$ .

But it's easily fixed...

Let  $p_1<\cdots<p_\ell<k$  be the prime numbers less than  $k$ , where  $\ell=\pi(k-1)$ . If  $n-i$  (for some  $0\le i\le k-1$ ) has a prime factor  $p\ge k$ , then  $\gcd(p,n-j)=1$  for all  $0\le j\ne i\le k-1$ , so for all such  $i$  we can get distinct prime factors no less than  $k$ . Now suppose that  $n-i_j=p_1^{\alpha_j(1)}\cdots p_\ell^{\alpha_j(\ell)}$  (for  $0\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le k-1$ ) only have prime divisors less than  $k$ .

If  $m>\ell$ , then as mentioned in the previous post there must be some  $j$  for which  $p_i^{\alpha_j(i)}<k\forall 1\le i\le \ell$  since  $\gcd(n-i_r,n-i_s)<k\forall 1\le r\ne s\le m$  and so
\[c^k-k+1<n-k+1\le n-i_j < k^\ell \le k^{\pi(k)} < k^{\frac{Ck}{\ln(k)}} = e^{Ck}\]for some constant  $C$  independent of  $k$  (by the PNT), which is false for sufficiently large  $c$ .

Thus  $m\le\ell$ . Using the same logic as in the previous paragraph, we can show that the largest prime powers dividing  $n-i_1,\ldots,n-i_m$  are pairwise relatively prime. Suppose that  $q^r$  is the largest prime power dividing  $n-i_j$  so that
\[q^r \ge \sqrt[\ell]{n-i_j} \ge \sqrt[\pi(k-1)]{n-k+1} > n^{\frac{\ln(k)}{C'k}} > c^{\frac{\ln(k)}{C'}} > k\]for sufficiently large  $c$  ( $C'$  is another constant independent of  $k$  again determined by the PNT). Then
\[v_q\left(\binom{n}{k}\right) = \sum_{s\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{q^s}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{k}{q^s}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{n-k}{q^s}\right\rfloor \ge \left\lfloor\frac{n}{q^r}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{k}{q^r}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{n-k}{q^r}\right\rfloor = 1,\](note that  $q^r>k$  and  $n-k<n-i_j\le n$ ) where we have used the fact that
\[0\le\lfloor{a+b}\rfloor-\lfloor{a}\rfloor-\lfloor{b}\rfloor\le1\]for all reals  $a,b$ .

Hence we have at least  $(k-m)+m=k$  prime factors, as desired.

stem_md:
Let  $ f(n)$  be that largest integer  $ k$  such that  $ n^k$  divides  $ n!$ , and let  $ F(n)\equal{} \max_{2 \leq m \leq n} f(m)$ . Show that \[ \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \frac{F(n) \log n}{n \log \log n}\equal{}1.\] 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
Solution. First, we find an upper estimate for  $f(n)$ . Let  $n=\prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\alpha_i}$  be the prime factorization of  $n$ . Since  $n^{f(n)} \mid n$  !, we have  $$ \alpha_i f(n) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\left[\frac{n}{p_i^j}\right]<\frac{n}{p_i-1}, $$  that is,  $$ \alpha_i \log p_i \leq \frac{n}{f(n)} \frac{\log p_i}{p_i-1}, $$  for all  $i$ . Summing these inequalities, we obtain  $$ \log n=\sum \alpha_i \log p_i \leq \frac{n}{f(n)} \sum \frac{\log p_i}{p_i-1} . $$  Let  $q_1<q_2<\ldots$  be the sequence of all primes. Since  $(\log p) /(p-1)$  is decreasing, we have  $$ \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\log p_i}{p_i-1} \leq \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\log q_i}{p_i-1}=\log k+O(1) . $$  Combining the last two inequalities, we get  $$ f(n) \leq(1+o(1)) \frac{n \log k}{\log n} . $$  On the other hand,  $$ n=p_1^{\alpha_1} \ldots p_k^{\alpha_k} \geq q_1 \ldots q_k \geq 2^k . $$  Consequently,  $k \ll \log n, \log k \leq \log \log n+O(1)$ , and the previous estimate of  $f(n)$  yields  $$ f(n) \leq(1+o(1)) \frac{n \log \log n}{\log n} $$  as wanted.
Now we construct a number  $m \leq n$  with a large value of  $f(m)$ .
Define  $m_1$  by  $\left(m_1+1\right)!\leq n<\left(m_1+2\right)!$ . We have  $m_1 \sim(\log n) /(\log \log n)$  as  $n \rightarrow \infty$ . Let  $p$  be the largest prime up to  $\left(n / m_{1}!\right)^{1 / 3}$ , and put  $m=$   $p^3 m_{1}!$ . We have  $m \leq n$  obviously, and, since  $n / m_{1}!>m_1 \rightarrow \infty$ , we have  $p \sim\left(n / m_{1}!\right)^{1 / 3}$ , that is,  $m \sim n$ .

Verify that for every  $ x > 0$ , \[ \frac{\Gamma'(x\plus{}1)}{\Gamma (x\plus{}1)} > \log x.\]

solution_md: Solution: $\frac{\Gamma'(x+1)}{\Gamma (x+1)}= \log \Gamma (x+1)'$ ,  $\log \Gamma (z)=-\gamma z-\log z+\sum_{n\geq 1}(\frac{z}{n}-\log (1+\frac{z}{n}))$ , so  $\log \Gamma(x+1)=-\gamma (x+1)-\log (x+1)+\sum_{n\geq 1}(\frac{x+1}{n}-\log (1+\frac{x+1}{n}))$ ,  $\log \Gamma (x+1)'=-\gamma-\frac{1}{x+1}+\sum_{n\geq 1}(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+x+1})$ ,  $\gamma =\lim_{n\to \infty}(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}-\log n)$ , so we need to prove that  $\lim_{n\to \infty}(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}-\log n+\log x)<\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{1}{n}-\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{1}{n+x}=\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{x}{n(n+x)}$ , it is equivalent to  $\lim_{n\to \infty}(-\log \frac{n}{x}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{k}-\frac{x}{k(k+x)}))=\lim_{n\to \infty}(-\log \frac{n}{x}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k+x})=lim_{n\to \infty} \left(-\int_{0}^{n-x}\frac{1}{t+x}dt+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k+x} \right) <0$ ,  $f(t)=\frac{1}{t+x}\downarrow \downarrow$ , so  $lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \int_{0}^{n-x}\frac{1}{t+x}dt-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k+x} \right) =lim_{n\to \infty} ( (\int_{1}^{n-x}\frac{1}{t+x}dt-\sum_{k=2}^{[n-x]}\frac{1}{k+x})+((\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{t+x}dt-\frac{1}{1+x})-\sum_{k=[n-x]+1}^{n}\frac{1}{k+x}))>0$ . done

stem_md:
Let  $ G$  be a  $ 2$ -connected nonbipartite graph on  $ 2n$  vertices. Show that the vertex set of  $ G$  can be split into two classes of  $ n$  elements such that the edges joining the two classes form a connected, spanning subgraph. 

*L. Lovasz*
solution_md:
In any way we split the vertex set  $V$  of  $G = (V,E)$  into two classes  $A$  and  $B$ , the set of edges  $E(A)\cup E(B)$  contained in  $A$  or  $B$  is non-empty (since the graph is non-bipartite), thus the edges crossing between  $A$  and  $B$  make up a proper subgraph  $G'$  of  $G$ . 

The problem asks to find such a split, with  $|A|=|B|=n$ , such that  $G'$  is connected, and spanning  $G$  - meaning the vertex set of  $G'$  (the ends of the edges crossing between  $A$  and  $B$ ) is equal to  $V$ . Notice that neither connectivity, nor the spannning property are guaranteed for a random such split.

stem_md:
Prove that a necessary and sufficient for the existence of a set  $ S \subset \{1,2,...,n \}$  with the property  that the integers  $ 0,1,...,n\minus{}1$  all have an odd number of representations in the form  $ x\minus{}y, x,y \in S$ , is that  $ (2n\minus{}1)$  has a multiple of the form  $ 2.4^k\minus{}1$  

*L. Lovasz, J. Pelikan*
solution_md:
Prove that a necessary and sufficient for the existence of a set $ S \subset \{1,2,...,n \}$ with the property that the integers $ 0,1,...,n\minus{}1$ all have an odd number of representations in the form $ x\minus{}y, x,y \in S$ , is that $ (2n\minus{}1)$ has a multiple of the form $ 2.4^k\minus{}1$ *L. Lovasz, J. Pelikan*
The statement is clearly true for $n=1$ . So we can assume $n>1$ . Define $s(x):=\sum_{s\in S}x^{s-1}\in\mathbb{F}_2[x]$ . Then the condition is equivalent to $x^{n-1}s\left(\tfrac{1}{x}\right)s(x)=x^{2n-2}+x^{2n-3}+\ldots+x+1=\frac{x^{2n-1}-1}{x-1}$ . Note that this polynomial has no multiple roots in $\overline{\mathbb{F}_2}$ . Let $r=\mathrm{ord}_{2n-1}(2)$ and let $a$ be a element of order $2n-1$ in $\mathbb{F}_{2^r}$ . We have $x^{2n-2}+x^{2n-3}+\ldots+x+1=\prod_{i=1}^{2n-2}\left(x-a^i\right)$ . If $y$ is a root of $s(x)$ then $\frac{1}{y}$ is a root of $x^{n-1}s\left(\tfrac{1}{x}\right)$ . So if the condition holds we can write $s(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(x-a^{\pm i}\right)$ . On the other hand if we can choose signs so that $t(x):=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(x-a^{\pm i}\right)$ has coeffitients in $\mathbb{F}_2$ (in this case the constant coeffitient is automatically $1$ ) both $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(x-a^{\mp i}\right)$ and $x^{n-1}t\left(\tfrac{1}{x}\right)$ are monic degree $n-1$ polynomial with the same set of roots. So they are equal and we get a choice for $s$ . Since $s$ has coeffitients in $\mathbb{F}_2$ it must be the product of the minimal polynomial of its roots. In particular if the minimal polynomial of $a^i$ has $a^{-i}$ as a root there is no possible choice for $s$ . But if there is no such $i$ then we can construct $s$ by choosing one factor at a time so that we multiple the minimal polynomial of $a^j$ if neither $a^j,a^{-j}$ are roots. (This is possible because $x^{\deg(f)}f\left(\tfrac{1}{x}\right)$ is the minimal polynomial of $a^{-i}$ where $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $a^i$ .) The roots of the minimal polynomial of $a^j$ are the images of $a^j$ under the Galois-transformations of $\mathbb{F}_{2^r}/\mathbb{F}_2$ . But $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{2^r}/\mathbb{F}_2)$ is generated by the Frobenius automorphism $x\mapsto x^2$ . So there is no choice for $s$ if, and only if there are $j,k$ with $a^{j2^k}=a^{-j}$ and $2n-1\nmid j$ . Since $a$ has order $2n-1$ this is the case if and only if there are $j,k$ with $2n-1\mid j\left(2^k+1\right)$ and $2n-1\nmid j$ , i.e. if $2n-1$ and $2^k+1$ are coprime for all $k\geq0$ . A prime $p$ divides a number of the form $2^k+1$ if, and only if $2\mid\mathrm{ord}_p(2)$ . So there exists such a set $S$ if and only if $\mathrm{ord}_p(2)$ is odd for all prime divisors of $2n-1$ , i.e. if $\mathrm{ord}_{2n-1}(2)$ is odd, i.e. if $2n-1$ has a multiple of the form $2^{2k+1}-1$ .

Let  $ R$  be an infinite ring such that every subring of  $ R$  different from  $ \{0 \}$  has a finite index in  $ R$ . (By the index of a subring, we mean the index of its additive group in the additive group of  $ R$ .) Prove that the additive group of  $ R$  is cyclic.

solution_md:
Solution:

Part 1:

In this part we will prove that there exists  $\xi \in R: R=\{r_1\xi+r_2\xi^2+...r_k\xi^k+...\}_{r_1,r_2,...,r_k,...}$ .

Denote  $\wp$  as prime set.  $\lambda R=\{\lambda*a| a\in R\}$ .

Lemma 1: $\forall p\in \wp, pR\not= \{ 0\}$ From Lemma 1 we can prove that  $\forall a\in R\setminus \{ 0 \}, n\in Z\setminus 0$ ,  $an\not=0$  (because if  $pa=0$  for prime p, then  $R_p=\{ a\in R| pa=0 \}$  is subring of  $R$ , so  $|R/R_p|<\infty$  and  $|R_p|=\infty$ ,  $pR=\{ 0 \}$  and use Lemma 1).

Lemma 2: $\forall p\in \wp, pR\not= R$ Next Lemmas will work when  $R:$ Lemma 2 holds, for other rings  $R$  we will use modifications of this Lemmas wich are in Part 2.

From Lemma 2 we get that  $\cap_{i\in Z\backslash 0}p^iR=\{0\}$  (if  $\cap_{i\in Z\backslash 0}p^iR=R'\not=\{0\}$ , then  $pR'=R'$ ).

Denote function  $\nu_p(a)=max\{i\in Z|a\in p^iR\}$ ,  $\cap_{i\in Z\backslash 0}p^iR=\{0\}$ , so  $\forall a\in R, 0 \leq \nu_p(a)<\infty$ .

Lemma 3: $\forall p\in \wp , |R/pR|=p^n$ , for some positive integer  $n$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Construct rings  $pR=R_0\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2 \subseteq ...\subseteq R_{k-1}\subseteq R_k=R$ , such that  $\forall i, \forall R^*: R_i \in R^*\in R_{i+1}$ ,  $R^*=R_i$ , or  $R^*=R_{i+1}$ ,  $\forall i,\exists a_i\in R_{i+1}\backslash R_i$ .  $\alpha_i=a_i+R_i$ , from defenition of  $R_i$ ,  $R_{i+1}/R_i=\{x_1\alpha_i+x_2\alpha_i^2+...+x_h\alpha_i^h+...\}_{x_1,x_2,...,x_h,...\in Z}$ ,  $\forall r\in R_{i+1}/R_i, p*r\in pR\subset R_{i}$ , so  $R_{i+1}/R_i$  is ring over field  $Z/pZ$ , so if  $f^*(x)=u_1x+u_2x^2+....+x^m$  is minimal polynom were  $f^*(a)=0$  (he exist because  $|R_{i+1}/R_i|<\infty$ ), then  $R_{i+1}/R_i\cong Z[x]/(px,x^m)$ , so  $|R_{i+1}/R_i|=|Z[x]/(px,x^m)|=p^{m-1}$ ,  $n=m-1$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 3': $\forall \lambda \in Z, q||R/\lambda R|\Leftrightarrow q|\lambda, q\in \wp$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Let  $\lambda = p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}$ , we will use Induction by  $k_1+k_2+...+k_i$ .  $\lambda R=p_1R'$ , were  $R_1=\frac{\lambda}{p_1}R$ , from Lemma 3  $|R/\lambda R|=|R/R'|*|R'/p_1R'|$  and from Lemma 3 and Induction we get Lemma 3'.  $\Box$ Lemma 4: $\forall p \not= q, p,q \in \wp$ ,  $pR\cap qR\not= pR$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Let  $pR\subseteq qR$ , then  $p^{n_1}=|R/pR|=|R/qR|*|qR/pR|=q^{n_2}|qR/pR|$ . Contradiction.  $\Box$ Lemma 5: $\forall a\in R, \exists N>0: \forall p\in \wp , p>N, a\in R\backslash pR$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Let exists  $\{p_i\}_{i=1}^{\infty}:p_i\in \wp$ ,  $p_1<p_2<p_3<...$ ,  $\forall i\in Z, a\in p_iR$ , then  $\cap_i p_iR=R^{\wp}\not= \{0\}$ .  $R^{\wp}$  is ring,  $|R/R^{\wp}|<\infty$ ,  $\forall i, R^{\wp}\subseteq p_iR$ , so  $|R/R^{\wp}|=|R/p_iR|*|p_iR/R^{\wp}|\geq p_i\to \infty (i\to \infty)$ . Contradiction.  $\Box$ Lemma 6: $\forall p \not= q, p,q \in \wp$ ,  $pR\cap qR= pqR$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Easy to see that  $pqR\subseteq pR\cap qR$ , from using ideas from Lemma 3 and from Lemma 4, we get that  $|pR/(pR\cap qR)|=q^{l}$ , where  $l\not=0$ . From Lemma 3,  $|pR/pqR|=p^{f}$ , so  $(pR\cap qR)/pqR=p^{f-l}$ , like the same  $(pR\cap qR)/pqR=q^y$ , so  $y=f-l=0$ ,  $pR\cap qR=pqR$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 6': $m,n\in Z: (m,n)=1$ , then  $mR\cap nR= mnR$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Like in Lemma 6  $|(mR\cap nR)/mnR|=H$ , from using Lemma 3',  $p\in \wp$ ,  $p|H\Leftrightarrow p|(m,n)$ , so  $H=1$ .  $\Box$ We will say that  $k|a\in R \Leftrightarrow \exists b\in R:a=k*b$ ,  $k\in Z$ . We say that  $a\in P_R\Leftrightarrow a\in R, \forall p\in \wp, p\nmid a$ . From property  $p|a, b=\lambda*a\Rightarrow p|b$ ,  $a,b\in R$  and Lemma 5 we get that  $P\setminus P_R\not=R$  and  $\forall a\in R, \exists e\in P_R, p_1<p_2<...<p_i\in \wp , k_1,k_2,...,k_i\in Z_{+}: a=p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}e$ .

Lemma 7:

If  $e_1,e_2\in P_R$ ,  $a\in R$  and  $p_1<p_2<...<p_i\in \wp , k_1,k_2,...,k_i\in Z_{+}: a=p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}e_1$ ,  $q_1<q_2<...<q_j\in \wp , l_1,l_2,...,l_j\in Z_{+}: a=q_1^{l_1}q_2^{l_2}...q_i^{l_i}e_2$ , then  $e_1=e_2$ ,  $i=j$ ,  $q_v=p_v$ ,  $l_v=k_v$ . $\bigtriangleup$ From Lemma 6' we get that if  $ p \in \wp \lambda \in Z, p\nmid \lambda a\in R$ ,  $p|a, \lambda |a\Rightarrow p\lambda |a$ , so if  $q_u\not= p_v, v\in [1,i]$ , then  $q_u|a$ ,  $p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}|a\Rightarrow q_vp_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}|a \Rightarrow \exists b\in R:a=q_vp_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}b=p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}e_1$ , from Lemma 1  $p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}(e_1-q_vb)=0$ , so  $q_v|e_1$  and  $e_1\in P\setminus P_R$ . Contradiction. 
So  $i=j$   $p_v=q_v, v\in [1,i]$ , and so easy to see that  $l_v=k_v, v\in [1,i]$ , so  $a=p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}e_1=p_1^{k_1}p_2^{k_2}...p_i^{k_i}e_2$ , so  $e_1=e_2$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 8:

If  $p\in \wp$ , ring  $R^*:pR\subseteq R^*\subseteq R$ , then  $R^*=pR$ , or  $R^*=R$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Let  $R^*\not= R$ , from using all previous construction to  $R^*$ , we get that  $\forall a\in R^*, \exists !\lambda \in Z, \xi^* \in P_{R^*}: a=\lambda*\xi^*$ ,  $\exists !\mu \in Z, \xi \in P_{R}: \xi^*=\mu*\xi$ , so  $a=\lambda \mu \xi$ ,  $\mu*\xi=\xi^*\in R^*$ , so from ideas of Lemma 3 we get that  $R/R^*\cong Z[x]/(px,f^*(x))$  and so  $p|\mu$ ,  $a=\lambda \mu \xi\in pR$ , so  $pR\subseteq R^*\subseteq pR$ , so  $R^*=pR$ .  $\Box$ Lemma 9: $\forall p\in \wp, |R/pR|=p$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Take ring  $R/pR$  if there exists  $f\in R/pR, f\not= 0, f^2=0$ , then from Lemma 8,  $R/pR=\{0,f,2f,...,(p-1)f\}$  and  $|R/pR|=p$ , if  $\forall g\in R/pR, g^2\not= 0$ , then take multiplicative group (maybe without 1)  $G=R/pR\setminus 0$ , well known  that from  $|G|<\infty$  then  $\exists e\in G: e^2=e$ , so  $R/pR=\{0,e,2e,...,(p-1)e\}$  and also  $|R/pR|=p$ .  $\Box$ Easy to see that from Lemma 9 by Indicton we get that  $\forall n\in Z, |R/nR|=n$  ( $|R/abR|=|R/aR|*|aR/abR|=ab$ ).

Lemma 10:

Let  $R'$  is ring in  $R$ , then there exists  $n\in Z: R'=nR$ . $\bigtriangleup$ Let  $n=|R/R'|$ , then  $nR\subseteq R'$  and from Lemma 9  $|R/nR|=n=|R/R'|$ , so  $R'=nR$ .  $\Box$ Now let's take  $\xi \in P_R$ , and ring  $R_1=\{r_1\xi+r_2\xi^2+...r_k\xi^k+...\}_{r_1,r_2,...,r_k,...}$ , from Lemma 10  $\exists n\in Z: R_1=nR$ , so exists  $b\in R: \xi=nb$ , so  $n=1$  and  $R=R_1$ . It finishes Part 1.

Let  $ f(x)\equal{}\sum_{n\equal{}1}^{\infty} a_n/(x\plus{}n^2), \;(x \geq 0)\ ,$  where  $ \sum_{n\equal{}1}^{\infty} |a_n|n^{\minus{} \alpha} < \infty$  for some  $ \alpha >  2$ . Let us assume that for some  $ \beta > 1/{\alpha}$ , we have  $ f(x)\equal{}O(e^{\minus{}x^{\beta}})$  as  $ x \rightarrow \infty$ . Prove that  $ a_n$  is identically  $ 0$ . 

*G. Halasz*
solution_md:
Solution (in case  $\beta>\alpha+1$ ):


We will prove in case  $\beta>6+\alpha$  that if  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_n}{x+n}=O(e^{-x^{\beta}})=\theta(x)e^{-x^{\beta}}$ , then  $a_1=0$ . Easy to see that  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(x+n)(x+n+1)}=\theta(x)e^{-x^{\beta}}-\theta(x+1)e^{-(x+1)^{\beta}}$ , like the same (by induction)  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_n}{(x+n)(x+n+1)...(x+n+k)}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\frac{1}{k!}(-1)^iC_k^i\theta(x+i)e^{-(x+i)^{\beta}}$ , so  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_n(x+1)...(x+k+1)}{(x+n)...(x+n+k)}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\frac{1}{k!}(-1)^iC_k^i(x+1)...(x+k+1)\theta(x+i)e^{-(x+i)^{\beta}}$ ,  $\beta>\alpha$ ,  $\forall \beta>\alpha'>\alpha, \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{|a_n|}{n^{\alpha'}}<\infty$ , so we can think that  $\alpha=\frac{p}{q}\in Q$ ,  $\frac{|a_n|(x+1)...(x+k+1)}{(x+n)...(x+n+k)}=\frac{|a_n|(x+1)...(x+[\alpha]+1)}{(x+n)...(x+n+[\alpha])}\frac{(x+[\alpha]+2)...(x+k+1)}{(x+n+[\alpha]+1)...(x+n+k)}\leq\frac{|a_n|}{n^{\alpha}}\frac{(x+1)...(x+[\alpha]+1)(x+[\alpha]+2)...(x+k+1)}{(x+n+[\alpha]+1)...(x+n+k)}\leq \frac{(x+1)...(x+[\alpha]+1)(x+[\alpha]+2)...(x+k+1)}{(x+2+[\alpha]+1)...(x+2+k)}$ ,  $\delta>0$ , we need function  $k:R_{\geq 0}\to Z_{>0}:\frac{(x+1)...(x+[\alpha]+1)(x+[\alpha]+2)...(x+k(x)+1)}{(x+2+[\alpha]+1)...(x+2+k(x))}\leq \delta $   $(*)$ ,  $\sum_{j=[\alpha]+2}^{k(x)+1}\ln(1+\frac{1}{x+j})\geq\sum_{y=1}^{[\alpha]+1}\ln(x+y)+\ln(\frac{1}{\delta})$ ,  $\sum_{j=[\alpha]+2}^{k(x)+1}\ln(1+\frac{1}{x+j})\geq \sum_{j=[\alpha]+2}^{k(x)+1}\frac{1}{x+j+1}\geq^{k:}\sum_{y=1}^{[\alpha]+1}\ln(x+y)+\ln(\frac{1}{\delta})$ ,  $\sum_{j=[\alpha]+2}^{k(x)+1}\frac{1}{x+j+1}\geq \int_{[\alpha]+3}^{k(x)+1}\frac{1}{x+j+1}dj=\ln(x+j+1)|_{j=[\alpha]+3}^{k(x)+1}\geq^{k:}\sum_{y=1}^{[\alpha]+1}\ln(x+y)+\ln(\frac{1}{\delta})$ , so let's find  $k:\ln(x+k(x)+2)\geq \sum_{y=1}^{[\alpha]+4}\ln(x+y)+\ln(\frac{1}{\delta})$ ,  $x+k(x)+2\geq \frac{1}{\delta}\prod_{y=1}^{[\alpha]+4}(x+y)$ , so take  $k(x)=x^{6+\alpha}$  (for  $x^{\frac{1}{q}}\in Z_{\geq 0}$ ), for  $\forall \delta>0$ ,  $\exists x$  large enough with  $(*)$ .

Denote  $\gamma =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{|a_n|}{n^{\alpha}}$ ,  $\forall \delta>0$ , for  $x'\in Z$  large enough  $x=x'^q$ ,  $|\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_n(x+1)...(x+k(x)+1)}{(x+n)...(x+n+k(x))}|=|a_1+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{a_n(x+1)...(x+k(x)+1)}{(x+n)...(x+n+k(x))}|\geq |a_1|-\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{|a_n|(x+1)...(x+k(x)+1)}{(x+n)...(x+n+k(x))}\geq |a_1|-\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{|a_n|}{n^{\alpha}}\delta=\gamma\delta+|a_1|$ , so  $|\sum_{i=0}^{k(x)}\frac{1}{(k(x))!}(-1)^iC_{k(x)}^i(x+1)...(x+k(x)+1)\theta(x+i)e^{-(x+i)^{\beta}}|\geq |a_1|+\gamma\delta$ , so we need only to prove that  $\lim_{x\to \infty, x\in Z}\sum_{i=0}^{x^{6q+p}}\frac{1}{(x^{6q+p})!}(-1)^iC_{x^{6q+p}}^i(x^q+1)...(x^q+x^{6q+p}+1)\theta (x^q+i)e^{-(x^q+i)^{\beta}}=0$ ,  $0\leq |\theta(x)|\leq M$  $|\sum_{i=0}^{x^{6q+p}}\frac{1}{(x^{6q+p})!}(-1)^iC_{x^{6q+p}}^i(x^q+1)...(x^q+x^{6q+p}+1)\theta (x^q+i)e^{-(x^q+i)^{\beta}}|\leq \sum_{i=0}^{x^{6q+p}}Mx^{12px^{6q+p}}e^{-x^{q\beta}}\leq Mx^{20px^{6q+p}}e^{-x^{q\beta}}$ ,  $q\beta>6q+p$ ,  $\lim_{x\to \infty, x\in Z}x^{20px^{6q+p}}e^{-x^{q\beta}}=e^{\lim_{x\to \infty, x\in Z}20p\ln(x)x^{6q+p}-x^{q\beta}}=e^{-\infty}=0$ ,so  $a_1=0$ , like the same  $a_i=0$ . Like the same we can prove this for  $\beta>\alpha+1$ . done
