stem_md:
Let  $ \mathcal{A}_n$  denote the set of all mappings  $ f: \{1,2,\ldots ,n \} \rightarrow \{1,2,\ldots, n \}$  such that  $ f^{-1}(i) :=\{ k \colon f(k)=i\ \} \neq \varnothing$  implies  $ f^{-1}(j) \neq \varnothing, j \in \{1,2,\ldots, i \} .$  Prove \[ |\mathcal{A}_n| = 
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{k^n}{2^{k+1}}.\] 

*L. Lovasz*
solution_md:
Given naturals \(\text{n}\) and \(\text{k}\), denote by \(\text{hom}\left(\text{n},\text{k}\right)\) and \(\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k}\right)\) the number of functions and surjections respectively of type \(\left\{0,\dots,\text{n}-1\right\}\to\left\{0,\dots,\text{k}-1\right\}\). Observe (by straightforward counting; but the identity is also familiar from the discrete Taylor series\(^{\text{[A]}}\) of \(\text{k}\mapsto\text{k}^{\text{n}}\)) that for such \(\text{n}\) and \(\text{k}\), \begin{align*}\text{k}^{\text{n}}\ &=\ \text{hom}\left(\text{n},\text{k}\right) &=\ \sum_{\text{k’}\colon\omega}\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k}\right)\binom{\text{k}}{\text{k’}}\end{align*} (here the index \(\text{k’}\colon\omega\) indicates iterating over \(\text{k’}\in\left\{0,1,\dots\right\}\), although of course all but finitely many of these summands are \(0\)). Observe moreover (as proven inductively\(^{\text{[B]}}\) by the hockey-stick identity) that for all naturals \(\text{k’}\), \[\sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega}\binom{\text{k}}{\text{k’}}2^{-\text{k}}\ =\ 2\text{.}\] Finally, observe (again by just counting) that \[\left|\mathcal{A}_{\text{n}}\right|\ =\ \sum_{\text{k’}\colon\omega}\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k’}\right)\] (all but finitely many of the summands again \(0\)), from which we conclude that \begin{align*}\left|\mathcal{A}_{\text{n}}\right|\ &=\ \sum_{\text{k’}\colon\omega}\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k’}\right) &=\ \sum_{\text{k’}\colon\omega}\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k’}\right)\sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega}\binom{\text{k}}{\text{k’}}2^{-\text{k}-1} &=\ \sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega} \sum_{\text{k’}\colon\omega}\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k’}\right)\binom{\text{k}}{\text{k’}}2^{-\text{k}-1} &=\ \sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega} \text{k}^{\text{n}}2^{-\text{k}-1}\end{align*} as claimed—the swapping of sums justified by the evident overall absolute convergence. \(\blacksquare\)

-----

\(\textbf{[A]}\) I.e., by the theory of finite differences we have that \[\text{k}^{\text{n}}\ =\ \sum_{\text{k’}\colon\omega}\left(\sum_{\text{i}\colon\text{k’}+1}\left(-1\right)^{\text{k’}-\text{i}}\binom{\text{k’}}{\text{i}}\text{i}^{\text{n}}\right)\binom{\text{k}}{\text{k’}}\text{,}\] and it’s not hard to see that the bracketed expression within the sum (i.e., the \(\text{k’}^{\text{th}}\) finite difference of \(\text{k}\mapsto\text{k}^{\text{n}}\)) is an inclusion-exclusion count of \(\text{epi}\left(\text{n},\text{k}\right)\).

\(\textbf{[B]}\) Of course, \[\sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega}\binom{\text{k}}{0}2^{-\text{k}}\ =\ 2\text{.}\] As for the induction step, observe that by the hockey-stick identity \begin{align*}\sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega}\binom{\text{k}}{\text{k’}+1}2^{-\text{k}}\ &=\ \sum_{\text{k}\colon\omega}\sum_{\text{i}\colon\text{k}}\binom{\text{i}}{\text{k’}}2^{-\text{k}} &=\ \sum_{\text{i}\colon\text{k}}\sum_{\text{j}\colon\omega}\binom{\text{i}}{\text{k’}}2^{-\text{i}-\text{j}-1} &=\ \sum_{\text{i}\colon\text{k}}\binom{\text{i}}{\text{k’}}2^{-\text{i}} &=\ 2\text{,}\end{align*} where the penultimate equality comes from the index substitution \(\text{j}+1\ :=\ \text{k}-\text{i}\) and the interchange of sums is as above justified by absolute convergence.

\(\textbf{[C]}\) Indeed, the above two footnotes are shadows of that the discrete-calculus identity (insofar as the sums in question are well-defined) \[\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\colon\omega}\sum_{\text{d}\colon\omega}a\left(\text{d}\right)\binom{x}{\text{d}}2^{-x}\ =\ \sum_{\text{d}\colon\omega}a\left(\text{d}\right)\] that we implicitly leverage here is formally analogous to the calculus identity \[\int_{x\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\sum_{\text{d}\colon\omega}a\left(\text{d}\right)\frac{x^{\text{d}}}{\text{d}!}e^{-x}\cdot\text{d}x\ = \ \sum_{\text{d}\colon\omega}a\left(\text{d}\right)\] (again insofar as the integrals and sums in question are well-defined), with \(x\mapsto 2^{x}\) in particular the discrete-calculus analogue of the natural exponential. Indeed, the latter can be “proved”  (at least modulo casting the magic chain of adjectives that rids us of the usual analytic subtleties resulting from manipulating infinite sums and improper integrals) by an analogous induction, with base case \[\int_{x\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\frac{x^{0}}{0!}e^{-x}\cdot\text{d}x\ =\ 1\] and inductive step \begin{align*} \int_{x\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\frac{x^{\text{d}+1}}{\left(\text{d}+1\right)!}e^{-x}\cdot\text{d}x\ &=\ \int_{x\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\int_{y\colon\left[0,x\right]}\frac{y^{\text{d}}}{\text{d}!}e^{-x}\cdot\text{d}y\cdot\text{d}x &=\ \int_{y\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\int_{z\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\frac{y^{\text{d}}}{\text{d}!}e^{-y-z}\cdot\text{d}z\cdot\text{d}y &=\ \int_{y\colon\left[0,\infty\right)}\frac{y^{\text{d}}}{\text{d}!}e^{-y}\cdot\text{d}y &=\ 1\end{align*} where the penultimate equality comes from the index substitution \(z\ :=\ x-y\). (This integral is, of course, familiar from the definition of the gamma function.)

Now, let us denote  $f_n=|\mathcal{A}_n|$ . It remains to establish that  $f_n$  comply with the same recurrence relation.
Consider the set  $A_1=f^{-1}(1)$  and fix it. Suppose  $|A_1|=j$ . It's clear that  $1\le j\le n$ . The restrictions of  $\{f\mid f\in\mathcal{A}_n, f^{-1}(1)=A_1\}$  on the set  $[n]\setminus A_1$  are exactly  $f_{n-j}$  different functions. Hence, we get:
\[f_n= \sum_{j=1}^{n} \binom{n}{j}f_{n-j}= \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \binom{n}{j} f_j\]
where, for convenience, we have set  $f_0=1$ . 
Since  $s_0=f_0=1$ , the result follows.

stem_md:
Prove that the set of rational-valued, multiplicative arithmetical functions and the set of complex rational-valued, multiplicative arithmetical functions form isomorphic groups with the convolution operation  $ f \circ g$  defined by \[{ (f \circ g)(n)= %Error. "displatmath" is a bad command.
\sum_{d|n} f(d)g(\frac nd}).\] (We call a complex number  $ \textit{complex rational}$ , if its real and imaginary parts are both rational.) 

*B. Csakany*
solution_md:
We prove this via several isomorphisms.

For any field  $K$ , the group of  $K$ -valued multiplicative arithmetic functions (under convolution) is isomorphic, via the Euler product of its Dirichlet series, to the infinite product  $(1 + TK[[T]])^\Bbb N$ , where the group operation in  $1 + TK[[T]] = \{\sum_{n \geq 0} a_n T^n: \forall n, a_n \in K; a_0 = 1\}$  is the product of formal power series.
This isomorphism is given explicitly as follows: if  $f$  is a  $K$ -valued multiplicative arithmetic function, then we map it to  $\left(\sum_{n \geq 0} f(p_i^n) T^n\right)_{i \in \Bbb N}$ , where  $p_i$  denotes the  $i$ -th prime number.

If  $K$  is a field of characteristic  $0$ , then the group  $(1 + TK[[T]], \cdot)$  is isomorphic to  $(TK[[T]], +)$  via  $\log$  and  $\exp$ , which are defined as:  $\log(1 + F) = \sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{(-1)^{n - 1}} n F^n$  and  $\exp(F) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac 1{n!} F^n$  for any  $F \in TK[[T]]$ .
Moreover, it is clear that the group  $(TK[[T]], +)$  is isomorphic to  $K^\Bbb N$ .

Thus we have shown that, when  $K$  is a field of characteristic  $0$ , the group of  $K$ -valued multiplicative arithmetic functions is isomorphic to the group of  $\left(K^\Bbb N\right)^\Bbb N$ , which is again isomorphic to  $K^\Bbb N$ , as there is a bijection between  $\Bbb N \times \Bbb N$  and  $\Bbb N$ .

It only remains to note that  $\Bbb Q(i) \simeq \Bbb Q^2$  as additive groups, and hence  $\Bbb Q(i)^\Bbb N \simeq \left(\Bbb Q^2\right)^\Bbb N \simeq \Bbb Q^\Bbb N$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ \{ f_n \}$  be a sequence of Lebesgue-integrable functions on  $ [0,1]$  such that for any Lebesgue-measurable subset  $ E$  of  $ [0,1]$  the sequence  $ \int_E f_n$  is convergent. Assume also that  $ \lim_n f_n\equal{}f$  exists almost everywhere. Prove that  $ f$  is integrable and  $ \int_E f\equal{}\lim_n \int_E f_n$ . Is the assertion also true if  $ E$  runs only over intervals but we also assume  $ f_n \geq 0 ?$  What happens if  $ [0,1]$  is replaced by  $ [0,\plus{}\infty) ?$  

*J. Szucs*
solution_md:
First let's see  $f$  is integrable. Suppose on the contrary  $f\not\in L^1[0,1]$ . We will construct  $E$ , and subsequence  $n_1<n_2 <\ldots $  for which  $|\int_E f_{n_k}| \ge k$ .
Since  $f\not\in L[0,1]$  and  $f_n\to f$  a.e. ,  $\int_0^1 |f_n|$  diverges (by Fatou's lemma), thus there exists  $n_1$  with  $\int_0^1 |f_{n_1}| > 4$ . Hence,  $|\int_{E_1} f_{n_1}| > 2$  ,where  $E_1$  is one of the sets where  $f_{n_1}$  takes positive or negative values.  Suppose, we have already constructed  $n_1<n_2,\ldots<n_{k-1}$  and  $E_1,E_2,\ldots, E_{k-1}$ . We choose  $\delta\,,\, 0<\delta<2^{-k} $  s.t.  $\int_{\Delta} |f_{n_i}| <2^{-k}, i=1,2,\ldots k-1$ , whenever  $m(\Delta) <\delta$ . 
One of the two possibilities holds for sure:

1)  $\int_{[0,1]\setminus E_{k-1}} |f| =\infty$ 2)  $\int_{E_{k-1}} |f| =\infty$ If 1) holds, we choose a set  $ \Delta_k $  with:  $ \Delta_k  \subset [0,1]\setminus E_{k-1}\,,\,  m(\Delta_k)<\delta $  and so that  $\int_{\Delta_k} |f|=\infty$ . Then, with the same argument as above, there exists  $n_k$  and  $\Delta^*_k \subset \Delta_k$  such that  $|\int_{E_{k-1}\cup \Delta^*_k} f_{n_k}| > k+1$ . Now, we set  $E_k=E_{k-1}+\Delta^*_k$ .
If 2) holds, we choose  $ \Delta_k$  with:  $\Delta_k  \subset E_{k-1}\,,\,  m(\Delta_k)<\delta $  and so that  $\int_{\Delta_k} |f|=\infty$ . Using convergence of  $\int_{E_{k-1}}f_n$ , similarly, there exists  $n_k$  and  $\Delta^*_k \subset \Delta_k$  such that  $|\int_{E_{k-1}\setminus \Delta^*_k} f_{n_k}| > k+1$ . In this case, we set  $E_k=E_{k-1}\setminus \Delta^*_k$ .
Notice that correction of  $E_{k-1}$ , on each step, by some small set  $\Delta^*_k$  doesn't affect much  $\int_{E_{k-1}} f_j\,,\, j=1,2,\ldots,k-1$ .
Let  $E=\lim_{n\to\infty} E_n $ . It can be checked that  $|\int_E f_{n_k}| \ge k\,,\, k=1,2,\ldots $ , a contradiction with the convergence of  $\int_E f_n$ . Therefore  $ \int_0^1 |f| < \infty$ .

It remains to see that  $\int_E f_n \to \int_E f$ . Suppose again it's not true. Set  $g_n=f_n-f $ . Hence,  $g_n \to 0 $  a.e. and  $\int_E |g_n|$  doesn't converge to  $0$ . **Claim**: There exists  $\epsilon>0$ , such that for any  $\delta>0$  there exists  $\Delta \subset E\,,\, m(\Delta)< \delta$  with  $\int_{E\setminus \Delta} |g_n| \to 0$  but  $\int_{\Delta} |g_n| > \epsilon$  for infinitely many  $n$ . 
Proof: Using for example Egorov's theorem and the fact  $\int_E |g_n|$  doesn't converge to  $0$ .  $\square$ The idea is to construct, in a similar way as above, sets  $E_k\subset E$  with  $|\int_{E_k} g_{n_k}| >\epsilon/4$ , when  $k$  is even, and small enough, when  $k$  is odd.
Lets choose  $E_1$ ,  $n_1$  with  $\int_{E_1}|g_1|<\epsilon/8$ . Suppose,  $E_1,\ldots,E_{k-1}\,,\, n_1<n_2,\ldots <n_{k-1}$  are already chosen, where  $k$  is even. 
We choose  $\delta\,,\, 0<\delta<2^{-k} $  s.t.  $\int_{\Delta} |g_{n_i}| <2^{-k}, i=1,2,\ldots k-1$ , whenever  $m(\Delta) <\delta$ . The above claim yeilds there exists  $\Delta_k\,,\, m(\Delta_k) < \delta$ ,  $\int_{E\setminus\Delta_k} |g_{n_k}|<\epsilon/8 \,,\,   \int_{\Delta_k} |g_{n_k}|>\epsilon$ . Thus for some  $\Delta^*_k\subset \Delta_k$ , it holds  $|\int_{E_{k-1}\cup\Delta^*_k} g_{n_k}|>\epsilon/4$ . We set  $ E_k=E_{k-1}\cup\Delta^*_k $ .
The next step, for  $ k+1 $ , is similar: choose  $ \delta\,,\, 0<\delta<2^{-k-1} $  s.t.  $ \int_{\Delta} |g_{n_i}| <2^{-k-1}, i=1,2,\ldots k $ , whenever  $m(\Delta) <\delta$ . For some  $\Delta_{k+1}\subset E\,,\, m(E_{k+1})<\delta$ , we choose  $g_{n_{k+1}}$  with  $\int_{E_k \setminus \Delta_{k+1}}|g_{n_{k+1}}|<\epsilon/8$  and set  $E_{k+1}=E_k \setminus \Delta_{k+1}$ . 
Finally, we check out that for  $E^*=\lim_{k\to\infty} E_k$  , the sequence  $|\int_{E^*}g_{n_k}|$  alternatively is less than  $\epsilon/8$  and greater than  $\epsilon/4$ , thus it cannot converge, a contradiction.

The assertion remains true if  $[0,1] $  is replaced by  $[0,\infty)$ . We just apply the proven fact on  $[0,N], N\to \infty$ .
The assertion is false if  $E$  runs over intervals and  $f_n\ge 0$ . As a counterexample one can take  $f_n(x)=n\,,\, x\in [0,1/n]$  and  $f_n(x)=0, x\in  (1/n,1]$ .**Comment**. As a motivation to the above construction, one can consider a sequence of functions  $f_n\,;\, f_n(x)=1/x, x\in [1/n,1]$  and  $f_n$  being some negative constant on  $[0,1/n]$  such that  $\int_0^1 f_n=0$ . Clearly  $f_n\to 1/x \not \in L^1[0,1]$ . Thus, if the problem claim is true, there must exist  $E\subset [0,1]$  with  $\int_E f_n$  not converging. Finding such  $E$  gives us the basic idea of the above construction.

stem_md:
Let  $ f$  be a differentiable real function and let  $ M$  be a positive real number. Prove that if \[ |f(x\plus{}t)\minus{}2f(x)\plus{}f(x\minus{}t)| \leq Mt^2 \; \textrm{for all}\ \;x\ \; \textrm{and}\ \;t\  , \] then \[ |f'(x\plus{}t)\minus{}f'(x)| \leq M|t|.\] 

*J. Szabados*
solution_md:
For any  $n\in \mathbb{N}$  We have
\[|(f(x+nt)-f(x+(n-1)t))-(f(x)-f(x-t))|\]
\[=|\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x+(i+1)t)-2f(x+it)+f(x+(i-1)t)|\]
\[\leq\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} | f(x+(i+1)t)-2f(x+it)+f(x+(i-1)t)|\]
\[\leq nMt^2\]
Let  $nt=y$ . By dividing by  $t$  we get
\[\big|\frac{f(x+y)-f(x+y-t)}{t}-\frac{f(x)-f(x-t)}{t}\big|\leq My\]
Letting  $y$  constant and  $n \rightarrow \infty$  it follows that  $t \rightarrow 0$  and therefore
\[|f'(x+y)-f'(x)|\leq  My\]

stem_md:
Let  $ a<a'<b<b'$  be real numbers and let the real function  $ f$  be continuous on the interval  $ [a,b']$  and differentiable in its interior. Prove that there exist  $ c \in (a,b), c'\in (a',b')$  such that \[ f(b)\minus{}f(a)\equal{}f'(c)(b\minus{}a),\] \[ f(b')\minus{}f(a')\equal{}f'(c')(b'\minus{}a'),\] and  $ c<c'$ . 

*B. Szokefalvi Nagy*
solution_md:
By the mean value theorem, there exist  $a < x_1 < a^\prime < x_2 < b < x_3 < b^\prime$  such that \[f^\prime (x_1) = \frac{f(a^\prime) - f(a)}{a^\prime - a},\] \[f^\prime (x_2) = \frac{f(b) - f(a^\prime)}{b - a^\prime},\] \[f^\prime (x_3) = \frac{f(b^\prime) - f(b)}{b^\prime - b}. \] 

Since the value of  $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$  lies between  $\frac{f(a^\prime) - f(a)}{a^\prime - a}$  and  $\frac{f(b) - f(a^\prime)}{b - a^\prime}$ , there exists a  $x_1 \le c \le x_2$  such that \[ f(b) - f(a) = f^\prime (c) (b-a)\] by Darboux's theorem. Likewise, there exists a  $x_2 \le c \le x_3$  such that \[f(b^\prime)-f(a^\prime) = f^\prime (c^\prime) (b^\prime-a^\prime).\] Except for the case  $c = c^\prime = x_2$ , we are done. 

If  $c = c^\prime = x_2$ , then we can check that the points  $(a,f(a)), (a^\prime, f(a^\prime)), (b,f(b)), (b^\prime, f(b^\prime))$  are collinear. Thus we can apply the mean value theorem again to find points  $C \in (a,a^\prime), C^\prime \in (b,b^\prime)$  so that the derivatives at that point equals the slope the the line.

stem_md:
Let  $ X_1,X_2,...,X_n$  be (not necessary independent) discrete random variables. Prove that there exist at least  $ n^2/2$  pairs $ (i,j)$  such that \[ H(X_i\plus{}X_j) \geq \frac 13 \min_{1 \leq k \leq n} \{ H(X_k) \},\] where  $ H(X)$  denotes the Shannon entropy of  $ X$ . 

*GY. Katona*
solution_md:
Consider the graph  $G$  with  $ n$  vertices, in which  $ i$  and  $j$  are connected iff we have   $$ H(X_i+X_j)< \frac{1}{3} \min_{1\leqslant k \leqslant n}\{H(X_k)\}. $$  We will show that  $G$  is a triangle-free graph.
Assume for the sake of contradiction that we can find  $3$  vertices  $m$ ,  $ n$  and  $p$  that form a triangle in  $G$ .

Notice that   $$ H(X_m)=H\big( (X_m+X_n)+(X_m+X_p)-(X_n+X_p)\big) \leqslant H(X_m+X_n)+H(X_n+X_p)+H(X_p+X_m). $$  Therefore   $$ \min_{1\leqslant k \leqslant n}\{ X_k \}\leqslant H(X_m)\leqslant 3\max \{H(X_m+X_n),H(X_n+X_p),H(X_p+X_m)\}. $$  which is a contradiction since  $m$ ,  $n$ , and  $p$  are connected.

So  $G$  is triangle free and  $G$  has no self-loops.
Therefore, by Turan, we know that  $G$  has at most  $n^2/4$  edges.

Hence the number of pairs we are searching for is at least  $n^2-2\cdot(n^2/4)=n^2/2.$

stem_md:
Assume that a face of a convex polyhedron  $ P$  has a common edge with every other face. Show that there exists a simple closed polygon that consists of edges of  $ P$  and passes through all vertices. 

*L .Lovasz*
solution_md:
Strange, it looks like this problem may be solved by some stupid induction. 

Consider the planar graph instead polyhedron so that our specific facet is outer polygon  $ A_1A_2\dots A_k$ . Note that the degree of each  $ A_i$  equals 3. Remove the vertices of outer face and edges passing from them. It is easy to see that the rest graph is a tree. It has some vertice  $ B$  of degree 1. Let  $ B$  be joined with  $ A_m$  and  $ A_n$ . Then the broken line  $ A_mBA_n$  divides our polygon onto two parts, in one of which our tree lies. Clearly, the vertex  $ B$  is joined with all  $ A_i$ 's between  $ A_i$  and  $ A_j$  in the other part. Relace all these vertices, including  $ A_i$ ,  $ A_j$  and  $ B$  to the new vertice and get a smaller graph with the same structure. It has Hamiltonian cycle, easy to see that hence initial graph also has. Some cases, when  $ k$  becomes equal to 1 or 2 after our operation, are analagous.

stem_md:
Assume that  $ R$ , a recursive, binary relation on  $  \mathbb{N}$  (the set of natural numbers), orders  $ \mathbb{N}$  into type  $ \omega$ . Show that if  $ f(n)$  is the  $ n$ th element of this order, then  $ f$  is not necessarily recursive. 

*L. Posa*
solution_md:
We will explicitly construct a Turing machine  $T$ , that computes such relation  $R$ , so that  $f$  is not recursive, i.e. there does not exist any Turing machine that computes  $f$ .
We will call a Turing machine  $T'$  good if  $T'(j) $ ( $T'$  with input  $j\in \mathbb{N}$ ) halts with output  $f(j)\in \mathbb{N}$  for every  $j\in \mathbb{N}$  and  $f(j),j=1,2,\ldots$  is a rearrangement of  $\{1,2,\ldots\}$ .
Here is the construction: $T$  starts with successively enumerating all Turing machines  $T_1, T_2,\ldots$  and simulates  $T_i$  running on the input  $i$ . Denote this process by  $T_i(i)$ . It can be done, as usual, by running a fixed number of cycles consecutively on each process  $T_1(1); T_1(1),T_2(2);T_1(1),T_2(2),T_3(3);\ldots$ Some of the processes (e.g. the good Turing machines)  $T_i(i)$  will halt with an output  $i'\in \mathbb{N}$ , the others will run forever.
Let  $T_i(i)$  be the first process which halts with an output  $i'$ . If  $i'\neq 1$ , we place  $i$  in the first place on a row and tag it with the number  $i'$ . If not, we just tag it and proceed to the next machine that halts. In that way, after a while, there will be a process  $T_j(j)$  that halts with an output  $j'\neq 1$ . We place  $j$  in the first place on the row and tag it with  $j'$ . The other tagged numbers are placed on the same row watching that the tag  $i'$  not equals to the number of the place. If the first  $i$  places are already filled, but  $T_i(i)$  is still running we place  $i$  in the first empty place and keep  $T_i(i)$  running. 
In this manner we consecutively put the natural numbers on the row. 
Suppose at some moment a machine  $T_i(i)$ , still running, with the corresponfing number  $i$ , put at the  $n$ -th place in the row, halts with an output  $i'$ . We consider if  $i'$  coincides with  $n$ . If it does, the next machine  $T_j(j)$  that halts with an output  $j'\,, j'\neq n$  , will be put in the  $n$ -th place and all placed numbers after that will move right by one position. If some of their tagged numbers match their new position we do the same thing, insert consecutively in their places some other machines that will halt and move them right by one position.
To sum up. We have constructed a machine  $T$  that places the natural numbers in a row, i.e. orders  $\mathbb{N}$  into type  $\omega$ . If denote by  $f(i)$  the number of the position where  $i$  is finally placed, we have  $f(i) \neq T_i(i)$  for every good Turing machine  $T_i$ . It just means there does not exist any good Turing machine that computes  $f$ . On the other hand the relation  $R$  of the order is computable by  $T$ , since once any two numbers are placed in the row, their precedence relationship never changes.

stem_md:
Let  $ G$  be an infinite graph such that for any countably infinite vertex set  $ A$  there is a vertex  $ p$ , not in  $A$ , joined to infinitely many elements of  $ A$ . Show that  $ G$  has a countably infinite vertex set  $ A$  such that  $ G$  contains uncountably infinitely many vertices  $ p$  joined to infinitely many elements of  $ A$ . 

*P. Erdos, A. Hajnal*
solution_md:
Guess we'll never know what infinite lemma they were talking about.

Call an infinite graph "good" if it satisfies the constraints of the problem, and "amazing" if it is good and further for any finite set of vertices  $A$ , there are uncountably many vertices not adjacent to any vertex in  $A$ . Clearly any good graph is uncountable, else we can look at the entire vertex set of the graph to get a contradiction.

We first prove that removing any finite set of vertices from a good graph retains its goodness. Indeed, let  $A$  be the finite set of vertices removed from a graph  $H$ . Now, for any countably infinite vertex set  $B$  in  $H \setminus A$ , consider the countably infinite set  $A \cup B$  in  $H$ . There exists a vertex  $v$  in  $H$  adjacent to infinitely many vertices from  $A \cup B$ . This  $v$  is not in  $A$ , and further  $A$  has only finitely many elements, so  $v$  is in fact adjacent to infinitely many elements of  $B$ , proving goodness of  $H \setminus A$ .

We return to the given problem. We have two cases:**Case I:**  $G$  has no amazing subgraph.

We define a sequence of good graphs  $G=G_1,G_2,G_3, \dots$  of graphs such that for each  $i \geq 1$ ,  $G_{i+1}$  is creating by removing a finite non-empty set of vertices  $A_i$  from  $G_i$  which "almost covered"  $G_i$ , i.e., all but countably many vertices of  $G_i$  were adjacent to at least one vertex from  $A_i$ . Such an  $A_i$  always exists since  $G$  has no amazing subgraphs. Let  $B_i$  be the countable set not covered by  $A_i$  in  $G_i$ . Consider  $A=\bigcup_{i \geq 1} A_i$  and  $B=\bigcup_{i \geq 1} B_i$ .  $A$  is countably infinite,  $B$  is countable, and for any vertex  $v$  not in  $B$ ,  $v$  is adjacent to at least one vertex in each  $A_i$ , so adjacent to infinitely many vertices in  $A$ . This is true for all vertices not in  $B$ , of which there are uncountably many since  $G$  is uncountable but  $B$  is countable.**Case II:**  $G$  has an amazing subgraph.

Proving the result for the amazing subgraph would imply it for  $G$ , so we can WLOG assume  $G$  is amazing. Assume FTSOC that for any countably infinite vertex set  $A$ , there are at most countably many vertices  $p$  adjacent to infinitely many elements of  $A$ .

We define a sequence  $A_1,A_2, \dots$  of disjoint countably infinite sets of vertices as follows. Let  $A_1$  be an arbitrary countably infinite set of vertices. For all  $i \geq 1$ , we create  $A_{i+1}$  as follows. Start off with  $A_{i+1}$  empty. Let  $C_i=\bigcup_{j \leq i} A_j$ , so  $C_i$  is countably infinite. First, we add to  $A_{i+1}$  all vertices adjacent to infinitely many vertices from  $C_i$ . Next, we enumerate all non-empty finite subsets of  $C_i$ , say  $S_1,S_2, \dots $ . Since  $G$  is amazing, each  $S_i$  misses uncountably many vertices, and all vertex sets that we have considered so far are countable. Thus we can inductively find countably infinite subsets  $T_1,T_2, \dots$  such that each  $T_k$  is disjoint from  $C_i$ , current  $A_{i+1}$ , and all  $T_j$  for  $j<k$ , and no vertex from  $T_k$  is adjacent to any vertex from  $S_k$ . Add all the  $T_k$  to  $A_{i+1}$  to get our final  $A_{i+1}$ . Thus  $A_{i+1}$  is countably infinite and disjoint from  $C_i$ , and we can continue this process.

Now, consider  $A=\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty A_i$ , which is countably infinite. Hence there exists a non-empty countable set  $P=\{p_1,p_2, \dots\}$  of all vertices not in  $A$  but having infinitely many neighbors in  $A$ . If  $P$  is finite, say of size  $n$ , we define  $p_n=p_{n+1}=p_{n+2}=\cdots$  for convenience. Let  $B_i$  be the set of neighbors of  $p_i$  in  $A$ . Clearly  $B_i$  is a countably infinite set, but since  $p_i \notin A_{k+1}$  for any  $k$ ,  $B_i \cap A_k$  is finite for all  $i,k$ .

Further, fix an enumeration  $a_1,a_2, \dots$  of the elements of  $A$ . For all  $i \geq 1$ , let  $B_i'$  be the set of neighbours of  $\{a_1,a_2, \dots, a_i\}$  in  $A$ . Let  $Q_{i,k}$  be the set of elements in  $A_k$  that are not in  $B_i'$ . We claim that, for a fixed  $i$ ,  $Q_{i,k}$  is infinite for all sufficiently large  $k$ . Indeed, let  $b_i$  be the smallest index such that  $\{a_1,a_2, \dots, a_i\} \subset C_{b_i}$ . Then, by construction, each  $A_j$  for  $j>b_i$  has an infinite subset that is not adjacent to any vertex from  $\{a_1,a_2, \dots, a_i\}$ . Thus  $Q(i,j)$  is infinite for all  $j>b_i$ .

We streamline the sequence  $b_1,b_2, \dots$  slightly. Define  $c_1=b_1+1$ , and for  $i \geq 1$ , define  $c_{i+1}=\max\{b_{i+1}+1,c_i+1\}$ . This ensures that  $c_1<c_2<c_3<\cdots$  and  $Q(i,c_i)$  is infinite for all  $i$ .

Now we construct a countably infinite set  $W$  by picking  $1$  element each from  $A_{c_1},A_{c_2},A_{c_3}, \dots$ . For each  $k \geq 1$ , pick an element from  $Q(k,c_k) \subset A_{c_k}$  that is not in any  $B_i$  for  $i \leq k$ ; this can be done since  $Q(k,c_k)$  is infinite while each  $B_i \cap A_{c_k}$  is finite. 

Now, there exists a vertex adjacent to infinitely many elements from  $W$ . Can this vertex be outside  $A$ ? In that case, the vertex is adjacent to infinitely many vertices from  $A$ , so it must be in  $P$ ; say it is  $p_j$ . Thus  $B_j \cap W$  is infinite, which is impossible since  $|B_j \cap W|<j$  by construction.

Thus this vertex must be in  $A$ , say it is  $a_j$  in the fixed enumeration. Let  $x$  be a neighbour of  $a_j$  in  $W$ . Then  $x \in B_i'$  for all  $i \geq j$ , and hence  $x \notin Q(i,c_i)$  for all  $i \geq j$ . Therefore by our construction of  $W$ ,  $\{x\}=W \cap A_{c_k}$  for some  $k < j$ , and we have at most  $j-1$  such choices for  $x$ , which contradicts the fact that there must be infinitely many neighbours of  $a_j$  in  $W$ . $\blacksquare$

Let  $ f_1,f_2,\dots,f_n$  be regular functions on a domain of the complex plane, linearly independent over the complex field. Prove that the functions  $ f_i\overline{f}_k, \;1 \leq i,k \leq n$ , are also linearly independent. 

*L. Lempert*
solution_md:
A generalization:

Let  $ f_i,\ i \equal{} \overline{1,n}$  be linearly independent holomorphic functions on a domain and let  $ g_j,\ j \equal{} \overline{1,m}$  be linearly independent antiholomorphic functions on the same domain. Then the functions  $ f_ig_j$  are linearly independent.
 $ \partial$  and  $ \bar\partial$  denote, as usual, the differential operators  $ \frac 12\left(\frac\partial{\partial x} \minus{} i\frac\partial{\partial x}\right)$  and  $ \frac 12\left(\frac\partial{\partial x} \plus{} i\frac\partial{\partial x}\right)$  respectively. Now assume we have a relation of the form  $ \sum a_{ij}f_ig_j \equal{} 0$  (where  $ a_{ij}$  are complex numbers). This can be written as  $ \sum h_if_i \equal{} 0\ (*)$ , where the  $ h_i$  are linear combinations of  $ g_j$ 's with the coefficients  $ a_{ij}$  (and are hence antiholomorphic). Because  $ \partial f_i \equal{} 0$ , applying a power  $ \bar\partial^k$  of  $ \bar\partial$  to  $ (*)$  yields the equation  $ \sum\bar\partial^k(h_i)f_i \equal{} 0$ . If not all  $ h_i$  are zero,  $ k$  can be chosen such that  $ \bar\partial^k h_i$  are constants and not all zero; this contradicts the linear independence of the  $ f_i$ 's, so all  $ h_i$  must be zero. But as noted before,  $ h_i \equal{} \sum_j a_{ij}g_j$ , so, since  $ g_j$  are linearly independent, all  $ a_{ij}$  must be zero.

stem_md:
Prove that the set of all linearly combinations (with real coefficients) of the system of polynomials  $ \{ x^n\plus{}x^{n^2} \}_{n\equal{}0}^{\infty}$  is dense in  $ C[0,1]$ . 

*J. Szabados*
solution_md:
This one is surprisingly simple: Assume that there is a signed measure  $ \mu$  annihilating all  $ x^n\plus{}x^{n^2}$ . Let  $ a_m\equal{}\int_{[0,1]}x^m\,d\mu$ . Then, on one hand,  $ a_m\to \mu\{1\}$  by the dominated convergence theorem and, on the other hand, if  $ a_m\equal{}a\ne 0$ , then  $ a$  and  $ \minus{}a$  occur among  $ a_m$  infinitely often, so we get a contradiction. Thus, our measure must annihilate every  $ x^m$  and we have reduced everything to the classical Weierstrass theorem.

Let's upgrade the problem to the same question about the sequence  $ \{x^n\plus{}x^{n^2}\plus{}x^{n^3}\}$  ;).

stem_md:
Suppose that  $ \tau$  is a metrizable topology on a set  $ X$  of cardinality less than or equal to continuum. Prove that there exists a separable and metrizable topology on  $ X$  that is coarser that  $ \tau$ . 

*L. Juhasz*
solution_md:
The aim is to prove that we can find countably many real-valued continuous functions on  $ (X,\tau)$  which separate the points of  $ X$  (that is, for every two  $ x\ne y\in X$  there is a function  $ f$  in this countable family with  $ f(x)\ne f(y)$ ). Such functions give a one-to-one continuous map of  $ (X,\tau)$  into a countable product of real lines, and the topology on  $ X$  generated by this map has the required properties (it identifies  $ X$  to a subspace of a countable product of real lines, and this latter space is a separable metric space). 

Now to find our countable family of functions on  $ X$ . For each  $ n\ge 1$ , let  $ X_n$  be a maximal family of points in  $ X$ , each two at a distance  $ \ge\frac 1n$  from each other. Then, for each  $ m > n$ , let  $ X_n^m$  be the union of the closed balls of radius  $ \frac 1n \minus{} \frac 1m$  centered at the points of  $ X_n$ . The set  $ X_n$  has at most continuum cardinality, by the hypothesis, and the set  $ X_n^m$  is closed for every pair  $ m > n$  of positive integers. Moreover, each of the balls of radius  $ \frac 1n \minus{} \frac 1m$  mentioned above is an open subset of  $ X_n^m$ . It follows that we can find a real-valued continuous function  $ f_{n,m}$  defined on  $ X_n^m$  which is constant on each ball, but which assigns different values to different balls. Extend  $ f_{n,m}$  to a continuous real-valued function on  $ X$  (Tietze Extension Theorem) denoted by the same symbol. It should be clear now that the functions  $ f_{n,m}$  separate the points of  $ X$  (two distinct points will be members of different balls in some set  $ X_n^m$ ), and this finishes the proof, according to the previous paragraph.

stem_md:
Prove that if  $ a,x,y$  are  $ p$ -adic integers different from  $ 0$  and  $ p | x, pa | xy$ , then \[ \frac 1y \frac{(1\plus{}x)^y\minus{}1}{x} \equiv \frac{\log (1\plus{}x)}{x} \;\;\;\; ( \textrm{mod} \; a\ )   .\] 

*L. Redei*
solution_md:
Using the power series expansions for the  $p$ -adic [exponential and logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_exponential_function), we have for  $\log(1+x)=z$  that
\[
\frac{(1+x)^y-1}{y} = \frac{\exp\big(y\log(1+x)\big)-1}{y}=z+\frac{yz^2}{2!}+\frac{y^2z^3}{3!}+\dots
\]
Therefore, the problem reduces to
\[
S=\frac{yz^2}{2!}+\frac{y^2z^3}{3!}+\dots\equiv 0\pmod{ax},
\]
where it suffices to show  $pS\equiv 0\pmod{x^2y}$  because  $pa|xy$ . However, this follows from the fact that  $x^2|p\cdot \frac{z^k}{k!}$ , where
\[
\frac{z}{x}=\frac{\log(1+x)}{x}=1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{3}\mp\dots
\]
is a  $p$ -adic integer (due to  $v_p(x^{k-1})\ge k-1\ge v_p(k)$ ), so our divisibility in turn reduces to  $p\cdot \frac{z^{k-2}}{k!}$  being a  $p$ -adic integer, which is clear, because by [Legendre's formula](http://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php?title=Legendre%27s_Formula),  $v_p(k!)\le \frac{k-1}{p-1}\le (k-2)v_p(z)+1$ .  $\blacksquare$

solution_md:
As a sidenote, Erdos spent a long time working on (and left as an famous open conjecture) the following variant of the posted problem:

Let  $ A$  be a set of non-negative integers such that every sufficiently large number can be represented as the sum of two elements of  $ A$ .  Must it be true that for every positive integer  $ k$  there is a integer that can be represented in at least  $ k$  different ways as the sum of two elements of  $ A$ ?

The problem is known as the [Erdos-Turan conjecture for additive bases](http://garden.irmacs.sfu.ca/?q=op/the_erdos_turan_conjecture_on_additive_bases), and has remained open for nearly 70 years despite a bounty of 500 dollars on it.

stem_md:
Let  $ 1<a_1<a_2< \ldots <a_n<x$  be positive integers such that  $ \sum_{i\equal{}1}^n 1/a_i \leq 1$ . Let  $ y$  denote the number of positive integers smaller that  $ x$  not divisible by any of the  $ a_i$ . Prove that \[ y > \frac{cx}{\log x}\] with a suitable positive constant  $ c$  (independent of  $ x$  and the numbers  $ a_i$ ). 

*I. Z. Ruzsa*
solution_md:
We have: 
\[ y(x)\geq (1-s)x\,,\, \forall x>1\]. 
where  $ s= \sum_{i=1}^n 1/a_i $ .
Indeed, the number of positive integers multiple of  $a_j$  and smaller than  $x$  is at most  $\frac{x}{a_i}$ , hence those of them not divisible by any of the  $a_i$  are at least  $x-x\cdot \sum_{i=1}^n 1/a_i=(1-s)x $ . 
Thus, if  $s$  is not very close to  $1$ , we can use that estimate. The problem is what to do when  $s$  is  $1$  or very close to  $1$ .
One more preliminary fact. Using prime number theorem one can get that the number of primes in the interval  $(x/2,x]$  is greater than  $C_1\frac{x}{\log x}$  for some absolute constant  $C_1>0$ .

Let us now denote  $\alpha : = \sum_{a_i\leq x/2} 1/a_i$ . The idea is as follows: if  $\alpha$  is "small" , we can use the above approach to estimate the integers in  $[1,x/2]$  not divisible by any  $a_i$ . If  $\alpha$  is "close" to  $1$ , there will be enough primes in  $(x/2, x]$  that are different to any of  $a_i$  's.**Case a)** :  $1-\alpha \geq \frac{C_1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\log x}$ . Then:
\[y(x) \geq \# \{m : m\leq x/2\,,\, m \text{ is not divisible by any }a_i \}\geq \frac{C_1}{2}\cdot \frac{x}{\log x}\]**Case b)**:  $1-\alpha < \frac{C_1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\log x}$ . Then, it holds:
\[ \#\{i : x/2 < a_i \leq x \} \leq \frac{C_1}{2}  \frac{x}{\log x} \]
Indeed, assuming it's not true, we get: 
\[1-\alpha \geq \sum_{a_i > x/2} 1/a_i \geq \frac{C_1}{2} \frac{x}{\log x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}=\frac{C_1}{2 \log x} \] 
a contradiction.
Hence, the number of primes in  $(x/2,x]$  not equal to any of  $a_i$  is at least  $\#\{p\in (x/2,x] : p\in \mathbb{P} \} - \frac{C_1}{2\log x}$ . Thus,
\[y(x) \geq \#\{p\in (x/2,x] : p\in \mathbb{P} \} - \frac{C_1}{2\log x} \geq  C_1\frac{x}{\log x} - \frac{C_1}{2\log x}= \frac{C_1}{2\log x}\]

Combining a) and b) , the result follows.

stem_md:
Let  $ \mathbb{Q}$  and  $ \mathbb{R}$  be the set of rational numbers and the set of real numbers, respectively, and let  $ f : \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  be a function with the following property. For every  $ h \in \mathbb{Q} , \;x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ , \[ f(x\plus{}h)\minus{}f(x) \rightarrow 0\] as  $ x \in \mathbb{Q}$  tends to  $ x_0$ . Does it follow that  $ f$  is bounded on some interval? 

*M. Laczkovich*
solution_md:
No,  $f$  may be unbounded on any interval.**A counterexample**.
Let  $p_1,p_2,\ldots$  be an enumeration of the primes. Set  $q_n=(p_1 p_2\ldots p_n)^n\,,\, n\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let us denote: $A_n =\left \{\frac{m}{q_n}\mid m\in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\,,\, n=1,2,\ldots$ . 

Clearly we have:

1)  $A_n \subset A_{n+1}$ .
2)  $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} A_n = \mathbb{Q}$ .
3) For every fixed  $h\in \mathbb{Q}$  , for all sufficiently big  $n$  ,  $x\in A_n \implies x+h \in A_n$ .  

Denote  $B_1=A_1\,,\, B_n=A_n\setminus A_{n-1}\,,n=2,3,\ldots$ . 
One can check that:

4)  $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}} B_n = \mathbb{Q}\,,\, B_n\cap B_m=\emptyset, m\neq n$ .
5) For every fixed  $h\in \mathbb{Q}$  , for all sufficiently big  $n$  ,  $ x\in B_n \implies x+h \in B_n$ .

Now, let us define the function  $f$ .
For any  $x\in \mathbb{Q}\,,\, f(x):=n$ , where  $n$  is such that  $x\in B_n$ .
Obviously  $f$  is unbounded on any interval. Let us fix  $h\in \mathbb{Q}$  and  $x_0\in \mathbb{R}$ . According to 5) we can choose  $N\in \mathbb{N}$ , s.t.  $\forall n>N\,,\, x\in B_n \implies x+h \in B_n$ . Let us take a neighbourhood  $U$  of  $x_0$  , free from members of  $B_1,B_2,\ldots, B_N$ , except eventually the point  $x_0$ . 

Thus,  $\forall x\in \mathbb{Q} \land x\in U\setminus \{x_0\} \implies f(x)=f(x+h)$ . 

Therefore  $\lim_{x\to x_0,x\ne x_0} f(x+h)-f(x)=0 $ .

Let the operation  $ f$  of  $ k$  variables defined on the set  $ \{ 1,2,\ldots,n \}$  be called  $ \textit{friendly}$  toward the binary relation  $ \rho$  defined on the same set if \[ f(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k) \;\rho\  \;f(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_k)\] implies  $ a_i \; \rho \ b_i$  for at least one  $ i,1\leq i \leq k$ . Show that if the operation  $ f$  is friendly toward the relations "equal to" and "less than," then it is friendly toward all binary relations. 

*B. Csakany*
solution_md:
The case  $n = 1$  is trivial.

We first look at the case  $n \geq 3$ . I will show by induction on  $k$  that, if  $f$  is friendly toward "equal to" and "less than", then there exists  $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$  such that  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = a_i$  for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k$ .

For  $k = 1$ , we have a function  $f$  from  $\{ 1, \dots, n\}$  to itself, which satisfies  $f(a) = f(b) \implies a = b$  (i.e.  $f$  is injective) and  $f(a) < f(b) \implies a < b$  (i.e.  $a \geq b \implies f(a) \geq f(b)$ , that is,  $f$  is non-decreasing). It follows that  $f(a) = a$  for all  $a \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ .

Now suppose that it's true for  $k - 1$  and let's prove the result for  $k$ .
We define  $g:(a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1})\mapsto f(a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1}, a_{k - 1})$ . It is clear from the definitions that  $g$  is friendly toward "equal to" and "less than". Thus by induction hypothesis, there exists  $i \in \{1, \dots, k - 1\}$  such that  $g(a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1}) = a_i$ .

If  $i \neq k - 1$ , then I claim that  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = a_i$  for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k$ .
In fact, for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k$  and any  $x \neq a_i$ , we may choose  $b_1, \dots, b_{k - 1}$  such that
-  $b_i = x$ ;
-  $b_j \neq a_j$  for any  $1 \leq j < k - 1$ ;
-  $b_{k - 1} \neq a_{k - 1}$  or  $a_k$  (notice that  $n \geq 3$ ).
It follows that  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) \neq f(b_1, \dots, b_{k - 1}, b_{k - 1}) = b_i = x$ . Thus the only possibility is  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = a_i$ .

If  $i = k - 1$ , then the same argument as above shows that, for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k$ , we have  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = a_{k - 1}$  or  $a_k$  (for any  $x\neq a_{k - 1}$  or  $a_k$ , choose  $b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}$  such that  $b_j \neq a_j$  and consider  $f(b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}, x, x)$ ).
Now consider the two numbers  $f(1, \dots, 1, 1, 2)$  and  $f(2, \dots, 2, 2, 1)$ . They must be different and both are equal to  $1$  or  $2$ . Therefore one of them is equal to  $1$ .
Without loss of generality, we assume in the following that  $f(1, \dots, 1, 1, 2) = 1$ .

For any  $a_1, \dots, a_{k - 2}$ , we choose  $b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}$  such that  $a_j \neq b_j$  and  $b_j \neq 1$  (which is possible because  $n \geq 3$ ).
It follows that  $f(b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}, 2, 1) = 2$  (because it is not equal to  $f(1, \dots, 1, 1, 2) = 1$ )  and hence  $f(a_1, \dots, a_{k - 2}, 1, 2) = 1$  (because it is not equal to  $f(b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}, 2, 1) = 2$ ).

For any  $a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1}$  such that  $a_{k - 1} \neq 1$ , we choose  $b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}$  such that  $a_j \neq b_j$ .
It follows that  $f(a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1}, 1) = a_{k - 1}$ , because it is not equal to  $f(b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}, 1, 2) = 1$ .
This is also true for  $a_{k - 1} = 1$ , hence we have  $f(a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1}, 1) = a_{k - 1}$  for any  $a_1, \dots, a_{k - 1}$ .

Finally, for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k$  such that  $a_k \neq 1$  or  $a_{k - 1}$ , we choose  $b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}$  such that  $a_j \neq b_j$ .
It follows that  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = a_{k - 1}$ , because it is not equal to  $f(b_1, \dots, b_{k - 2}, a_k, 1) = a_k$ .
This is also true for  $a_k = 1$  or  $a_{k - 1}$ , hence we have shown that  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = a_{k - 1}$  for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k$ .

-----
It remains to treat the case  $n = 2$ .

We view a relation  $\rho$  as a subset of  $\{1, 2\}^2$ .
Note that, if  $f$  is friendly toward two relations  $\rho_1, \rho_2$ , then  $f$  is also friendly toward the union  $\rho_1\cup \rho_2$ .
Since every subset of  $\{1, 2\}^2$  is a union of singletons, it suffices to prove that  $f$  is friendly toward each singleton relation.

There are only four singleton relations:
-  $\rho_1 = \{(1, 1)\}$ , i.e.  $a\textrm{ } \rho_1\textrm{ } b \iff a = b = 1$ ;
-  $\rho_2 = \{(2, 2)\}$ , i.e.  $a\textrm{ } \rho_2\textrm{ } b \iff a = b = 2$ ;
-  $\rho_3 = \{(1, 2)\}$ , i.e.  $a\textrm{ } \rho_3\textrm{ } b \iff a < b$ ;
-  $\rho_4 = \{(2, 1)\}$ , i.e.  $a \textrm{ }\rho_4 \textrm{ }b \iff a > b$ .
By assumption,  $f$  is friendly toward  $\rho_3$ , and this implies that  $f$  is also friendly toward  $\rho_4$ .

It remains to show that  $f$  is friendly toward  $\rho_1, \rho_2$ . We prove it for  $\rho_1$ , the other proof being identical.

Since  $f$  is friendly toward "equal to", for any  $a_1, \dots, a_k \in \{1, 2\}$ , we have  $f(3 - a_1, \dots, 3 - a_k) = 3 - f(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ .
Thus if  $f(a_1, \dots, a_k)\textrm{ } \rho_1\textrm{ } f(b_1, \dots, b_k)$ , then   $$ f(a_1, \dots, a_k) = 1 < 2 = f(3 - b_1, \dots, 3 - b_k) $$   which implies that there exists  $i$  such that  $a_i < 3 - b_i$ .
This is only possible when  $a_i = 1$  and  $3 - b_i = 2$ , or in other words,  $a_i\textrm{ } \rho_1\textrm{ } b_i$ .

solution_md:
Solution. Let us fix  $\varepsilon>0$ . We show that if  $n$  is large enough,  $0 \leq x_i<$   $1(i=1, \ldots, n)$ , then there exists a pair  $(i, j)$  of indices such that  $\| x_i-$   $x_j \|<\min (\varepsilon, 1 /$  over  $2|i-j|)$ . It suffices since it implies that by subdividing the infinite sequence  $x_1, x_2, \ldots$  into blocks of  $n$  terms, we can find a desired pair of indices in each block and the difference  $|i-j|$  does not change if the indices in the block are replaced by the indices in the whole sequence.

Let  $f:\{1, \ldots, n\} \rightarrow\{1, \ldots, n\}$  be a permutation such that  $$ 0 \leq x_{f(1)} \leq \cdots \leq x_{f(n)}<1 $$  We may assume that  $$ \left\|x_{f(i)}-x_{f(i+1)}\right\|<\min \left(\varepsilon, \frac{1}{2|f(i)-f(i+1)|}\right) $$  for  $i=1, \ldots, n$  since if it is not the case then we are done. Let  $A$  denote the set of the indices  $1 \leq i \leq n$  such that  $\left\|x_{f(i)}-x_{f(i+1)}\right\| \geq \varepsilon$ . Since the


cyclically taken intervals  $\left[x_{f(1)}, x_{f(2)}\right),\left[x_{f(2)}, x_{f(3)}\right), \ldots,\left[x_{f(n)}, x_{f(1)}\right)$  cover the cyclic interval  $[0,1)$   $$ 1 \geq \sum_{i=1}^n\left\|x_{f(i)}-x_{f(i+1)}\right\| \geq \sum_{i \in A} \varepsilon+\sum_{i \notin A} \frac{1}{2|f(i)-f(i+1)|}, $$  and  $|A| \leq 1 / \varepsilon$ . That is,  $$ 1-|A| \varepsilon \geq \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \notin A} \frac{1}{|f(i)-f(i+1)|} . $$  Applying the inequality between the arithmetic and harmonic means, we get the inequality  $$ \sum_{i \notin A}|f(i)-f(i+1)| \geq \frac{(n-|A|)^2}{2(1-|A| \varepsilon)} . $$  In the sum  $\sum_{i=1}^n|f(i)-f(i+1)|$ , every integer  $j \in\{1, \ldots, n\}$  appears exactly twice with positive or negative signs, so that the total sum of the signs is 0 . Obviously, the sum is maximum when the large numbers have coefficient +2 and the small numbers have coefficient -2 . Thus,  $$ \sum_{i=1}^n|f(i)-f(i+1)| \leq \frac{n^2}{2} $$  when  $n$  is even, and  $$ \sum_{i=1}^n|f(i)-f(i+1)| \leq \frac{n^2-1}{2} $$  when  $n$  is odd. Combining this fact with the preceding inequality, we obtain  $1-|A| \varepsilon \geq(1-|A| / n)^2$ , which is a contradiction if  $|A| \geq 1$  and  $n$  is sufficienly large. If  $A=\emptyset$ , then we get  $1=1$ , which means that  $n$  is even and the numbers  $|f(i)-f(i+1)|$  are equal (mean inequality). However, if  $f(i)>n / 2$ , then  $f(i)$  appears twice with positive sign, that is,  $f(i)>f(i-1), \quad f(i)>f(i+1)$ , implying that  $f(i-1)=f(i+1)$ , which is possible only if  $n \leq 2$ . But it is easy to see that equality cannot hold in this case either, and we got the desired contradiction in all cases.

stem_md:
We are given an infinite sequence of  $ 1$ 's and  $ 2$ 's with the following properties: 

(1) The first element of the sequence is  $ 1$ . 

(2) There are no two consecutive  $ 2$ 's or three consecutive  $ 1$ 's. 

(3) If we replace consecutive  $ 1$ 's by a single  $ 2$ , leave the single  $ 1$ 's alone, and delete the original  $ 2$ 's, then we recover the original sequence. 

How many  $ 2$ 's are there among the first  $ n$  elements of the sequence? 

*P. P. Palfy*
solution_md:
This is an interesting question, especially back in the year 1981.

However nowadays it is too easy to find the relevant information [on OEIS](http://oeis.org/A189572) (except that here it's using  $1, 2$  instead of  $0, 1$ ).
The number of  $2$ 's among the first  $n$  elements is just the partial sum of the above linked sequence.

To get a closed form result, I copy here the most useful information from the above OEIS page: $a(n) = \lfloor \alpha n + \beta\rfloor - \lfloor \alpha (n-1)+\beta\rfloor$ , with  $\alpha = \sqrt 2 -1$ ,  $\beta = 1 - \frac{\sqrt 2}2$ .

It follows that the number of  $2$ 's among the first  $n$  elements is given by  $\lfloor \alpha n + \beta \rfloor$  with  $\alpha, \beta$  as above.

This sequence is related to the so called [Hofstadter sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hofstadter_sequence).

stem_md:
Consider the lattice  $ L$  of the contradictions of a simple graph  $ G$  (as sets of vertex pairs) with respect to inclusion. Let  $ n \geq 1$  be an arbitrary integer. Show that the identity \[ x \bigwedge \left( \bigvee_{i\equal{}0}^n y_i \right) \equal{} \bigvee_{j\equal{}0}^n
\left( x \bigwedge \left( \bigvee_{0 \leq i \leq n, \;i\not\equal{}j\ } y_i \right)\right)\] holds if and only if  $ G$  has no cycle of size at least  $ n\plus{}2$ . 

*A. Huhn*
solution_md:
It can be seen that  $a, b \in \vee_{i=0}^k z_i$  holds if and only if there is a natural number  $l$  and a path  $a=u_o, u_1, \ldots, u_l=b$  such that for every  $0 \leq j<l,\left(u_i, u_{j+1}\right) \in z_i$  for some  $0 \leq i \leq k$ . Furthermore,  $(a, b) \in z_1 \wedge z_2$  holds if and only if there is a natural number  $l$  and a path  $a=u_o, u_1, \ldots, u_l=b$  such that  $\left(u_i, u_{i+1}\right) \in z_1$  and  $\left(u_i, u_{i+1}\right) \in z_2$  for every  $0 \leq i<l$ . The inequality  $\geq$  always holds in equality (1), so what we have to prove is that the inequality  $\leq$  holds if and only if  $G$  has no cycle of at least  $n+2$  vertices. Suppose that  $v_0, \ldots, v_k$  is a cycle with  $k \geq n+1$ . If  $x$  contracts  $\left(v_0, v_k\right), y_i$  contracts  $\left(v_i, v_{i+1}\right)(0 \leq i<n)$ , and  $y_n$  contracts the vertices  $v_n, v_{n+1}, \ldots, v_k$ , then the left-hand side of (1) is  $x$  and the right-hand side of it is not since  $\left(v_0, v_k\right)$  is not contracted in the right-hand side.

Conversely, suppose that  $G$  has no cycle of at least  $n+2$  vertices, and let  $(a, b) \in x \wedge \vee_{i=0}^n y_i$ . We show that  $(a, b)$  is an element of the right-hand side of (1) as well. The assumption  $(a, b) \in x \wedge \vee_{i=0}^n y_i$  implies that there is a path  $a=v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_k=b$  in  $G$  such that  $\left(v_t, v_{t+1}\right) \in x$  and  $\left(v_t, v_{t+1}\right) \in \wedge_{i=0}^n y_i$  for  $0 \leq t<k$ . Let us fix  $t$ . There is a path  $v_t=u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_l=v_{t+1}$  such that for every  $0 \leq s<l$ , we have  $\left(u_s, u_{s+1}\right) \in y_m$  for some  $0 \leq \leq n$ . Since the vertices  $u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_l$  constitute a cycle,  $l+1<n+2$ , that is,  $l \leq n$  and some of the  $y$  's do not appear among these  $y_m$ . Thus,  $$ \left(v_t, v_{t+1}\right) \in \bigvee_{i=0, \ldots, j-1, j+1, \ldots n} y_i $$  for some  $j$ , and hence  $(a, b)$  is contained in the right-hand side of (1).

stem_md:
Let  $ U$  be a real normed space such that, for an finite-dimensional, real normed space  $ X,U$  contains a subspace isometrically isomorphic to  $ X$ . Prove that every (not necessarily closed) subspace  $ V$  of  $ U$  of finite codimension has the same property. (We call  $ V$  of finite codimension if there exists a finite-dimensional subspace  $ N$  of  $ U$  such that  $ V\plus{}N\equal{}U$ .) 

*A. Bosznay*
solution_md:
At first, remark that it is sufficient to prove the statement for 1-codimensional subspaces: after that induction on codimention helps.

Then, the following lemma solves the problem:
**Lemma**. Let  $ X$  be a finite-dimensional normed space, then there is another finite-dimensional normed space  $ Y$  such that every 1-codimensional subspace of  $ Y$  contains an isometric copy of  $ X$ .
**Proof.** Take  $ Y\equal{} X \oplus X$  with the norm  $ \|(x_1, x_2)\|\equal{} \max\left\{\|x_1\|, \|x_2\|\right\}$ . Let  $ Z$  be a 1-codimensional subspace of  $ Y$ . Then  $ Z$  is the kernel of a functional  $ f\equal{}(f_1, f_2)$ ,  $ f_1, f_2 \in X^*$ . Without loss of generality we may (and do) asume that  $ \|f_1\| \le \|f_2\|\equal{}1$ . Take  $ e \in X$  with  $ \|e\|\equal{}f_2(e)\equal{}1$ . Then the subspace $ \{(x, \minus{}f_1(x)e): x \in X\}$  is the requested isometric copy of  $ X$  inside  $ Z$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ P$  be a probability distribution defined on the Borel sets of the real line. Suppose that  $ P$  is symmetric with respect to the origin, absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, and its density function  $ p$  is zero outside the interval  $ [\minus{}1,1]$  and inside this interval it is between the positive numbers  $ c$  and  $ d$  ( $ c < d$ ). Prove that there is no distribution whose convolution square equals  $ P$ . 

*T. F. Mori, G. J. Szekely*
solution_md:
I think that one could do something along these lines:
So a random variable  $ S$  has a density  $ 0 < c < D(x) < d$  with support  $ [ \minus{} 1; \plus{} 1]$ , and one tries to find two iid random variables  $ X_1,X_2$  such that  $ S \equal{} X_1 \plus{} X_2$ . Clearly  $ X_1$  and  $ X_2$  have their support equal to  $ [ \minus{} \frac12;\frac12]$ , are symetric (!), and have no atom.
Notice that if  $ X_1 \plus{} X_2 \in [ \minus{} 1; \minus{} 1 \plus{} \epsilon]$  then  $ X_1,X_2 \in [ \minus{} \frac12; \minus{} \frac12 \plus{} \epsilon]$ . So if  $ \mu$  is the measure  $ \mu([a;b]) \equal{} P(X_1 \in [a;b]) \equal{} P(X_1 \in [a;b]) \equal{} \mu([ \minus{} b; \minus{} a])$  then
\[ \mu([ \minus{} \frac12; \minus{} \frac12 \plus{} \epsilon])^2 \geq \int_{[ \minus{} 1; \minus{} 1 \plus{} \epsilon]} D(x)dx \geq c \epsilon
\]
Hence one could think of  $ X_1,X_2$  as random variables with density that looks like  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt {x \plus{} 1}}$  near  $ \minus{} 1^ \plus{}$  et like  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt {x \minus{} 1}}$  near  $ 1^ \minus{}$ . Thus, the density  $ \mu*\mu$  of  $ X_1 \plus{} X_2$  diverges near  $ 0$ , which is a contradiction since  $ \|D\|_{\infty} < d$ . To make this a little more precise, consider a fixed  $ N$  and
\[ a_k \equal{} \mu([ \minus{} 1 \plus{} \frac {k \minus{} 1}{N}; \minus{} 1 \plus{} \frac {k}{N}[) \equal{} \sqrt {c}(\sqrt {\frac {k}{N}} \minus{} \sqrt {\frac {k \minus{} 1}{N}}) \plus{} u_k
\]
with  $ \sum_1^n u_k \geq 0$  for all  $ 1 \leq n \leq N$ 

Now, because
\[ P(X_1 \plus{} X_2 \in [ \minus{} \frac1N; \frac1N]) \geq \sum_{k \equal{} 1}^N \mu([ \minus{} 1 \plus{} \frac {k \minus{} 1}{N}; \minus{} 1 \plus{} \frac {k}{N}[).\mu([1 \minus{} \frac {k \minus{} 1}{N};1 \minus{} \frac {k}{N}[)
\]
then one should have:
\[ \frac {2d}{N} \geq \sum_{k \equal{} 1}^N a_k^2
\]
which is false. Of course:
\[ \sum_{k \equal{} 1}^N a_k^2 \equal{} \frac {c}{N} \sum_1^N (\sqrt {k} \minus{} \sqrt {k \minus{} 1})^2 \plus{} \sum_1^N u_k^2 \plus{} 2 \sqrt {c} \sum_1^N u_k(\sqrt {k} \minus{} \sqrt {k \minus{} 1})
\]
and  $ \sum_1^N u_k(\sqrt {k} \minus{} \sqrt {k \minus{} 1}) \geq 0$  since  $ (\sqrt {k} \minus{} \sqrt {k \minus{} 1})$  decrease to  $ 0$  and  $ \sum_1^n u_k \geq 0$  for all  $ n$ . This is why
\[ \frac {2d}{N} \geq \sum_{k \equal{} 1}^N a_k^2 \geq \frac {c}{N} \sum_1^N (\sqrt {k} \minus{} \sqrt {k \minus{} 1})^2 \approx C\frac {\ln(N)}{N}
\]
which give the contradiction.

A map  $ F : P(X) \rightarrow P(X)$ , where  $ P(X)$  denotes the set of all subsets of  $ X$ , is called a  $ \textit{closure operation}$  on  $ X$  if for arbitrary  $ A,B \subset X$ , the following conditions hold: 

(i)  $ A \subset F(A);$  

(ii)  $ A \subset B \Rightarrow F(A) \subset F(B);$  

(iii)  $ F(F(A))\equal{}F(A)$ . 

The cardinal number  $ \min \{ |A| : \;A \subset X\ ,\;F(A)\equal{}X\ \}$  is called the  $ \textit{density}$  of  $ F$  and is denoted by  $ d(F)$ . A set  $ H \subset X$  is called  $ \textit{discrete}$  with respect to  $ F$  if  $ u \not \in F(H\minus{}\{ u \})$  holds for all  $ u \in H$ . Prove that if the density of the closure operation  $ F$  is a singular cardinal number, then for any nonnegative integer  $ n$ , there exists a set of size  $ n$  that is discrete with respect to  $ F$ . Show that the statement is not true when the existence of an infinite discrete subset is required, even if  $ F$  is the closure operation of a topological space satisfying the  $ T_1$  separation axiom.

stem_md:

stem_md:
Let  $ G(V,E)$  be a connected graph, and let  $ d_G(x,y)$  denote the length of the shortest path joining  $ x$  and  $ y$  in  $ G$ . Let  $ r_G(x)\equal{} \max \{ d_G(x,y) : \; y \in V \ \}$  for  $ x \in V$ , and let  $ r(G)\equal{} \min \{ r_G(x) : \;x \in V\ \}$ . Show that if  $ r(G) \geq 2$ , then  $ G$  contains a path of length  $ 2r(G)\minus{}2$  as an induced subgraph. 

*V. T. Sos*
solution_md:
Solution 1. Let  $n=r(G)$ , and let  $x$  be a vertex of  $G$  such that  $r_G(x)=n$  and the cardinality of the set  $\{y: d(x, y)=n\}$  is minimum. Let  $x_n$  be a vertex such that  $d\left(x, x_n\right)=n$ , and let  $x=x_0, x_1, y=x_2, \ldots, x_n$  be a path joining  $x$  and  $x_n$ . We show that if  $G$  does not contain a path of length  $2 n-2$  as an induced subgraph then  $r_G(y)=n$  and that  $d(x, z)<n(z \in V)$  implies that  $d(y, z)<n$ , which contradicts the choice of  $x$ , and  $d\left(y, x_n\right)=n-2$ . $r_G(y)=n$  follows from the other statement, so it is sufficient to prove that one.

Since  $d(y, z) \leq d(x, z)+2$ , it is sufficient to consider the cases  $d(x, z)=$   $n-2$  and  $d(x, z)=n-1$ . Let  $x=z_0, z_1, \ldots, z_k=z(k=n-2$  or  $n-1)$  be a path of length  $d(x, z)$  between  $x$  and  $z$ . By the minimality of the paths, if  $x_i=y_j \quad(i>0, j>0)$  then  $i=j$ , but then the length of the path  $y=x_2, \ldots, x_i=z_i, \ldots, z_k$  is at most  $k$  and we are done. Similarly, if  $x_i z_j$  is an edge of the graph, then  $i-1 \leq j$ . If this is an edge of  $G$  and  $i \geq 2$ , then the length of the path  $y=x_2, \ldots, x_i, z_j, \ldots, z_k$  is at most  $k(<n)$  and if  $i=1$  then the length of the path  $y, x_1, z_j, \ldots, z_k$  is  $k-j+2$ . We are done if either  $j \geq 2$  or  $k=n-2$ , so we may assume that  $j=1$  and  $k=n-1$  and then  $x_n, \ldots, x_1, z_1, \ldots, z_k$  is an induced path of length  $2 n-2$ . If  $G$  does not contain any edge  $x_i z_j$ , then  $x_n, \ldots, x_1, x_0, z_1, \ldots, z_k$  is an induced path of length  $2 n-2$  or  $2 n-1$ , which we wanted to prove.

Solution 2. (sketch) Every graph  $G$  with  $r(G)=n$  contains a connected, induced subgraph  $G^{\prime}$  such that  $r\left(G^{\prime}\right)=n$  and  $r\left(G^{\prime \prime}\right)<n$  for every connected, induced, proper subgraph  $G^{\prime \prime}$  of  $G^{\prime}$ , and it is sufficient to take such a graph  $G^{\prime}$ .
1. If  $G^{\prime}$  is a path, then its length is  $n-1$ .
2. If  $G^{\prime}-\{x\}$  is not connected, then it has two components and one of them is a path.
3. Let  $C$  be the set of vertices  $x$  such that there is no vertex  $y$  such that  $G-\{y\}$  is not connected and the component of  $G-\{y\}$  containing  $x$  is a path. Then  $C$  induces a 2-connected subgraph.
4. For every vertex  $x \in C$ , we get a path of length  $k$  if we delete the vertices of the component of  $G-\{x\}$  containing  $C-\{x\}$ .
5. For every vertex  $x \in C$ , there is exactly one vertex  $y \in C$  such that  $d(x, y)=n-k$ .
6. For such a pair of vertices  $\{x, y\}$ , the graph induced by  $C-\{x, y\}$  is not connected, that is, joining  $x$  and  $y$  in two components, we get a cycle of length at least  $2(n-k)$ .
7. For some  $0 \leq k \leq n-2$ , the graph  $G^{\prime}$  is a cycle of length  $2(n-k)$  with a pending path of length  $k$  at each vertex of it.
Remarks.
1. The second solution shows that the statement is sharp; it is false for path of length  $2 n-1$ .
2. There is an infinite graph  $G$  such that  $r(G)=3$ , and every induced path in  $G$  is of length at most 3.

stem_md:
Let \[ f(n)=  \sum_{p|n , \;p^{\alpha} \leq n < p^{\alpha+1} \ } p^{\alpha} .\] Prove that \[ \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty}f(n) \frac{ \log \log n}{n \log n}=1 .\] 

*P. Erdos*
solution_md:
Solution. It is well known that the number  $\omega(n)$  of different prime divisors of  $n$  is at most  $(1+o(1)) \cdot(\log n) /(\log \log n)$ . Since obviously  $f(n) \leq n \omega(n)$ , we conclude immediately that  $$ \underset{n \rightarrow \infty}{\limsup } f(n) \frac{\log \log n}{n \log n} \leq 1 . $$  To prove the other inequality, we select a parameter  $k$  and try to compose an  $n$  from primes below  $k$ . The number of these primes is  $\sim k / \log k$  by the prime number theorem. Now take another number  $m$ , which we shall later specify in terms of  $k$ . Every prime  $p \leq k$  has a power between  $m$  and  $\mathrm{km}$ . We cover the interval  $[m, \mathrm{~km}]$  with intervals of the type  $[m(1+$   $\left.\varepsilon)^{i-1}, m(1+\varepsilon)^i\right]$ , where  $i=1, \ldots,[c \log k], c$  depends only on  $\varepsilon$ . For a suitable  $i$ , there are at least  $l=\left[c_1 k /(\log k)^2\right]$  primes  $p \leq k$  that have a power in this interval. We select  $l$  of them; let  $P$  be the product of these  $l$  primes. If  $P<\varepsilon m$ , then there is a multiple of  $P$  in the interval  $\left[m(1+\varepsilon)^i, m(1+\varepsilon)^{i+1}\right]$ ; let  $n$  be such a multiple. We have  $$ f(n) \geq \operatorname{lm}(1+\varepsilon)^{i-1}>\ln (1-\varepsilon)^2 . $$  We have to estimate  $n$  in terms of  $l$ . We have  $P \leq k^l$  anyway; thus the choice  $m=k^{l+1}$  guarantees  $P<\varepsilon m$  if  $k>1 / \varepsilon$ . Further, we have  $$ n \leq m(1+\varepsilon)^{i+1}<k m(1+\varepsilon)^2<k^{l+2}, $$  hence  $l \geq(\log n) /(\log k)-2$ . Also  $n<k^k$  from the above inequality. Thus  $k \gg(\log n) / \log \log n$ , and we obtain  $$ l \geq(1-\varepsilon) \frac{\log n}{\log \log n}, \quad f(n)>(1-\varepsilon)^3 \frac{n \log n}{\log \log n}, $$  for large  $k$ .
Remark. It can be shown that  $$ \max _{n \leq x} f(n) \sim \frac{n \log n}{\log \log n} $$

stem_md:
Suppose that  $ K$  is a compact Hausdorff space and  $ K\equal{} \cup_{n\equal{}0}^{\infty}A_n$ , where  $ A_n$  is metrizable and  $ A_n \subset A_m$  for  $ n<m$ . Prove that  $ K$  is metrizable. 


*Z. Balogh*
solution_md:
The idea is to reduce the problem to the case when  $A_n$  are closed and afterwards to prove it for this special case.
Denote by  $d_m$  the metrict of  $A_m\,,m\in \mathbb{N}$ . WLOG, we can assume  $d_m(x,y)\leq 1, \forall x,y\in A_m$ , otherwise we can take  $\overline{d_m}=\min\{d_m,1\}$ .
EDIT>: Proceeding, will we need that: $d_{m_1}(x,y) \ge C d_{m_2} (x,y) \,, \forall x,y\in A_{m_1} \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \text{(1)}$ for any  $m_2>m_1$ , where  $C$  is a constant depending only on  $m_1$  and  $m_2$ . It is not guaranteed, but we can ensure it by changing the metrics and  leaving the induced topologies intact. Namely let us define:
\[\overline{d_n}(x,y)=\sum_{m\ge n}2^{n-m}d_m(x,y)\,\, \forall x,y\in A_n  \]
Clearly  $\overline{d_n} \ge \frac{1}{2} \overline{d_{n+1}}$ . Thus, WLOG we can assume  $\text{(1)}$  is true.
>end of EDIT.
Fix  $n$ . To show that  $\overline{A_n}$  is metrizable, it is natural somehow to extend by continuity the metric  $d_m$  over  $A_m\,,m\geq n$  to a metric over  $\overline{A_n}$ . The problem is that it can happen it couldn't be done for some set of "bad" points of  $\overline{A_n}\setminus A_m$ . We will prove that when  $m\to\infty$  these "bad" points will eventually vanish. 
Let us denote by  $B_{n,m}\,\,, n\le m$  the set of these "bad" points, i.e.: $ B_{n,m}=\left\{x\in \overline{A_n}\mid \exists \varepsilon>0\,,\forall U\in\tau(K),x\in U,\, \exists u_1,u_2\in U\cap A_m\,,\,d_{m}(u_1,u_2)>\varepsilon  \right\} $ .

Some properties of  $B_{n,m}$ 1)  $B_{n,m} \subset \overline{A_n}\setminus A_m$ 2)  $B_{n,m}$  is closed. 
3)  $B_{n,m_{2}}\subset B_{n,m_{1}}\,,\, m_2>m_1 $ To prove 2) let  $b$  is a limit point of  $B_{n,m}$ , we must show  $b\in B_{n,m} $ . Clearly  $b\in \overline{A_n} $ . Take some neighbourhood  $U$  of  $b$ . There exists  $b_1\in B_{n,m}$  with  $b_1\in U$ . Since  $K$  is compact and Hausdorff, it is regular (in fact it is normal), thus we can separate  $b_1$  from  $K\setminus U$ , in particular there exists open set  $V$ ,  $b_1\in V\,, V\subset U$ . Applying the definition of  $B_{n,m}$ , with respect to  $b_1\,,V$  we establish the existence of "not close"point  $u_1,u_2\in U$ , thus  $b\in B_{n,m}$ .
3) can be proved in a similar way.
Now, since  $B_{n,n}\supset B_{n,n+1}\supset \ldots$  ,  $B_{n,m}$  are compact and  $\bigcap_{m} B_{n,m}=\emptyset$ , it follows  $B_{n,m}=\emptyset$  for all sufficiently big  $m$ . Then, we can extend by continuity the metric  $d_m$  over  $\overline{A_n}$ .

It remains to consider the case  $A_n$  are closed. The idea is to embed  $K$  into the cube  $[0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$  with the product topology. 
Since each  $A_n$  is a compact metric space, it is separable. (one can consider the finite  $1/k$  nets,  $k=1,2,\ldots$ ). Let  $a^{(n)}_i\in A_n \,,i\in\mathbb{N}$  be a dense set in  $A_n$ . 
Define functions  $f^{(n)}_i :A_n \to [0,1]\,, f^{(n)}_i(x)=d_n(x,a^{(n)}_i )$ . They are continuous functions on a closed sets of normal topological spase  $K$ . Applying the Tietze extension theorem, we can extend  $f^{(n)}_i $  to continuous map  $f^{(n)}_i : K\to [0,1]$ . Let us denote  $F=\{f^{(n)}_i \mid n,i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ . We consider the map:  $\phi : K\to [0,1]^F\,, \phi(x)=\langle f(x) \rangle_{f\in F}$ . 
One can check straightforwardly that:

1)  $\phi$  is continuous. ( considering  $[0,1]^F$  with the product topology)
2)  $\phi$  is injective.
3)  $\phi$  is open mapping. (in  $\phi(K)$  with the induced topology)

It follows that  $\phi$  is a homeomorphism between  $K$  and  $\phi(K)$ . Since  $[0,1]^F$  is metrizable, the result follows.

stem_md:
Let  $ p_0,p_1,\ldots$  be a probability distribution on the set of nonnegative integers. Select a number according to this distribution and repeat the selection independently until either a zero or an already selected number is obtained. Write the selected numbers in a row in order of selection without the last one. Below this line, write the numbers again in increasing order. Let  $ A_i$  denote the event that the number  $ i$  has been selected and that it is in the same place in both lines. Prove that the events  $ A_i \;(i\equal{}1,2,\ldots)$  are mutually independent, and  $ P(A_i)\equal{}p_i$ . 


*T. F. Mori*
solution_md:
We will prove that for any finite set  $ S \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0 $ , we have    $$ \mathbb{P}\left(\prod_{i \in S} A_i \right) = \prod_{i \in S} p_i. $$  (Side note: the probability of obtaining an infinite sequence is  $ 0 $ .)  

To do this, we introduce a altered process. In addition to stopping whenever we select  $ 0 $  or a number that has already been obtained, we will also stop when we select any number in  $ S $ .  

Call an outcome sequence of the original process  $ S $ -valid if it contains all elements of  $ S $ . Let  $ u $  be an  $ S $ -valid sequence. Removing these elements from  $ u $  yields a sequence  $ u' $  in the altered process. Notice that  $ u $  is uniquely determined by  $ u' $ , thus we have a bijection between the set of  $ S $ -valid sequences and the outcome sequences of the altered process.  

Since selections happen independently, the probability of obtaining any  $ S $ -valid sequence  $ u $  in the original process is    $$ \mathbb{P}(u) = \mathbb{P}_{\text{altered}}(u') \cdot \prod_{i \in S} p_i. $$  Summing over all outcome sequences in the altered process gives  $$ \mathbb{P}\left(\prod_{i \in S} A_i \right) = \prod_{i \in S} p_i. $$  This concludes the proof.  $ \square $

stem_md:
Let  $ f : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  be a twice differentiable,  $ 2 \pi$ -periodic even function. Prove that if \[ f''(x)\plus{}f(x)\equal{}\frac{1}{f(x\plus{} 3 \pi /2 )}\] holds for every  $ x$ , then  $ f$  is  $ \pi /2$ -periodic. 


*Z. Szabo, J. Terjeki*
solution_md:
Since  $f$  is even, we get that \[\frac{1}{f(x+3\pi/2)}=f''(x)+f(x) = f''(-x)+f(-x)=\frac{1}{f(-x+3\pi/2)}=\frac{1}{f(x-3\pi/2)}\]

Therefore  $f$  is  $3\pi$ -periodic and  $2\pi$ -periodic, therefore  $f$  must be  $\pi$ -periodic
That means 
\begin{align*}
&f''(x)+f(x)=\frac{1}{f(x+\pi/2)}
&f''(x+\pi/2)+f(x+\pi/2)=\frac{1}{f(x+\pi)}=\frac{1}{f(x)}\
\end{align*}
That means that \[f''(x)f(x+\pi/2)-f''(x+\pi/2)f(x)=0 \Rightarrow (f'(x)f(x+\pi/2)-f(x)f'(x+\pi/2))'=0\]
Therefore \[f'(x)f(x+\pi/2)-f(x)f'(x+\pi/2) = c\]
Since  $f(x+\pi/2)=f(x-\pi/2)$  ( $f$  is even and has period  $\pi$ ), by setting  $x\rightarrow -x$  we get that \[-f'(x)f(x+\pi/2)+f(x)f'(x+\pi/2) = c\]

So, we got that  $c=0$ .
\begin{align*}
&f'(x)f(x+\pi/2)-f(x)f'(x+\pi/2) = 0 
\Rightarrow &(f(x)/f(x+\pi/2))'=0 
\Rightarrow &f(x)=kf(x+\pi/2)=k^2f(x+\pi)=k^2f(x) 
\Rightarrow &k^2=1 \Rightarrow k\in\{1,-1\}\
\end{align*}
Since  $f$  doesn't vanish and is continuous,  $f$  must have the same sign on  $\mathbb{R}$ . That forces  $k$  to be  $1$ , which means  $f$  has period  $\pi/2$ .

Let  $ g : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  be a continuous function such that  $ x+g(x)$  is strictly monotone (increasing or
decreasing), and let  $ u : [0,\infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  be a bounded and continuous function such that \[ u(t)+  \int_{t-1}^tg(u(s))ds\] is constant on  $ [1,\infty)$ . Prove that the limit  $ \lim_{t\rightarrow \infty} u(t)$  exists. 


*T. Krisztin*
solution_md:
Define f(x) = x + g(x). Since x + g(x) is monotone, so f'(x) > 0 \ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}. We have the equation: u(t) + \int_{t-1}^{t} g(u(s)) \, ds = c This implies: u(t) - \int_{t-1}^{t} u(s) \, ds + \int_{t-1}^{t} \left( u(s) + g(u(s)) \right) ds = c Taking the limit as t \to \infty: \lim_{t \to \infty} u(t) - \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_{t-1}^{t} u(s) \, ds + \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_{t-1}^{t} \left( u(s) + g(u(s)) \right) ds = c Since u(s) + g(u(s)) is monotonic, we have: \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_{t-1}^{t} \left( u(s) + g(u(s)) \right) ds \text{ is finite, say } M Also, \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_{t-1}^{t} u(s) \, ds = 0, as u(s) is bounded. Therefore: \lim_{t \to \infty} u(t) + M = c Thus, \lim_{t \to \infty} u(t) = c - M = N, which shows that \lim_{t \to \infty} u(t) exists.

stem_md:
Prove that if the function  $ f : \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow [0,1]$  is continuous and its average on every circle of radius  $ 1$  equals the function value at the center of the circle, then  $ f$  is constant. 


*V. Totik*
solution_md:
An idea using fourier transform of distributions is shown in the link above. The other approach, discussed there, to show that  $f$  is harmonic, maybe wiil be more difficult than the problem itself. Moreover, I have a doubt about it being true; I mean, given only "the radius  $1$  mean value property" is rather not enough to say the function is harmonic!?
A discrete version of this problem was given at Bulgarian TST for the Balkan MO (2003). "In every knot of  $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$  lattice is written a real number between  $0$  and  $1$  with the property every number is the average of its four neighbours. Show that all numbers are equal". 
You can see [here](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=41&t=5327) for many comments and various ideas including using the Krein-Milman theorem, random walks, etc. 
I'd like to show here how the idea of [the official solution of the discrete version](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?p=2832968#p2832968) (which btw is pretty elementary) can be adapted in this continuous case.

Suppose on the contrary  $f$  is not constant. Then there exist  $x_1,x_2\in \mathbb{R}^{2}\,,\|x_2-x_1\|=1\,,\, f(x_2) > f(x_1)$ . Let us denote  $\Delta f(x) := f(x+h) - f(x)$ , where  $h=x_2-x_1$ . We have:
(i)  $\Delta f(x)$  also satisfies "radius  $1$  mean value property".
(ii)  $\Delta f(x)$  is also bounded (between -1 and 1).
Since  $\Delta f(x_1) > 0$ , and because of (ii), we conclude  $\infty > M := \sup_{x\in \mathbb{R}} \Delta f(x) > 0$ .

Let us fix  $\varepsilon >0$ , and choose  $x_0$  s.t.  $M-\varepsilon < \Delta f(x_0) \leq M$ . Imagine for a moment that  $\Delta f(x)$  is smooth enough, say Lipschitz. Thus, having  $\Delta f(x_0)$  is close to  $M$  and "radius  $1$  mean value property" will imply  $\Delta f(x_0+h)$  is close to  $M$  too, i.e.  $M-K \varepsilon < \Delta f(x_0+h) \leq M$ , where  $K$  is a constant, not depending on  $\varepsilon$  or  $x_0$ . 
Thus, by induction, we obtain:
\[ \Delta f(x_0+j h) > M-K^{j}\varepsilon \,,\, j=0,1,\ldots \]
Therefore:
\[ f(x_0+j h) - f(x_0)= \sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\Delta f(x_0+i h) > j M - \varepsilon \sum_{i=1}^{j} K^{i} \]
Now, look at the above inequality. The LHS is bounded, while we can make the RHS as big as we want, taking  $\varepsilon$  small enough. Thus, we get a contradiction.

Well, going back, the only obstacle to carry out this idea is that we can't be sure  $\Delta f$  is a Lipschitz function. To get around it, we could average  $f$ . So, the proof goes like that:
Suppose  $f(x_2)> f(x_1)$ , where  $\|x_2-x_1\|=1$ . Let  $\overline{f}(x)= \frac{1}{|B_r|}\int_{B_r} f(x+u)\,d u$ , where  $B_r$  is the ball with radius  $r$ , centered at the origin. We can take  $r$  small enough, so that  $\overline{f}(x_2) > \overline{f}(x_1)$ . Of course  $\overline{f}$  is bounded. By changing order of integration, one can check that  $\overline{f}$  also satisfies the "radius  $1$  mean value property". And the most important thing is that  $\overline{f}$  is a Lipschitz function, which follows from the boundness of  $f$ . It means  $\Delta \overline{f} (x)$  is Lipschitz  too, and the rest goes as above.

stem_md:
Prove that if  $ E \subset \mathbb{R}$  is a bounded set of positive Lebesgue measure, then for every  $ u < 1/2$ , a point  $ x\equal{}x(u)$  can be found so that \[ |(x\minus{}h,x\plus{}h) \cap E| \geq uh\] and \[ |(x\minus{}h,x\plus{}h) \cap (\mathbb{R} \setminus E)| \geq uh\] for all sufficiently small positive values of  $ h$ . 


*K. I. Koljada*
solution_md:
Solution:
We will prove problem for every  $u<1/4$ , let  $u=1/4-\varepsilon$  for  $\varepsilon>0$ . First let's find interval  $I^1:\frac{|I\cap E|}{|I|}=\frac{|I\cap (\mathbb{R}\setminus E)|}{|I|}=\frac{1}{2}$ . After Lebesgue's density theorem we get that there exists point  $a:\exists lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{|(a-h,a+h)\cap E|}{2h}=1$ , so there exists  $h:\frac{|(a-h,a+h)\cap E|}{2h}>\frac{1}{2}$ , E is bounded set, so there exists point  $b:\frac{|(a-h,a+h)\cap E|}{2h}=0<\frac{1}{2}$ , denote function  $\phi:[a,b]\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ , where  $\phi(x)=\frac{|(x-h,x+h)\cap E|}{2h}$ ,  $\phi\in C([a,b])$ , so there exist point  $c\in (a,b):\frac{|(c-h,c+h)\cap E|}{2h}=\frac{1}{2}$ , so  $I^1=(c-h,c+h)$ . Let intervals  $I_1,I_2:|I_1|=|I_2|=\frac{|I^1|}{2},I_1\sqcup I_2=I^1$ , easy to see that  $min(\frac{I_1\cap E}{|I_1|},\frac{I_2\cap E}{|I_2|})\leq \frac{1}{2}\leq max(\frac{I_1\cap E}{|I_1|},\frac{I_2\cap E}{|I_2|})$ , so there exist interval  $I^2:\frac{|I^2\cap E|}{|I^2|}=\frac{1}{2}-\delta,|\delta| \leq2\varepsilon,[I^2]\subset  I^1,|I^2|=|I_1|=|I_2|=\frac{|I^1|}{2}$ . Like the same construct intervals  $I^2,I^3,...$ , where  $[I_{n+1}]\subset  I_n, |I_{n+1}|=\frac{|I_n|}{2}\ \forall n$ , let  $x(u)=\cap_{i=1}^{\infty}I^{i}$ ,  $x(u)\in I^1$ , so there exist  $\tau >0:O_{\tau}(x(u))\subset I^1$ , for every  $h<\tau$  there exist  $n_h\in N:I^{n_h}\subset O_h(x(u)),|I^{n_h}|\geq \frac{h}{2}$ , so  $|(x(u)-h,x(u)+h)\cap E|\geq |I^{n_h}\cap E|\geq (\frac{1}{2}-2\varepsilon)|I^{n_h}|\geq (\frac{1}{4}-\varepsilon)h=uh$ , like the same  $|(x(u)-h,x(u)+h)\cap (\mathbb{R}\setminus E)|\geq uh$ . done

stem_md:
**3.** Let  $a$  and  $b$  be positive integers such that when dividing them by any prime  $p$ , the remainder of  $a$  is always less than or equal to the remainder of  $b$ . Prove that  $a=b$ . (**N.16**)
[P. Erdos, P. P. Pálify]
solution_md:
At first I thought this solution was (ex)^2 (extremely extraordinary),  but I think that after reviewing some ideas on classical prime estimates it makes a lot of sense (still it is quite incredible regardless). 
---------------------------------
Let  $p$  big, then we can conclude that  $a < b$  (ignore the trivial equality case), now if  $\frac{b}{2} < a$ , then we can notice that we may let  $b \rightarrow b - a$ , as the problem condition will be preserved anyway. So, assume that  $\frac{b}{2} \ge a$ , now we only need to show that there's no pair satisfying this. 

Now, in a similar fashion to Bertrand Postulate, we will track where the issue of this statement is by using the binomial  $\binom{b}{a}$  to convey the contradiction by using the Legendre formula and size due to a seemingly microscopic optimization (but due to the very strong conditions that we got on  $b$ , and  $a$  it will be enough anyway). Notice that the numerator and denominator will be the product of  $b$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $b - a + 1$  and  $1$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $a$  respectively, let these products be  $A$ , and  $B$ . Denote  $A(p^k)$  and  $B(p^k)$  the number of terms divisable by  $p^k$  on each product, then 
\[A(p^k) = \lfloor\frac{a}{p^k}\rfloor \text{ and } B(p^k) = \lfloor\frac{b}{p^k}\rfloor - \lfloor\frac{b-a}{p^k}\rfloor\]
notice that the relation  $B(p^k) - A(p^k) \in \{0, 1\}$  (this is just algebra), now the gist is that **Claim**.  $A(p) \ge B(p)$  for every  $p$ . **Proof**. Notice that if we go decreasing  $1$  from  $a$ , the first multiple of  $p$  that will appear will be  $a - a \mod p$ , similar for  $b$ , but because by the problem condition  $a \mod p \le b \mod p$  and the fact that both sequences have the same size we are done.  $\Box$ With the other observations, we have  $A(p) = B(p)$ , so we can conclude that  $p > a$  won't contribute to the terms  $A$  or  $B$ . This observation will also render another incredible deep observation, so we have that 
\[A = \prod_{p \le a}p^{A(p) + A(p^2) + \dots} \text{ and } B = \prod_{p \le a}p^{B(p) + B(p^2) + \dots}\]
then  $\binom{b}{a} = \frac{B}{A} = \prod_{p \le a}p^{B(p^2) - A(p^2) + B(p^3) - A(p^3) + \dots}$ Let  $m(p)$  the largest number such that  $B(p^k) \neq 0$ , then we conclude that the above is a divisor of  $\prod_{p \le a}p^{m(p)-1}$ , rearranging this expression, implies that 
\[\frac{B}{\prod_{p\le a}p^{m(p)}} \mid \frac{A}{\prod_{p \le a} p}\]
This clearly can't happen, because the RHS will be atmost  $a^{a - \pi(a)}$ , and in the LHS every term that wasn't cancelled in the denominator will be bigger than  $a$ , and there will be more than  $a-\pi(a)$  of them, as desired  $\Box$

For example, what about  $a=3,b=9$ ? The same primes divide them, but they're not equal. A prime greater than  $9$  won't do it either. Your argument fails here. (It's not a counterexample to the original problem; the remainders mod  $7$  flip the order)
It is true only when  $b$  is square free.

Clearly  $a\leq b$  (to see this, take  $p$  greater than both of  $a$  and  $b$ ).

Now, let us assume that  $a<b$ . [Theorem of Sylvester and Schur](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1934-01.pdf) tells us that there exists a prime  $p > \min(a, b-a)$  such that  $p \mid {b\choose k}$ . This prime contradicts the assumption, as we will now show, and so  $a=b$ .

Since  $p\mid b(b-1)\dots (b-k+1)$ , the residue of  $b$ , which we will denote by  $r$ , is not greater than  $k-1$ . Now let us consider two cases:
I)  $a\leq \frac b2$ We then have  $k=a<p$ , so the residue of  $a$  is  $a$ , which is greater than  $r$ .

II)  $a > \frac b2$  
Now we have  $k=b-a$ . Write  $b=qp+r$  and we obtain  $$ a-p(q-1)=(b-k)-p(q-1)=p+r-k $$  and  $p+r-k\leq p-1$ , so  $p+r-k$  is the residue of  $a$ , and as it can be seen, it is larger than  $r$ .

This concludes the proof.

This is a very nice problem!
