stem_md: Determine all finite groups  $G$  that have an automorphism  $f$  such that  $H\not\subseteq f(H)$  for all proper subgroups  $H$  of  $G$ . [B. Kovacs]
solution_md:
We will prove that these groups are exactly  $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$  for some prime  $p$ . In what follows, we let  $G$  and  $f$  be a group and an automorphism with the above property.

To begin, suppose  $f$  has a (nontrivial) fixed point. Since the cyclic subgroup generated by that element is fixed under  $f$ , it must coincide with  $G$ , so  $G\cong\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ . Since in this case every proper subgroup is preserved,  $n$  must be prime.

Now suppose  $f$  has no nontrivial fixed points. This implies that the function  $g(x)=x^{-1}f(x)$  is injective, and thus surjective as well.
Consider  $H$  a Sylow  $p$ -group.  $f(H)$  is also a Sylow  $p$ -group and thus conjugate to  $H$  by some  $x$ , i.e.  $f(H)=xHx^{-1}$ . By the above claim, there is a  $y\in G$  s.t.  $y^{-1}f(y)=x^{-1}$ , so   $$ f(yHy^{-1})=f(y)f(H)f(y)^{-1}=yx^{-1}f(H)xy^{-1}=yHy^{-1}. $$   Since  $yHy^{-1}$  is nontrivial and preserved,  $yHy^{-1}$  must be  $G$  and thus  $|G| =p^n$  for some prime  $p$ . Finally, by the class equation,  $Z(G)$  must be nontrivial, and is obviously preserved, so  $Z(G)=G$ , implying that  $G$  is abelian. The latter makes the set  $M=\{x\in G\mid x^p=e\}$  a subgroup, and since it's preserved as well,  $M=G$  and thus all elements of  $G$  have order  $p$ . We have thus obtained that  $G$  is  $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$ .

Now we shall see why all such groups have an automorphism with no invariant proper subgroups. Notice that we can extend the group automorphism  $f$  to a vector space automorphism,  $T:\mathbb{F}_p^n\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_p^n$ . The condition on  $f$  translates to  $T$  having no invariant subspace. In general, it's well-known that there is a bijection between the invariant subspaces of  $T$  and the irreducible factors of  $p_T$ , its characteristic polynomial. Thus taking any irreducible polynomial  $P\in\mathbb{F}_p[X]$  of degree  $n$  and letting  $T$  be described by the companion matrix  $C(P)$ , we get ourselves a linear map with no invariant subspace.

stem_md: Let  $p_1$  and  $p_2$  be positive real numbers. Prove that there exist functions  $f_i\colon \mathbb R \rightarrow \mathbb R$  such that the smallest positive period of  $f_i$  is  $p_i\, (i=1, 2)$ , and  $f_1-f_2$  is also periodic. [J. Riman]
solution_md:
Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be positive real numbers. Prove that there exist functions $f_i\colon \mathbb R \rightarrow \mathbb R$ such that the smallest positive period of $f_i$ is $p_i\, (i=1, 2)$ , and $f_1-f_2$ is also periodic. [J. Riman]
Does this work? Note that the claim is trivially true if $\frac{p_1}{p_2} \in \mathbb{Q}$ . From now assume $i \in {1,2}$ . Suppose $\frac{p_1}{p_2} \not \in \mathbb{Q}$ . Define [center] $\[f_i =\ \begin{cases} A_{3-i} &: x = A_1p_1 + A_2p_2 \: \text{for} \: A_i \in \mathbb{Z} 1 &: \text{else} \end{cases} \]$ [/center] By our assumption, such a function exists. We claim $f_1, f_2$ satisfy the given conditions. Indeed note that $f_i$ is periodic with fundamental period $p_i$ . Also, note that the function $f_1 - f_2$ is periodic with period $p_1 + p_2$ . $\blacksquare$

Take  $f_2(x)=x\,,\, x\in[0,p_2)$  , and extended periodically on  $\mathbb{R}$ . So far, so good. We have done  $1/2$  of the job :). Denote  $g(x)=f_1(x)-f_2(x)$ . Let  $t$  be a real number such that  $t\neq r_1 p_1 + r_2p_2$  for any rationals  $r_1,r_2$ . Our aim is to construct  $g$  with period  $t$  and in the same time  $g+f_2$  to have (minimal) period  $p_1$ . 

Let's define a relation  $\sim$  on  $\mathbb{R}$  as  $x\sim y$  iff  $x-y=m t+np_1 + kp_2 $  for some integer  $m,n,k$ . Then  $\sim$  is a equivalence relation. Take a representative of each equivalence clase and let it be  $\mathbb{R}/\sim$ . Define arbitrary  $f_1$  on  $\mathbb{R}/\sim$  just under condition to be an injection. 

Let us take some  $x_0\in \mathbb{R}/\sim$  and spread  $f_1(x_0)$  on the the equivalence class  $[x_0]=\{x : x\sim x_0\}$ . First we define  $f_1$  on the set  $A_0=\{x_0+mp_1+np_2 : m,n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$  complying the condition:  $f_1\restriction_{A_0}$  takes pairwise different values except when  $x-y=mp_1, x,y\in A_0,\,m\in \mathbb{Z}$ , for which  $f_1(x)=f_1(y)$ . 

That can be easily done inductively on  $n$  and  $m$ . Thus  $f_1$ , respectively  $g=f_1-f_2$  is defined correctly on  $A_0$ . Now, for any  $m\in \mathbb{Z}, x\in A_0$ , we define  $g(x+mt)=g(x)$ . Due to the choice of  $t$ ,  $(A_0+m_1t)\cap (A_0+m_2t) =\emptyset$ , so we rule out the possible crashes. 

Thus,  $g$  is defined on  $[x_0]$ , and hence on the  $\mathbb{R}$ . 
Because of the construction,  $g$  is periodic with period  $t$  (possibly not the minimal one),  $f_1$  is periodic with period  $p_1$  and all other periods of  $f_1$  are multiple of  $p_1$ .           **Comment**: The motivation is to try consecutively defining  $f_1,f_2$ . First, define them on a single point  $x_0$  and see the dependencies it should spread out on the set  $x_0 + mt + np_1 +kp_2$ . Then, if one can deal with that set, the solution could be completed using transfinite induction, but I preferred a clearer way as above. 
Such approaches, using AC, usually leads to weird functions, like  $f_1$ , but probably it cannot be done without AC.

stem_md: Let  $\frac{2}{\sqrt5+1}\leq p < 1$ , and let the real sequence  $\{ a_n \}$  have the following property: for every sequence  $\{ e_n \}$  of  $0$ 's and  $\pm 1$ 's for which  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty e_np^n=0$ , we also have  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty e_na_n=0$ . Prove that there is a number  $c$  such that  $a_n=cp^n$  for all  $n$ . [Z. Daroczy, I. Katai]
solution_md:
Let  $(\lambda_n)$  be a positive strictly deceasing sequence. 
Call it  $\textbf{\textit{interval filling}}$  if  $S=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\lambda_i < \infty$  and for every  $x \in [0,S]$  there is a sequence  $(\varepsilon_n)$  of  $0$ 's and  $1$ 's  such that   $$ x=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_i\lambda_i $$  <details><summary>Lemma 1</summary>If a sequence  $(\lambda_n)$  satisfies  $S=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\lambda_i < \infty$  and  $\lambda_n \leqslant \sum_{i=n+1}^{\infty}\lambda_i$  then it is interval filling. $\textbf{Proof}$ Let  $x \in [0,S]$  
Define  $(\varepsilon_n)$  inductively as follows:  $$  
\varepsilon_n = \begin{cases} 
0 & \text{if   } \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \varepsilon_i \lambda_i+\lambda_n \geqslant x  
1 &\text{if    } \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \varepsilon_i \lambda_i +\lambda_n < x 
\end{cases}  $$  One can easily check that this sequence works.</details>

<details><summary>Corollary of lemma 1</summary>For  $\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}+1}\leqslant \delta < 1$ , the sequence  $$ \delta, \delta^2, \dots, \delta^{n-1}, \delta^{n+1}, \delta^{n+2}, \dots  $$  is interval filling for any natural number  $n$ .</details>

<details><summary>Lemma 2</summary>Let  $ A$  and  $B$  be two nonempty sets that partition the natural numbers, and let  $2/(\sqrt{5}+1) \leqslant \delta <1$ .
Then, there exist nonempty sets  $A' \subseteq A$  and  $B' \subseteq B$  such that  $$ \sum_{i \in A'}\delta^i=\sum_{i \in B'}\delta^i $$    $\textbf{Proof}$ Let  $S = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\delta^i$ , and  $S_A = \sum_{i \in A}\delta^i$ .
Now, choose  $n \in A$  such that  $S_A \leqslant S - \delta^n$ .  We know that the sequence   $$ \delta, \delta^2, \dots, \delta^{n-1}, \delta^{n+1}, \delta^{n+2}, \dots  $$  is interval filling, therefore, we can find a set  $X \subseteq \mathbb{N} \setminus \{n\}$  such that   $$ \sum_{i \in X}\delta^i = S_A = \sum_{i \in A}\delta^i $$  Let  $A' = A \setminus X$  and  $B' = C \setminus A$ .</details>

Now, assume for the sake of contradiction that there is no such  $c$ .
If  $(a_n)$  satisfies the hypothesis, then  $b_n = a_n - cp^n$  does as well.
Let  $A = \{n | b_n > 0\}$  and  $B = \{n | b_n \leqslant 0\}$ .
Our assumption implies that we can find  $c$  such that  $A$  and  $B$  are both nonempty sets.
Applying Lemma 2, we get two sets  $A'$  and  $B'$  such that   $$ \sum_{ i \in A'}p^i=\sum_{ i \in B'}p^i $$  Choose   $$  
\varepsilon_n = \begin{cases} 
1 & \text{if   } n \in A'  
-1 &\text{if    } n \in B' 
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}  $$  Then   $$ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_ip^i=\sum_{i \in A'}p^i - \sum_{i \in B'}p^i = 0 $$  So according to the hypothesis, we must have   $$ 0 = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_ib_i = \sum_{i \in A'}b_i - \sum_{i \in B'}b_i > 0 $$  which contradicts our assumption.

Szabo]
solution_md:
Drawing a sort of similar motivation as the above post of dgrozev we can try out a new approach for the problem.

We can do as follows :**<u>Case 1:</u>**

We also denote:
\[A_{k,n} := A\bigcap \left[\frac{k}{2^n},\frac{k+1}{2^n}\right)\,,\, n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, k=0,1,\dots, 2^n-1\]
The main idea is that we can build the interval  $[0,2)$  by the "bricks"  $A_{k,n}$ , each of them translated infinitely many times. These would imply the same for the interval  $[0,4)$  and the rest would be a routine.

stem_md: Show that if  $k\leq \frac n2$  and  $\mathcal F$  is a family  $k\times k$  submatrices of an  $n\times n$  matrix such that any two intersect then  $$ |\mathcal F|\leq \binom{n-1}{k-1}^2 $$  [Gy. Katona]
solution_md:
Let  $S$  be the family of  $k$ -element subsets of  $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ . Then each member of  $\mathcal{F}$  corresponds to some  $M=(A,B)\in S^2$ . If we consider the possible  $A$ 's for each  $M\in\mathcal{F}$ , we find that any two of them intersect, and the same holds for the possible  $B$ 's. By the [Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Ko%E2%80%93Rado_theorem), at most  $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$  possible  $A$ 's are possible, and the same holds for the  $B$ 's. Assuch,
\[
|\mathcal{F}|\le \binom{n-1}{k-1}^2.
\]
By the way, the bound is sharp, just take all possible  $k\times k$  submatrices containing a fixed entry of the  $n\times n$  matrix.

stem_md:
(a) Prove that for every natural number  $k$ , there are positive integers  $a_1<a_2<\ldots <a_k$  such that  $a_i-a_j$  divides  $a_i$  for all  $1\leq i, j\leq k, i\neq j$ .

(b) Show that there is an absolute constant  $C>0$  such that  $a_1>k^{Ck}$  for every sequence  $a_1,\ldots, a_k$  of numbers that satisfy the above divisibility condition.
[A. Balogh, I. Z. Ruzsa]
solution_md:
Here is the solution which is essentially taken from "Problems from the book":
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The important thing to note is that for any prime  $p$ , we have that  $a_i \equiv a_j \mod p$  already implies  $p \mid a_i,a_j$ . Hence there are at most  $p-1$  elements of our sequence not divisible by  $p$ . Repeating that argument among the multiples of  $p$ , we further conclude that there are at most  $2p-2$  elements not divisible by  $p^2$  etc.
Morally, this already shows that the elements of our sequence must be divisible by quite a lot of numbers and hence must be quite large. Since  $a_k \le 2a_1$ , this should imply that  $a_1$  must be quite large.
The rest of the solution will be to get the necessary analytic estimates to make this idea rigorous.
First of all, we count how often  $p$  divides the product  $a_1\dotsc a_n$ :
At least  $n-(p-1)$  elements must be divisible by  $p$ , at least  $n-2(p-1)$  elements divisible by  $p^2$  etc. So we find that
\[v_p(a_1\dots a_n) \ge (n-(p-1))+(n-2(p-1))+\dots+(n-\lfloor \frac{n}{p-1}\rfloor (p-1))\]
and it's quite easy to show that this is  $\ge \frac{n^2}{2p}-100 \frac{n^{3/2}}{p}$  for all  $p<\sqrt{n}$ .
In particular, for any  $c<\frac{1}{2}$ , this is  $\ge c \cdot\frac{n^2}{p}$  for all  $n$  sufficiently large.
We then obtain that
\[a_1\dots a_n \ge \prod_{p<\sqrt{n}} p^{c\frac{n^2}{p}}=exp\left(cn^2\sum_{p<\sqrt{n}} \frac{\log p}{p}\right)\]
But it is a well-known fact due to Mertens that
\[\sum_{p \le x} \frac{\log p}{p}=\log x+\mathcal{O}(1)\]
so that we have found that
\[a_1\dots a_n > n^{Cn^2}\]
for all  $C<1/4$  and  $n$  sufficiently large. Since  $a_k \le 2a_1$  for all  $k$ , this implies that
\[a_1>n^{Cn}\]
for all  $C<1/4$  and  $n$  sufficiently large.</details>

stem_md: Determine all real numbers  $x$  for which the following statement is true: the field  $\mathbb C$  of complex numbers contains a proper subfield  $F$  such that adjoining  $x$  to  $F$  we get  $\mathbb C$ . [M. Laczkovich]
solution_md:
Let  $\overline{\Bbb Q}$  denote the subfield of  $\Bbb C$  consisting of all algebraic numbers.
The key result we need is that the group of automorphisms  $\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbb C)$  acts transitively on  $\Bbb C\setminus \overline{\Bbb Q}$ , and the restriction map  $\operatorname{Aut}(\Bbb C) \rightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(\overline{\Bbb Q})$  is surjective.
This can be proved by using transcendental basis. I omit the details here.

Using this result, we see that for any  $x \in \Bbb R$  which is not a totally real algebraic number, there exists  $y \in \Bbb C\setminus \Bbb R$  and  $\sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}(\Bbb C)$  such that  $\sigma(y) = x$ . As  $\Bbb C = \Bbb R[y]$  holds, applying  $\sigma$  gives us  $\Bbb C = F[x]$  with  $F = \sigma(\Bbb R)$ .

It remains to consider the case that  $x$  is a totally real algebraic number. We suppose that there exists such an  $F$  and deduce a contradiction.
In this case, the extension  $\Bbb C/F$  has finite degree, hence a theorem of Artin-Schreier says that the degree  $[\Bbb C : F]$  is equal to  $2$ .
A reference for this theorem is [this pdf by K. Conrad](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/artinschreier.pdf).
Let  $\iota$  denote the nontrivial element of  $\operatorname{Gal}(\Bbb C/F)$ .

Write  $E = F \cap \overline{\Bbb Q}$ . It is a proper subfield of  $\overline{\Bbb Q}$  as  $x \in \overline{\Bbb Q} \setminus E$ .
Moreover, for any element  $y \in \overline{\Bbb Q}$ , we can write  $y = a + bx$  with  $a, b\in F$ . Applying  $\iota $  gives  $\iota(y) = a + b\iota(x)$ , from which we may express  $a, b$  in terms of  $x, y, \iota(x), \iota(y)$ .
This shows that  $a, b$  are elements of  $\overline{\Bbb Q}$  and hence are elements of  $E$ .
Taking  $y = x^2$ , we see that the extension  $\overline{\Bbb Q}/E$  has degree  $2$ .

Therefore the extension  $\overline{\Bbb Q}/E$  corresponds to a nontrivial  $2$ -torsion element of  $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\Bbb Q}/\Bbb Q)$ , which we still write as  $\iota$ .
We know that all nontrivial  $2$ -torsion elements of  $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\Bbb Q}/\Bbb Q)$  are conjugate to each other (this is also stated in the above linked pdf, on page 5, with references). 
Thus there exists  $\sigma \in \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\Bbb Q}/\Bbb Q)$  such that  $\iota = \sigma^{-1}\circ c \circ \sigma$  holds on  $\overline{\Bbb Q}$ , where  $c$  is the complex conjugation on  $\Bbb C$ .
Since  $\sigma(x)$  is real by assumption, we have  $(c \circ \sigma)(x) = \sigma(x)$ , which implies  $\iota(x) = x$ , a contradiction.

stem_md:
Let  $a_0=0$ ,  $a_1, \ldots, a_k$  and  $b_1, \ldots, b_k$  be arbitrary real numbers.
(i) Show that for all sufficiently large  $n$  there exist polynomials  $p_n$  of degree at most  $n$  for which  $$ p_n^{(i)} (-1)=a_i,\,\,\,\,\, p_n^{(i)} (1)=b_i,\,\,\,\,\, i=0, 1, \ldots, k $$  and  $$ \max_{|x|\leq 1} |p_n (x)|\leq \frac{c}{n^2}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, (*) $$  where the constant  $c$  depends only on the numbers  $a_i, b_i$ .

(ii) Prove that, in general, (*) cannot be replaced by the relation  $$ \lim_{n\to\infty} n^2\cdot \max_{|x|\leq 1} |p_n (x)| = 0 $$  [J. Szabados]
solution_md:
**(ii)** We will prove that providing  $a_1,b_1$  are not both  $0$ , it's not possible  $\max_{|x|\leq 1} |p_n (x)|=o(n^{-2}) $ . Suppose on the contrary, it holds. Then, using [Markov brothers' inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_brothers%27_inequality), we get:
\[\max_{|x|\leq 1} |p'_n (x)|\leq n^2\cdot \max_{|x|\leq 1} |p_n (x)| =o(1) \]
Since we can raise  $n$  to infinity, it yields  $p'(-1)=p'(1)=0$ , a contradiction.**(i)** A sketch: To show the main idea, let  $k=1$ . We search for a polynomial  $p_n(x)$  with:   $$ p_n(-1)=p_n(1)=0\,;\,p'_n(-1)=a, p'_n(1)=b $$  and   $$ \max_{|x|\leq 1} |p_n (x)|\leq \frac{c}{n^2} $$   
where  $c$  depends only on  $a$  and  $b$ .

Let  $T_n(x)$  be the [Chebyshev polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials#Definition). The essential things we use are: 1)  $T_n$  oscillates between  $-1$  and  $1$  when  $x\in [-1,1]$ ; 2)  $T_n$  grows very very quickly on the left of  $-1$  and on the right of  $1$ . 
Let  $\varepsilon>0$  be such that  $|T_n(-1-\varepsilon)|=|T_n(1+\varepsilon)|=n^2$ . For example  $\varepsilon\sim \frac{(\ln n)^2}{n^2}$ . Now, let us shrink  $[-1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$  into  $[-1,1]$  and flatten  $T_n$  by multiplying it by  $\frac{1}{n^2}$ . That's, we set: 
\[t_n(x)= \frac{1}{n^2}\cdot T_n((1+\varepsilon) \cdot x)\]
If follows:
\[|t_n(x)|\leq \frac{1}{n^2}\,,\, \forall x\in[-1+1/(1+\varepsilon), 1-1/(1+\varepsilon)] \]

Consider now  $p_n(x) := (x-1)(x+1)t_n(x)$ . Using the fact that  $1-x$ , resp.  $1+x$  is "small" when  $x$  approaches  $1$  resp.  $-1$ , one can get:
\[\max_{|x|\leq 1}|p_n(x)|< \frac{c}{n^2}\]
for an absolute constant  $c$ .
Furthermore  $p'_n(1)= 1$  and  $p'_n(-1)=\pm 1$  depending on the parity of  $n$ . Thus, some linear combination of  $p_n$  and  $p_{n-1}$ :  $$ P_n(x) := \alpha p_n(x)+\beta p_{n-1}(x)  $$  will satisfy the requirement.

stem_md: Prove that if the  $a_i$ 's are different natural numbers, then  $\sum_ {j = 1}^n a_j ^ 2 \prod_{k \neq j} \frac{a_j + a_k}{a_j-a_k}$  is a square number.
solution_md: Let  $P(x):=\frac{1}{2}x^2(x-a_1)(x-a_2)\cdots (x-a_n).$ 	Then, the expression in question is exactly the [divided difference](https://dgrozev.wordpress.com/2020/10/06/imo-2019-shortlist-a5-an-application-of-divided-differences/)  $P[0,a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n].$  The divided difference of  $x^k,$  for  $k<n$ , taken at points  $0,a_1,\dots,a_n$  is  $0$ . Using the standard formulas for  $x^k[0,a_1,\dots,a_n], k=n,n+1,n+2$  yields	  $$ P[0,a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n]=(a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n)^2. $$

stem_md: Let K be the field formed by the addition of a root of the polynomial  $x^4 - 2x^2 - 1$  to the rational field. Prove that there are no exceptional units in the ring of integers of K. (A unit  $\varepsilon$  is called exceptional if  $1-\varepsilon$  is also a unit.)
solution_md:
We perform a  $2$ -adic study of the field  $K$ .

It is clear that  $K=\Bbb Q(\sqrt{1 + \sqrt 2})$ .
Write  $t = \sqrt{1 + \sqrt 2} - 1$ . We have  $t(t + 2) = \sqrt 2$ .
We fix any embedding  $K \hookrightarrow \overline{\Bbb Q_2}$ . Let  $v_2$  denote the normalized  $2$ -adic valuation on  $\overline{\Bbb Q_2}$  such that  $v_2(2) = 1$ .
Since  $t$  (and hence  $t + 2$ ) has nonnegative  $2$ -adic valuation, we have  $v_2(t) \leq v_2(\sqrt 2) = \tfrac12$ . Consequently, we have  $v_2(t + 2) = v_2(t)$  by ultrametric triangle inequality and therefore  $v_2(t) = \tfrac12v_2(\sqrt2) = \tfrac14$ .

We conclude that the prime  $2$  has ramification degree  $4$  in  $K$ , i.e.  $2 \mathcal O_K = \mathfrak p^4$  for some maximal ideal  $\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathcal O_K$ , where  $\mathcal O_K$  denotes the ring of integers of  $K$ .
It follows that the residue field  $\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak p$  is isomorphic to  $\Bbb F_2$ . Hence for any  $\varepsilon \in \mathcal O_K$ , either  $\varepsilon$  or  $1 - \varepsilon$  belongs to  $\mathfrak p$  and therefore is not a unit.

stem_md: Let H be a Hilbert space over the field of real numbers  $\Bbb R$ . Find all  $f: H \to \Bbb R$  continuous functions for which  $$ f(x + y + \pi z) + f(x + \sqrt{2} z) + f(y + \sqrt{2} z) + f (\pi z) $$    $$ = f(x + y + \sqrt{2} z) + f (x + \pi z) + f (y + \pi z) + f(\sqrt{2} z) $$  is satisfied for any  $x , y , z \in H$ .
solution_md:
Write  $u = \pi$  and  $v = \sqrt2$ .

For each  $z \in H$ , define  $g_z(t) = f(t + uz) - f(t + vz)$  and  $h_z(t) = g_z(t) - g_z(0)$ .
We have  $g_z(x + y) + g_z(0) = g_z(x) + g_z(y)$  and then  $h_z(x + y) = h_z(x) + h_z(y)$ .
The standard argument shows that the map  $h_z: H\rightarrow\Bbb R$  is  $\Bbb Q$ -linear and hence  $\Bbb R$ -linear as  $h_z$  is continuous.
Riesz representation theorem implies that there exists  $r_z \in H$  such that  $h_z(t) = \langle r_z, t\rangle$  for all  $t \in H$ , where  $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$  is the inner product of  $H$ .

Write  $c_z = g_z(0)$ . We have
(i)  $f(t + uz) - f(t + vz) = g_z(t) = c_z + \langle r_z, t\rangle$ .

For any  $t, z, w \in H$ , we have  $f(t + u(z + w)) - f(t + v(z + w)) = (f((t + uz) + uw) - f((t + uz) + vw)) + (f((t + vw) + uz) - f((t + vw) + vz))$ , which gives  $c_{z + w} + \langle r_{z + w}, t\rangle = c_w + \langle r_w, t + uz\rangle + c_z + \langle r_z, t + vw\rangle$ .
This being true for all  $t \in H$ , we conclude that
(ii)  $c_{z + w} = c_z + c_w + u\langle r_w, z\rangle + v\langle r_z, w\rangle$ ;
(iii)  $r_{z + w} = r_z + r_w$ .

In (ii), exchanging  $z$  and  $w$  gives  $\langle r_w, z\rangle = \langle r_z, w\rangle$ .
Thus for any  $\lambda \in \Bbb R$ , we have  $\langle \lambda r_z, w\rangle = \lambda\langle r_z, w\rangle = \lambda \langle r_w, z\rangle = \langle r_w, \lambda z\rangle = \langle r_{\lambda z}, w\rangle$ .
Taking  $w = r_{\lambda z} - \lambda r_z$  shows that  $r_{\lambda z} = \lambda z$  for all  $\lambda \in \Bbb R$  and all  $z \in H$ .
Combined with (iii), we see that the map  $z \mapsto r_z$  is an  $\Bbb R$ -linear map from  $H$  to  $H$ .
It is also symmetric, hence [Hellinger–Toeplitz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellinger%E2%80%93Toeplitz_theorem) tells us that it is continuous, i.e. a self adjoint operator on  $H$ .

Now (ii) can be rewritten as  $c_{z + w} = c_z + c_w + (u + v)\langle r_z, w\rangle$ .
If we write  $d_z = c_z - \tfrac{u + v}2\langle r_z, z\rangle$ , which is again continuous in  $z$ , then the above equality becomes  $d_{z + w} = d_z + d_w$ .
It follows that the map  $z \mapsto d_z$  is a continuous  $\Bbb R$ -linear map from  $H$  to  $\Bbb R$ .

In (i), we replace  $t$  with  $-vz$  to get  $f((u - v)z) = f(0) + c_z - v\langle r_z, z\rangle = f(0) + \tfrac{u - v}2\langle r_z, z\rangle + d_z$ .
Replacing  $z$  with  $\tfrac z{u - v}$ , we get  $f(z) = f(0) + \tfrac1{2(u - v)}\langle r_z, z\rangle + \tfrac1{u - v}d_z$ .

In conclusion, we have  $f(z) = a + b(z) + \langle c(z), z\rangle$  where:
-  $a$  is a real number;
-  $b:H \rightarrow \Bbb R$  is a continuous linear functional on  $H$ ;
-  $c:H \rightarrow H$  is a continuous self-adjoint operator on  $H$ .

Conversely, it is easy to verify that any function  $f$  of the above form satisfies the required identity.

stem_md: Let  $F^2$  be a closed, oriented 2-dimensional smooth surface,  $f : F^2 \to F^2$  is a smooth homeomorphism whose order is an odd prime p (i.e., the p-th iterate  $f \circ f \circ \cdots \circ f$  is the identity). In the tangent plane at the fixed point  $P_i$ , a positively directed (i.e., compatible with the direction of the surface) base can be chosen in which f is differentiated by a rotation with positive angle  $2\pi k_i/p$  , where  $k_i$  is a natural number,  $0 < k_i < p$  . Prove that   $$ \sum_{i = 1}^s k_i^{p-2}\equiv0\pmod{p} $$

stem_md: Given  $f,g\in L^1[0,1]$  and  $\int_0^1 f = \int_0^1 g=1$ , prove that there exists an interval I st  $\int_I f = \int_I g=\frac12$ .
solution_md:
We use the fact that Lebesgue integral is continuous. Thus there exists $m \in [0, 1]$ such that $\int_0^m f = \int_m^1 f = \frac 1 2$ . Moreover, for each $x \in [0, m]$ , there exists $s(x) \in [x, 1]$ such that $\int_x^{s(x)} f = \frac 1 2$ . We have $s(0) = m$ and $s(m) = 1$ . Again by continuity of Lebesgue integral, the function $x \mapsto s(x)$ is continuous. This implies that the function $U: [0, m] \rightarrow \Bbb R$ sending $x$ to $\int_x^{s(x)}g$ is continuous. We have $U(0) + U(m) = \int_0^1 g = 1$ . Hence one of $U(0)$ is $\geq \frac 1 2$ and the other is $\leq \frac 1 2$ . Thus there exists $a \in [0, m]$ such that $U(a) = \frac 1 2$ . It follows that the interval $I = [a, s(a)]$ works.
Generally, the claim in red is not true. For example, take $f$ to be $1$ in $[1/2,1]$ so, $m=1/2$ . Let $f$ takes very large negative values inside $[1/4,1/2]$ and $f$ takes large positive values in $[0,1/4]$ so that to compensate it. Now, for $x=1/4$ there does not exist $s(x)\in[x,1]$ with the required property. It could be fixed if one takes $m$ to be the minimal one with the same property.**EDIT**. But there is one more issue. You should clearly define what exactly $s(x)$ is, because for some values of $x$ it may happen that many values of $s(x)$ could do the job. So, to claim $s(x)$ is continuous you should define $s(x)$ more clearly. But there is some problem if you want $s(0)=m, s(m)=1$ . It means in the first case $s(0)$ would be the minimal one with this property, but then $s(m)$ should be the maximal one with this property?!

stem_md: Let  $X =\{ X_1 , X_2 , ...\}$  be a countable set of points in space. Show that there is a positive sequence  $\{a_k\}$  such that for any point  $Z\not\in X$  the distance between the point Z and the set  $\{X_1,X_2 , ...,X_k\}$  is at least  $a_k$  for infinitely many k.
solution_md:
We take  $b_k = \tfrac12\min\{|X_i - X_j|: 1 \leq i < j \leq k + 1\}$  and  $a_k = \min\{b_k, \tfrac 1 k\}$ , which ensures that the sequence  $(a_k)_k$  converges to zero.

Let  $Z$  be a point such that for sufficiently large  $k$ , the distance between  $Z$  and the set  $\{X_1, \dots, X_k\}$  is strictly smaller than  $a_k$ . We want to show that  $Z \in X$ .
The assumption means that for sufficiently large  $k$ , there exists  $i_k \in \{1, \dots, k\}$  such that  $|Z - X_{i_k}| < a_k \leq b_k$ .
Replacing  $k$  with  $k + 1$ , we get that there exists  $i_{k + 1} \in \{1, \dots, k + 1\}$  such that  $|Z - X_{i_{k + 1}}| < b_{k + 1} \leq b_k$ .
These two inequalities imply that  $|X_{i_k} - X_{i_{k + 1}}| < 2b_k = \min\{|X_i - X_j|: 1 \leq i < j \leq k + 1\}$ .
Since both  $i_k$  and  $i_{k + 1}$  belong to the set  $\{1, \dots, k + 1\}$ , the above inequality forces  $i_k = i_{k + 1}$ .
Thus we must have  $i_k = i_{k + 1} = i_{k + 2} = \dots$  for sufficiently large  $k$ . Let  $i$  denote this common value.
We then have  $|Z - X_i| < a_k$  for all sufficiently large  $k$ . Taking limit  $k \rightarrow \infty$  shows that  $Z = X_i$ .

stem_md: For odd numbers  $a_1 , ..., a_k$  and even numbers  $b_1 , ..., b_k$  , we know that  $\sum_ {j = 1}^k a_j^n = \sum_{j = 1}^k b_j^n$  is satisfied for n = 1,2, ..., N. Prove that  $k\geq 2^N$  and that for  $k = 2^N$  there exists a solution  $(a_1,...,b_1,...)$  with the above properties.
solution_md:
For the bound, we will actually prove the stronger fact that  $2^N | k:$  Indeed, first note that the problem is *translation invariant:* that is, if  $(a_1,\dots,a_k; b_1,\dots,b_k)$  is an admissible sequence for the problem, so is  $(a_1 + l,a_2 + l,\dots,a_k+l;b_1+l,b_2+l,\dots,b_k+l)$  for any integer  $l$  - since it at most inverts the parity of the numbers involved, and the polynomial identities remain the same. 

Hence, without loss of generality, suppose  $a_i,b_i > 0$  for all  $i.$  Consider the polynomial  $P(x) = \sum_{i=1}^k (x^{a_i} - x^{b_i}).$  Notice that  $P(1) = P'(1) = \cdots = P^{(N)}(1) = 0$  - in fact, this is equivalent to the condition given by the problem. Hence,  $(x-1)^{N+1}$  divides  $P(x).$  Since both polynomials have integer coefficients, taking  $x = -1$  implies  $2^{N+1}$  divides  $P(-1) = -2k,$  i.e.,  $2^N | k,$  as desired. 

For the desired example, we proceed by induction: for  $n=1,$  just take, for instance,  $a_1 = 1, a_2 = 3$  and  $b_1 = b_2 = 2.$  Given an admissible sequence  $(a_1,\dots,a_{2^N}; b_1,\dots,b_{2^N})$  for  $N,$  consider  $(a_1,\dots,a_{2^N},b_1+1,b_2+1,\dots,b_{2^N} + 1; b_1,\dots,b_{2^N},a_1+1,\dots,a_{2^N}+1).$  Clearly, this is admissible for  $N.$  A direct computation shows that this is admissible for  $N+1$  as well, which finishes the inductive step.

stem_md: Let A be a subset of the set  $\{1,2, ...,n\}$  with at least  $100\sqrt n$  elements. Prove that there is a four-element arithmetic sequence in which each element is the sum of two different elements of the set A.
solution_md:
Let A be a subset of the set $\{1,2, ...,n\}$ with at least $100\sqrt n$ elements. Prove that there is a four-element arithmetic sequence in which each element is the sum of two different elements of the set A.
There are $|A|(|A|-1)\geq10^4n-10^2\sqrt{n}$ ordered pairs $(a,b)\in A^2$ with $a\neq b$ . For $a,b\in A$ we have $3\leq 2a+b\leq 3n$ . So by the pidgeonhole principle there is a $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that at least $\frac{10^4n-10^2\sqrt{n}}{3n-2}>3$ ordered pairs $(a,b)\in A^2$ with $a\neq b$ and $2a+b=k$ exist. So there are pairwise distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$ with $2a+b=2c+d=k$ . But now $a+d,c+d,a+b,c+b$ form an arithmetic progression of length four.

stem_md: Prove that a harmonic function that is not identically zero in the plane cannot vanish on a two-dimensional positive-measure set.
solution_md:
Let us prove the result for harmonic functions on general  $\Bbb R^n$ .

A harmonic function  $H$  is real analytic. We let  $Z$  denote the set of zeros of  $H$ .
For any point  $P\in Z$ , one of the partial derivatives  $\partial_i H$  does not vanish at  $P$  (otherwise the function  $H$  is identically zero).
By implicit function theorem, there is an open neighborhood  $U_P$  of  $P$  such that  $U_P \cap Z$  is the graph of a continuous function from an open set in  $\Bbb R^{n - 1}$  to  $\Bbb R$ , which then has zero measure in  $\Bbb R^n$ .

Now for any  $R > 0$ , the compact set  $Z_R = \{P \in Z: |P| \leq R\}$  is covered by the family of open sets  $(U_P)_{P \in Z_R}$  and hence there exists a finite subcover  $(U_{P_i})_i$ . Since each  $U_{P_i} \cap Z$  has zero measure, we see that  $Z_R \subseteq \bigcup\nolimits_i(U_{P_i} \cap Z)$  has zero measure.
This allows us to conclude that  $Z = \bigcup\nolimits_{R = 1}^\infty Z_R$  has zero measure.

stem_md: Denote  $\langle x\rangle$  the distance of the real number x from the nearest integer. Let f be a linear, 1 periodic, continuous real function. Prove that there exist natural n and real numbers  $a_1 , ..., a_n , b_1 , ..., b_n , c_1 , ..., c_n$  such that   $$ f(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^n c_i \langle a_ix + b_i \rangle $$   for every x iff there is a k such that   $$ \sum_{j = 1}^{2^k} f \left(x+{j\over2^k}\right) $$   is constant.
solution_md:
In the [original problem statement](http://www.math.u-szeged.hu/~mmaroti/schweitzer/schweitzer-1995.pdf), it seems that  $f$  is supposed to be "piecewise linear".

Let us first prove the implication  $\implies$  in the problem statement.**Lemma**: Let  $f_1, \dots, f_m$  be continuous real functions and  $t_1, \dots, t_m$  be positive real numbers. Assume that
- for each  $i$ , the function  $f_i$  is  $t_i$ -periodic;
- for any  $i \neq j$ , the quotient  $t_i/t_j$  is irrational;
- the sum  $\sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^m f_i$  is a constant function.
Then each  $f_i$  is a constant function.**Proof**: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We prove by induction on  $m$ . For  $m = 1$  there is nothing to prove.
Now assume that the claim is true for  $m$  and we prove it for  $m + 1$ .
Let  $f_1, \dots, f_{m + 1}$  satisfy the assumptions. For  $i = 2, \dots, m+1$ , we define  $g_i(x) = f_i(x) - f_i(x + t_1)$ , which is still  $t_i$ -periodic.
Since  $\sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^{m + 1} f_i$  is constant and  $f_1$  is  $t_1$ -periodic, the sum  $\sum\nolimits_{i = 2}^{m+1}f_i$  is  $t_1$ -periodic. Consequently, we have  $\sum_{i = 1}^m g_i(x) = 0$ .
By induction hypothesis, we know that each  $g_i$  is constant. Integrating  $g_i$  over an interval of length  $t_i$ , we see that  $g_i$  must be equal to zero.
Therefore we have  $f_i(x) = f_i(x + t_1)$ , namely  $f_i$  is  $t_1$ -periodic. But it is also  $t_i$ -periodic, thus it is  $(\alpha t_1 + \beta t_i)$ -periodic for any integers  $\alpha, \beta$ . The assumption  $t_1/t_i \not\in \Bbb Q$  implies that  $(\alpha t_1 + \beta t_i)$  can be arbitrarily small, hence  $f_i$  must be constant by continuity.
We have shown that  $f_i$  is constant for each  $2 \leq i \leq m + 1$ , and hence  $f_1$  is also constant.</details>

Now assume that  $f$  is a  $1$ -periodic continuous real function that can be written as  $\sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n c_i\langle a_i x + b_i\rangle$ . Using the identy  $\langle x \rangle + \langle x + \tfrac12\rangle = \tfrac12$ , we may assume that none of the  $a_i$  is zero.
We group all the  $a_i$  according to the equivalence relation  $a_i \sim a_j \iff \exists r \in \Bbb Q^\times, ra_i = a_j$ .
We sum up the functions  $c_i \langle a_i x + b_i\rangle$  in each group, so that  $f(x) = \sum\nolimits_{j = 1}^s f_j(x)$  where each  $f_j(x)$  is a sum of functions  $c_i\langle a_ix + b_i\rangle$  where all the  $a_i$ 's differ by a rational multiple.
It is then clear that each  $f_j(x)$  is  $t_j$ -periodic for some  $t_j$ , and that  $t_j/t_k$  is irrational for  $j \neq k$ .
Thus by Lemma, for any  $j$  such that  $t_j$  is irrational ( $\iff$  all the  $a_i$ 's in that group are irrational), the function  $f_j(x)$  is constant and hence can be replaced with functions of the form  $c(\langle x \rangle + \langle x + \tfrac12\rangle)$ .
This shows that  $f$  can be written as  $\sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n c_i\langle a_i x + b_i\rangle$  where each  $a_i$  is nonzero rational.

For any positive real number  $T$  and any positive integer  $m$ , we define a linear operator  $[m]_T$  from the space of  $T$ -periodic functions to the space of  $\tfrac Tm$ -periodic functions, given by  $[m]_Th(x) = \tfrac 1m\sum\nolimits_{k = 1}^m h(x + \tfrac{kT}m)$  for any  $h$  and  $x$ .
It is easy to verify that  $[m']_{\tfrac Tm}[m]_T h = [m'm]_T h$  for any  $h, m, m'$ .

Let  $N$  be the common denominator of all  $a_i$  and write  $a_i = \tfrac{A_i}N$ . Let  $g_i$  denote the function  $\langle \tfrac{A_i}N x + b_i\rangle$ , which is  $N$ -periodic.
We know that  $f = \sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n c_ig_i$  is  $1$ -periodic, hence  $f = [N]_Nf = \sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n c_i[N]_Ng_i$ .
For each function  $g = \langle \tfrac ANx + b\rangle$ , we write  $A = 2^s B$  with  $B$  odd and note that  $g(x + \tfrac N{2^{s + 1}}) + g(x) = 1$ .
For  $r \geq s + 1$ , we have  $[2^r]_1[N]_Ng = [2^rN]_Ng$ . Since this function is  $\tfrac1{2^r}$ -periodic, we have  $[2^rN]_Ng(x) = [2^rN]_Ng(x + \tfrac N{2^{s + 1}})$  and hence  $2\cdot [2^rN]_Ng(x) = [2^rN]_N(g(x) + g(x + \tfrac N{2^{s + 1}})) = \tfrac12$ , i.e.  $[2^rN]_Ng = \tfrac14$  is constant.

Thus for sufficiently large  $r$ , we have that  $[2^rN]_Ng_i$  is constant for all  $i$ , and therefore  $[2^r]_1f = \sum\nolimits_{i = 1}^n c_i[2^rN]_Ng_i$  is constant, which is what we want to prove.

-----
Next we prove the other implication  $\impliedby$  in the problem statement.

We let  $F$  denote the  $\Bbb R$ -vector space of all  $1$ -periodic continuous piecewise linear real functions, which we also view as functions on  $S = \Bbb R/\Bbb Z$ .
For any function  $f \in F$  and any  $x \in \Bbb R/\Bbb Z$ , the left and right derivatives  $f'_-(x)$  and  $f'_+(x)$  both exist, and are equal for all but finitely many  $x \in S$ .
Let  $R = \Bbb R[S]$  be the group ring of the additive group  $S$  with coefficients in  $\Bbb R$ .
Thus we have an  $\Bbb R$ -linear map  $\phi: F \rightarrow R$  defined as  $\phi(f) = \sum\nolimits_{x \in S} (f'_+(x) - f'_-(x))\cdot \{x\}$ , where  $\{x\}$  denotes the basis element of  $\Bbb R[S]$  corresponding to  $x$ .
It is clear that the kernel of  $\phi$  is the one dimensional space of constant functions.
(In fact, one can show that  $\phi$  induces an isomorphism of  $\Bbb R$ -vector spaces from the quotient of  $F$  by constant functions to the augmentation ideal of  $\Bbb R[S]$ . We don't need this result here.)

For any  $k \geq 0$ , we write  $D_k = \phi(\langle 2^k x\rangle) = (1 - \{\tfrac 1{2^{k + 1}}\})\prod\nolimits_{i = 1}^k (1 + \{\tfrac 1{2^i}\})$ , where  $1$  denotes the unity in  $R$ , namely  $\{0\}$ .
Let  $I \subseteq R$  be the ideal generated by all  $D_k$ .
We prove by induction on  $k$  that  $1 - \{\tfrac 1{2^k}\}$  belongs to  $I$  for all  $k \geq 1$ .
Suppose the result is true for  $\leq k$ . We have  $0 \equiv D_{k + 1} \equiv (1 - \{\tfrac 1{2^{k + 1}}\}) \cdot 2^k\pmod I$ , hence  $\{\tfrac1{2^{k + 1}}\} \equiv 1\pmod I$ .

Now suppose that  $f$  is a function in  $F$  such that  $\sum\nolimits_{j = 1}^{2^r}f(x + \tfrac j{2^r})$  is constant for some  $r$ . This means that  $\beta\cdot z = 0$ , where  $\beta = \sum\nolimits_{j = 1}^{2^r}\{\tfrac j{2^r}\} \in R$  and  $z = \phi(f)$ .
We show that  $z$  belongs to  $\alpha R$  where  $\alpha = 1 - \{\tfrac 1{2^r}\}$ . It is clear that  $\alpha\beta = 0$ .
Since  $\{\tfrac j{2^r}\} = \{\tfrac 1{2^r}\}^j \equiv 1 \pmod{\alpha R}$  and hence  $\beta \equiv 2^r \pmod{\alpha R}$ , we see that  $\beta$  is invertible in the quotient  $R/\alpha R$  and thus we have  $R = \alpha R + \beta R$ . In particular, there exist  $u, v \in R$  such that  $\alpha u + \beta v = 1$ . Multiplying by  $\beta$ , we get  $\beta^2v = \beta$ .
We write  $z = \alpha s + \beta t$ . Multiplying by  $\beta$ , we get  $0 = \beta^2 t$ . It follows that  $\beta t = \beta^2 v t = 0$  and hence  $z = \alpha s \in \alpha R$ .

However, we have shown that  $\alpha$  belongs to  $I$ , which implies that  $z \in I$ . Consequently, there exist  $a_i, b_i, c_i$  such that the function  $g(x) = \sum\nolimits_i c_i\langle a_i x + b_i\rangle$  satisfies  $\phi(g) = \phi(f)$ . Thus  $f - g$  is constant and can be expressed as  $c\langle 0\cdot x + \tfrac12\rangle$ .

Let F(x) be a known distribution function, the random variables  $\eta_1 , \eta_2 ...$  be independent of the common distribution function  $F( x - \vartheta)$ , where  $\vartheta$  is the shift parameter. Let us call the shift parameter "well estimated" if there exists a positive constant c, so that any of  $\varepsilon> 0$  there exist a Lebesgue measure  $\varepsilon$  Borel set E ("confidence set") and a Borel-measurable function  $t_n( x_1 ,. .., x_n )$  ( n = 1,2, ...) such that for any  $\vartheta$  we have  $$ P ( \vartheta- t_n ( \eta_1 , ..., \eta_n ) \in E )> 1-e^{-cn}    \qquad( n > n_0 ( \varepsilon, F ) ) $$  Prove that

stem_md:
Let  $\{a_n\}$  be a bounded real sequence.
(a) Prove that if X is a positive-measure subset of  $\mathbb R$ , then for almost all  $x\in X$ , there exist a subsequence  $\{y_n\}$  of X such that   $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty (n(y_n-x)-a_n)=1 $$  (b) construct an unbounded sequence  $\{a_n\}$  for which the above equation is also true.
solution_md:
(a) We prove it's true for every Lebesgue point of  $X$  i.e.  $x\in X$  with   $$ \displaystyle \lim_{m(I)\to 0}\frac{m(X\cap I)}{m(I)}=1\qquad (1) $$   
where the limit is taken over intervals  $I$  centered at  $x$ . By Lebesgue's density theorem, almost all points of  $X$  have that property.  
Assume  $x\in X$  satisfies  $(1)$ . Let  $A>0$  such that  $|a_n|<A-1, \forall n\in \mathbb{N}$ .**Claim 1**. For any  $\varepsilon>0$  there exists  $N\in\mathbb{N}$  such that for  $n\ge N$  the set  $X_n:=n(X-x)=\{n(y-x) : y\in X\}$  meets every interval  $I\subset (-A,A)$  with length  $\varepsilon$ .

*Proof*. Assume, on the contrary, there is an interval  $I\subset (-A,A)$  with length  $\varepsilon$  which is free of elements of  $X_n$  for infinitely many  $n\in\mathbb{N}.$  For any  $n$  like that consider the interval  $J_n=(x-A/n, x+A/n).$  We have  $$ \frac{m(J_n\cap X)}{m(J_n)}=\frac{m(X_n\cap (-A,A))}{2A}\le \frac{2A-\varepsilon}{2A}\qquad (2)  $$  But since  $x$  is a Lebesgue point, the LHS of  $(2)$  tends to  $1$  as  $n\to\infty$ , contradiction.  $\blacksquare$  

Further, we use Claim 1 to obtain a sequence of natural numbers  $N_k, k=1,2,\dots$  so that for any  $n\ge N_k$  we are sure  $X_n$  meets any interval  $I\subset (-A,A)$  with length  $\frac{1}{2k}.$  It means that we can choose  $y'_n,y''_n\in X$  such that  $$ -\frac{1}{k}<n(y'_n-x)-a_n<-\frac{1}{2k}\,;\, \frac{1}{2k}<n(y''_n-x)-a_n<\frac{1}{k} $$  Thus, we consecutively choose  $y_n$  to be either  $y'_n$  or  $y''_n$  so that the partial sum of the series  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (n(y_n-x)-a_n)$  (from some place on, depending on  $k$ ) to oscillate about  $1$  with deviation no more than  $1/k.$  It yields  $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty (n(y_n-x)-a_n)=1. $$

candidates:
**(b)** The question is a bit ambiguous, maybe due to the translation. I believe that there does not exist an universal unbounded sequence like that, which does not depend on  $X$ . So, I interpret the question as to show that for any fixed set  $X\subset \mathbb{R},$  with positive measure, there exists an unbounded sequence (depending on  $X$ ) that satisfies the given condition.

According to Claim 1 in the previous post, for any Lebesgue's point  $x\in X$  and  $A>0, \varepsilon>0$  there exists  $N=N(x,A,\varepsilon)$  such that for each  $n\ge N(x,A,\varepsilon)$ , the set  $\{n(y-x) : y\in X\}$  meets every interval  $I\subset (-A-1, A+1)$  with length  $\varepsilon.$  Let now choose  $A_n>0, \varepsilon_n>0, n=1,2,\dots$  such that  $\lim_{n\to \infty} A_n=\infty$  and  $\lim_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_n=0.$  For any fixed  $n$  let us consider the set   $$ X_M:= \{x\in X \mid N(x,A_n,\varepsilon_n)\le M\} $$  where  $M>0$ . Since  $X_M$  is measurable and  $\bigcup_{M=1}^{\infty}X_M=X$ , we can choose  $M$  large enough so that  $m(X\setminus X_M)\le 2^{-n}.$  Denote this value of  $M$  as  $M=\varphi(n)$  and the set  $X_M$  by  $X_n.$  By Borel-Cantelli lemma, for almost all  $x\in X$  it holds that  $X_n$  covers  $x$  for some  $n$  on. Now, we choose an unbounded sequence  $\left(a_i\right)$  such that for all  $i,\, \varphi(n)\le i<\varphi(n+1)$  we have  $a_i=A_n, n=1,2,\dots.$  The same argument, as used in entry (a), shows that the requirement in entry (a) is satisfied.

stem_md: Let  $\xi_1 , \xi_2 , ...$  be a series of independent, zero-expected-value random variables for which  $\lim_{n\to\infty} E(\xi_n ^ 2) = 0$ , and  $S_n = \sum_{j = 1}^n \xi_j$  . Denote by I(A) the indicator function of event A. Prove that  $$ \frac{1}{\log n} \sum_{k = 1}^n \frac1k I\bigg(\max_{1\leq j\leq k} |S_j|>\sqrt k\bigg) \to 0 $$  with probability 1 if  $n\to\infty$  .
solution_md:
**Notations.**

For a family of centered random variables  $(X_{n})_{n \geq 1}$  with finite second moment, we let   $$ \begin{aligned}
    &\sigma_{n}^{2} = \operatorname{var}(X_{i}),
    &\varepsilon_{n}^{2} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}.
\end{aligned} $$  For a measure  $\mu$  and  $f$  a real function, we let  $$ \mu(f) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t) \, \mu(\mathrm{d}t). $$  For  $m\leq n$ , we define  $$ \begin{aligned}
&S_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i},
&T_{m,n}=\max_{m \leq i \leq n}|S_{i}-S_{m}|,
&\overline{T}_{m,n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}T_{m,n},
&T_{n}=\max_{0\leq i \leq n} |S_{i}|,
&\overline{T}_{n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}T_{n}
&\mu_{n}=\frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\delta_{\frac{T_{i}}{\sqrt{i}}},
\end{aligned} $$  where   $$ H_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}. $$  **Preliminaries.****Theorem. (Portemanteau)**
Let  $\lambda_{n}$ ,  $\lambda$  be probability measures on  $\mathbb{R}$ . The following statements are equivalent:
(i)  $\lambda_{n}$  converges in distribution to  $\lambda$ .
(ii) For any bounded Lipschitz function  $f$ ,  $\lambda_{n}(f) \longrightarrow \lambda(f)$ .**Theorem. (Doob's maximal inequality)**
Let  $(X_{n})_{n \geq 1}$  be a family of independent centered random variables with finite second moment, then  $$ \mathbb{E}\left(T_{n}^{2}\right)\leq 4n \varepsilon_{n}^{2} $$  **Main theorem**.

The key result we will need to prove is**Theorem 1.**
Let  $(X_{i})_{i \geq 1}$  be independent, centered random variables with variance  $\sigma_{i}^{2} \longrightarrow 0$ , then  $\mu_{n}$  converges almost surely in distribution to  $\delta_{0}$ .

To prove Theorem 1, we use the equivalent characterization of convergence in distribution given by Portemanteau theorem. More precisely, theorem 1 amounts into proving that**Proposition 2.**
Almost surely, for all  $f$  bounded and Lipschitz,  $$ \mu_{n}(f) \longrightarrow \delta_{0}(f)=f(0). $$  This result is quite hard to prove and we will consider first a weaker version of Proposition 2.**Proposition 3.**
Let  $f$  be bounded and Lipschitz, then  $\mu_{n}(f)$  converges almost surely to  $f(0)$ .**Proof of Proposition 3**
This part is dedicated to the proof of Proposition 3. Several technical lemmas are needed and listed below with their proof.

In all that part, we assume  $f$  to be a  $k$ -Lipschitz function bounded by some constant  $C$ . More generally,  $C$  refers to a constant that can change from line to line, but which is always independent of  $n$ . **Lemma 4.**
For  $m\leq n$ ,   $$ |T_{n}-T_{m,n}|\leq T_{m} $$  <details><summary>Proof Lemma 4</summary>We need to prove that  $$ T_{n}-T_{m}\leq T_{m,n} \leq T_{n}+T_{m}. $$  On one hand,  $$ T_{m,n}=\max_{m \leq i \leq n}|S_{i}-S_{m}|\leq \max_{m \leq i \leq n}|S_{i}| + |S_{m}|  \leq T_{n}+T_{m}. $$  On the other hand, note that  $T_{m}\leq T_{n}$ . Then, either  $T_{m}=T_{n}$  and in that case,  $T_{m,n}\geq T_{n}-T_{m}=0$ . 
Otherwise,  $T_{n}>T_{m}$  so that   $$ T_{n} = \max_{0 \leq i \leq n} |S_{i}|\leq \max_{m \leq i \leq n} |S_{i}|. $$   
In that case,  $$ T_{n,m} = \max_{m \leq i \leq n}|S_{i}-S_{m}| \geq \max_{m \leq i \leq n}|S_{i}|- |S_{m}|= T_{n}-|S_{m}|\geq T_{n}-T_{m} $$  This finishes the proof.</details>**Lemma 5.**
Let  $f$  be Lipschitz and bounded and  $m\leq n$ , then  $$ \left|\operatorname{cov}\left(f\left(\overline{T}_{m}\right), f\left(\overline{T}_{n}\right)\right)\right| \leq C\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}. $$  for some constant  $C>0$  independent of both  $m$  and  $n$ .

<details><summary>Proof Lemma 5</summary>As  $\overline{T}_{m,n}$  depends only on  $X_{m+1}, \dots, X_{n}$ , it is independent of  $\overline{T}_{m}$  and we have  $$ \operatorname{cov}\left(f(\overline{T}_{m}), f(\overline{T}_{n})\right)=\operatorname{cov}\left(f(\overline{T}_{m}), f(\overline{T}_{n})-f(\overline{T}_{m,n})\right). $$  It follows then that   $$ \begin{aligned}
\left|\operatorname{cov}\left(f(\overline{T}_{m}), f(\overline{T}_{n})\right)\right|&\leq \mathbb{E}\left(\left|f(\overline{T}_{m})-\mathbb{E}(\overline{T}_{m})\right| \, \left|f(\overline{T}_{n})-f(\overline{T}_{m,n})-\mathbb{E}(f(\overline{T}_{n}))+\mathbb{E}(f(\overline{T}_{m,n}))\right|\right)
\text{( $f$  bounded)}&\leq C \mathbb{E}\left(\left|f(\overline{T}_{n})-f(\overline{T}_{m,n})-\mathbb{E}(f(\overline{T}_{n})-f(\overline{T}_{m,n}))\right|\right)
\text{(triangular inequality)}&\leq C  \mathbb{E}\left(\left|f(\overline{T}_{n})-f(\overline{T}_{m,n})\right|\right)
&\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{n}} \mathbb{E}\left(|T_{n}-T_{m,n}|\right)
\text{(Lemma 4)}&\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{n}} \mathbb{E}\left(T_{m}\right)
\text{(Jensen's inequality)}&\leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{n}} \sqrt{\mathbb{E}(T_{m}^{2})}
\text{(Doob's maximal inequality)}&\leq C\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}\varepsilon_{m}.
\end{aligned} $$  As  $\sigma_{i}^{2}$  is bounded, so is  $\varepsilon_{m}^{2}$ . Hence, there exists some constant  $C>0$  independent of both  $m$  and  $n$  such that  $$ \left|\operatorname{cov}\left(f(\overline{T}_{m}), f(\overline{T}_{n})\right)\right|\leq C\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}. $$  This finishes the proof.</details>**Lemma 6.**
Let  $f$  be continuous and Lipschitz, then  $$ \mathbb{E}\left(\mu_{n}(f)\right) \longrightarrow f(0) $$  and   $$ \operatorname{var}(\mu_{n}(f))=O\left(\frac{1}{\log(n)}\right). $$  <details><summary>Proof Lemma 6</summary>By triangular inequality,  $$ \begin{aligned}
|\mathbb{E}\left(\mu_{n}(f)\right)-f(0)| &\leq \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\mathbb{E}\left(\left|f\left(\frac{T_{i}}{\sqrt{i}}\right)-f(0)\right|\right)
\text{( $f$  Lipschitz)}&\leq \frac{C}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\mathbb{E}\left(\left|\frac{T_{i}}{\sqrt{i}}\right|\right)
\text{(Jensen's inequality)}&\leq \frac{k}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{T_{i}^{2}}{i}\right)
\text{(Doob's maximal inequality)}&=\frac{2k}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\varepsilon_{i}.
\end{aligned} $$  As  $\sigma_{i}$  tends to  $0$ , so does  $\varepsilon_{i}$ . This implies immediately that   $$ |\mathbb{E}\left(\mu_{n}(f)\right)-f(0)| \longrightarrow 0. $$  Now, we consider the variance.  $$ \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\mu_{n}(f)) &= \frac{1}{H_{n}^{2}}\sum_{1 \leq p,q \leq n} \frac{1}{pq}\operatorname{cov}(f(\overline{T}_{m}),f(\overline{T}_{n}))
&\leq \frac{1}{H_{n}^{2}}\sum_{1 \leq p \leq q \leq n} \frac{1}{pq}|\operatorname{cov}(f(\overline{T}_{m}),f(\overline{T}_{n}))|
\text{(Lemma 5)}&\leq \frac{C}{H_{n}^{2}}\sum_{1 \leq p \leq q \leq n}\frac{1}{pq}\sqrt{\frac{p}{q}}
&\sim \frac{C}{\log(n)^{2}}\sum_{1 \leq p \leq q \leq n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}q^{3/2}}
&\sim \frac{C}{\log(n)^{2}} \int_{1}^{n}\int_{1}^{x} \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}x^{3/2}}\, \mathrm{d}y\, \mathrm{d}x
&\sim \frac{C}{\log(n)^{2}} \int_{1}^{n}\frac{1}{x} \,\mathrm{d}x
&\sim \frac{C}{\log(n)}.
\end{aligned} $$  This finishes the proof.</details>

We are now ready to complete the proof of Proposition 3.

<details><summary>Proof proposition 3</summary>By Chebyshev inequality and lemma 6,   $$ \begin{aligned}
    \mathbb{P}\left(|\mu_{n}(f)-f(0)+o(1)|\geq \varepsilon \right) \leq \frac{\operatorname{var}(\mu_{n}(f))}{\varepsilon^{2}}\leq \frac{C}{\log(n)}.
\end{aligned} $$  Take  $n=2^{k^{2}}$  so that  $$ \mathbb{P}\left(|\mu_{n}(f)-f(0)+o(1)|\geq \varepsilon \right)\leq \frac{C}{k^{2}}. $$  This is summable and Borel-Cantelli implies then that  $\mu_{2^{k^{2}}}(f)$  converges almost surely to  $f(0)$ . 

More generally, if  $n\geq 1$ , denote by  $k$  the unique integer such that  $2^{k^{2}} \leq n < 2^{(k+1)^{2}}$ . We know that  $\mu_{2^{k^{2}}}(f)$  converges almost surely to  $f(0)$ . In order to prove that  $\mu_{n}(f)$  does also, it suffices to prove that  $\mu_{2^{k^{2}}}(f)$  and  $\mu_{n}(f)$  are not far away. This is a consequence of the following estimate.  $$ \begin{aligned}
\left|\mu_{n}(f)-\frac{H_{2^{k^{2}}}}{H_{n}}\mu_{2^{k^{2}}}(f)\right|&=\frac{1}{H_{n}}\left|\sum_{i=2^{{k}^{2}}}^{n}\frac{1}{i}f\left(\frac{T_{i}}{\sqrt{i}}\right)\right|
\text{( $f$  bounded)}&\leq  \frac{C}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=2^{k^{2}}}^{2^{(k+1)^{2}}}\frac{1}{i}
&\sim \frac{C}{H_{n}}[(k+1)^{2}-k^{2}]
&\sim C\frac{k}{\log(n)}.
\end{aligned} $$  As  $2^{k^{2}}\leq n$ , we have  $k \leq \sqrt{\log(n)}$  so that   $$ \left|\mu_{n}(f)-\frac{H_{2^{k^{2}}}}{H_{n}}\mu_{2^{k^{2}}}(f)\right| \leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{\log(n)}}. $$  for some constant  $C>0$  independent of  $n$ .

Therefore, we have proved that  $$ \sup_{2^{k^{2}} \leq n < 2^{(k+1)^{2}}}\left|\mu_{n}(f)-\frac{H_{2^{k^{2}}}}{H_{n}}\mu_{2^{k^{2}}}(f)\right| \longrightarrow 0. $$  It remains to notice that  $H_{2^{k^{2}}}/H_{n} \to 1$  as  $n\to +\infty$ . This finishes the proof.</details>**Proof of proposition 2.**
So far, we have proved that for any  $f$  bounded Lipschitz function, almost surely,  $\mu_{n}(f)$  converges to  $f(0)$ . To prove proposition 2, we need to exchange the order of the quantifiers. We need to prove that almost surely, for any  $f$  bounded and Lipschitz,  $\mu_{n}(f)$  converges to  $f(0)$ . But, there is one problem as there are an uncountable number of bounded and Lipschitz functions. To circumvent this issue, we need a stronger version of Portemanteau theorem. This is the content of the following lemma. **Lemma 7.**
Let  $\lambda_{n}$ ,  $\lambda$  be probability measures. There exists a countable set  $D$  of bounded Lipschitz functions such that  $\lambda_{n}$  converges in distribution to  $\lambda$  if and only if  $\lambda_{n}(f)$  converges to  $\lambda(f)$  for any  $f$  in  $D$ .

<details><summary>Proof Lemma 7</summary>Define  $D$  as the set of functions   $$ f_{I,n}(t) = n \operatorname{dist}(t, {}^{c}I) \wedge 1. $$  where  $I$  is any open interval with rational or infinite extremities and  $n \geq 1$ .  $D$  is by definition countable.

It is also clear that  $f_{I,t}$  is bounded, Lipschitz (as dist is Lipschitz) and converges simply to  $1(t\in I)$ . This is a key property that allows to approximate any bounded continuous function by linear combination of elements of  $D$ . $\implies$  If  $\lambda_{n}$  converges in distribution to  $\lambda_{n}$ , then by definition,  $\lambda_{n}(f)$  converges to  $\lambda(f)$  for any  $f \in D$ . $\impliedby$  For the converse, assume that  $\lambda_{n}(f)$  converges to  $\lambda(f)$  for any  $f \in D$ . Approach  $g$  by a linear combination of elements of  $f$  such that  $||f-g||_{\infty} \leq \varepsilon$ . Then,  $$ \begin{aligned}
    |\lambda_{n}(g)-\lambda(g)|&\leq |\lambda_{n}(f)-\lambda(f)|+ |\lambda_{n}(f-g)|+|\lambda(f-g)|
    &\leq 2\varepsilon+|\lambda_{n}(f)-\lambda(f)|
    &\leq 3\varepsilon
\end{aligned} $$  for  $n$  large enough. Hence,  $$ \lambda_{n}(g) \longrightarrow \lambda(g), $$  or equivalently  $\lambda_{n}$  converges to  $\lambda$  in distribution.</details>

Lemma 7 and Proposition 3 implies immediately Proposition 2.**Conclusion.**
We are now ready to prove that:**Proposition 8.**
Almost-surely,  $$ \frac{1}{\log(n)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i} 1\left(\max_{0 \leq j \leq i}|S_{j}|>\sqrt{i}\right)\longrightarrow 0. $$  <details><summary>Proof proposition 8</summary>The proof is based on the following well-known result. If  $\lambda_{n}$  is a sequence of probability measures that converges in distribution to  $\lambda$  and  $f$  is  $\lambda$  almost surely continuous, then  $\mu_{n}(f)$  converges to  $\mu(f)$ .

According to Theorem 1, almost surely,  $\mu_{n}$  converges to  $\delta_{0}$ . Applying the latter result to  $\lambda_{n}=\mu_{n}$ ,  $\lambda=\delta_{0}$  and  $f(t)=1(|t|>1)$  (which is continuous at  $0$ ),  we have then that  $$ \mu_{n}(f) = \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}1(|T_{i}|>\sqrt{i}) $$  converges to  $0$ . As  $H_{n}\sim \log(n)$ , the conclusion follows.</details>

Absolutely stunning! This problem is a tale related to almost-sure central limit theorem, definitely one of my favorite problem from Miklós Schweitzer. I was very proud solving it. 

But before giving away the solution in a latter post, I will some background and ideas.**Background**.**Convergence in distribution.**
First, recall that a sequence of random variables  $X_{n} : \Omega \to E$  converges in distribution to  $X$  if   $$ \mathbb{E}[f(X_{n})]\longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[f(X)] $$  for any bounded continuous function on  $E$ . Hence, to define convergence in distribution, you simply need a topology on  $E$  in order to define properly continuity.**Almsot sure central limit theorem.**

The central limit theorem for iid random variables  $(X_{i})_{i\geq1}$  tells us that the sequence  $S_{n}/\sqrt{n}$  converges in distribution to a normal distribution and it is natural to wonder whether the preceding theorem can be enhanced to almost-sure convergence. Unluckily, this is a shattered dream as even convergence in probability fails miserably. 

Even though there was no almost sure convergence, mathematicians were still interesting in the trajectories of  $(S_{n}/\sqrt{n})_{n\geq 1}$  and some authors started studying the sequence of random probability measures  $$ \lambda_{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\delta_{S_{n}/\sqrt{n}}. $$  This is quite an exotic object as  $\lambda_{n}$  is a random variable tacking its values in the space of probability measures  $\mathcal{M}_{1}(\mathbb{R})$ . This space can be equipped with a natural topology and one can prove that  $\lambda_{n}$  converges in distribution to a random probability measure  $\lambda$ . Yet, there is still no almost-sure convergence, but we are almost there. We just need a last fundamental idea, that is Cesaro/Harmonic mean convergence.**Cesaro convergence.**
If  $(x_{n})_{n\geq 1}$  is a sequence of real numbers and  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ , then we know that   $$  \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\to x\right) \implies \left(\frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{x_{k}}{k}\to x\right) $$  where  $H_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k}$ . Yet, the reverse implications is not true. In particular,  $\frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{x_{k}}{k}$  can converge whereas  $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}$  diverges. This is the core idea of the almost-sure central limit theorem, which we state now.**Almost-sure central limit theorem.**
The random probability measure  $$ \mu_{n}=\frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\delta_{\frac{S_{i}}{\sqrt{i}}} $$  converges almost-surely in distribution to a standard normal random variable.

The latter theorem means that, for almost all  $\omega$ , the probability  $\mu_{n}(\omega)$  converges in distribution to a standard normal distribution. If we recall the definition of convergence in distribution, it equivalently means that for almost all  $\omega$ , for any  $f : \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$  continuous and bounded,  $$ \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}f\left(\frac{S_{i}(\omega)}{\sqrt{i}}\right)\to \mathbb{E}[f(X)] $$  where  $X \to \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ . This is such a beautiful result!**Back to the problem.**

Now, in our problem, the  $X_{i}$  are no longer iid but satisfy  $\operatorname{Var}(X_{i})\to 0$ . Hence,  $S_{n}/\sqrt{n}$  no longer converges to a standard normal distribution, but instead to  $0$ . Hence, if the almost-sure central limit holds true, we expect that   $$ \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}\delta_{S_{i}/\sqrt{i}} $$  converges almost-surely in distribution to  $0$ , that is almost surely, for any  $f$  continuous bounded  $$ \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}f\left(\frac{S_{i}}{\sqrt{i}}\right)\to f(0). $$  If we let  $f(t) = 1(|t|>1)$  (which is not continuous at  $\pm 1$  but this is a minor inconvenience), then  $$ \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}1(|S_{i}|>\sqrt{i})\to f(0)=0. $$  This is not exactly what we want as we would like  $\max_{0 \leq k \leq i}|S_{k}|$  instead of  $|S_{i}|$ , but we are clearly very close to a solution. This is the content of my next post.

I wanted to express my sincere gratitude for your exceptional contributions dear @Saucitom. Your posts are not only immensely enriching but also exhibit an elegance and pedagogical brilliance that truly stand out. The depth of knowledge and insight you share is both impressive and inspiring.

Thank you for your kind words, @oty! 

Here are some more context about almost-sure central limit theorems. It's not a topic I know very well or I'm very interested in, so feel free to correct me if I'm wrong.

An almost-sure central limit theorem is a result of the form:**Theorem (almost-sure central limit theorem).**
If  $(W_{n})_{n\geq1 }$  is a sequence of random variables such that
(i) it converges in distributions to  $W$  and,
(ii) it satisfies some technical conditions (*),
then almost-surely, for any bounded Lipschitz continuous function  $f$ ,  $$ \frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}f(W_{i})\longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[f(W)]. $$  I omit the technical conditions (*) but they are quite important. Usually you want a bound on the covariance on the form  $$ |\operatorname{cov}(f(W_{p}),f(W_{q}))| = O\left(\sqrt{\frac{p}{q}}\right) $$  if  $p\leq q$ . This is usually the hard part, but once you have it, you can derive an almost-sure central limit theorem (just mimic the proof I made above).

Now, it is possible the process you consider does not satisfy the above bound, making it impossible to derive an almost-sure central limit theorem. Yet, you can still get one if, instead of considering harmonic mean, you consider weaker forms of convergence such as  $$ \frac{1}{\log(\log(n))}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i\log(i)}f(W_{i}). $$  or (if it still not sufficient)  $$ \frac{1}{\log(\log(\log(n)))}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i\log(i)\log(\log(i))}f(W_{i}), $$  and so on...

In summary, the bound you have on the covariance will give you the mean you can expect in your almost-sure central limit theorem.
Wow! Incredible.

stem_md: Prove that for any finite graph G there is a constant c(G)>0 such that for every n-point graph that does not have an induced subgraph isomorphic to G, there are two disjoint sets of vertices, each with at least  $n^{c(G)}$  elements, between which either all edges are connected, or none of the edges are.
solution_md:
The statement means that;
For finite graph  $G$ , there is constant  $c(G), d(G)$  such that every  $G$ -free graph  $H$  or it's complement has complete bipartite induced subgraph which both vertice set has size at least  $d(G)n^{c(G)}$ , where  $n=|V(H)|$ .

This result is from the article [“Ramsey-type theorem for bipartite graphs”, Combinatorics
10 (2000), 64-68](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/A-Ramsey-type-theorem-for-bipartite-graphs-Erd%C3%B6s-Hajnal/6516d9839335e251cc0a6f84b4241512fa6837a4) written by **P. Erdös, A. Hajnal and J. Pach**.

Prove that there exists a function  $f\colon [\omega_1]^2 \rightarrow \omega _1$  such that
(i)  $f(\alpha, \beta)< \mathrm{min}(\alpha, \beta)$  whenever  $\mathrm{min}(\alpha,\beta)>0$ ; and 
(ii) if  $\alpha_0<\alpha_1<\ldots<\alpha_i<\ldots<\omega_1$  then  $\sup\left\{ a_i \colon i<\omega \right\} =\sup \left\{ f(\alpha_i, \alpha_j)\colon i,j<\omega\right\}$ .
solution_md:
The simplest idea is to find an appropriate function  $\phi: \omega_1\to \omega_1$  that satisfies  $\phi(\alpha)<\alpha, \forall \alpha<\omega_1$  and then set  $f(\alpha,\beta):=\min(\phi(\alpha),\phi(\beta))$ .
	Unfortunately, this idea is doomed due to Fodor's lemma. For any regressive function  $\phi: \omega_1\to \omega_1$  ( $\phi(\alpha)<\alpha$ ) there exists an ordinal  $\gamma<\omega_1$  such that  $\phi(\alpha)<\gamma, \forall \alpha\in A$  where  $A\subset \omega_1$  is uncountable set. Choosing  $\{\alpha_1<\alpha_2<\dots\}\subset A,\gamma<\alpha_1$  and  $(ii)$  does not hold.

stem_md: Let  $a_1<a_2<a_3$  be positive integers. Prove that there are integers  $x_1,x_2,x_3$  such that  $\sum_{i=1}^3 |x_i | >0$ ,  $\sum_{i=1}^3 a_ix_i= 0$  and  $$ \max_{1\le i\le 3} | x_i|<\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{a_3}+1 $$  .
solution_md:
Let  $t = \left \lfloor \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{a_3} \right \rfloor.$  Consider the multiset  $S$  of nonnegative integers of form  $a_1u_1 + a_2u_2$  for integers  $0 \le u_1,u_2 \le t,$  which has size  $(t+1)^2 > \frac{4}{3}a_3.$  All these integers are  $<2a_3t.$  

If three elements of  $S$  have same residue  $\pmod{a_3}$  then at least two of them are within  $a_3t$  of each other, and we're done by taking their difference. 

Otherwise, there are more than  $\frac{1}{3}a_3$  unordered pairs of integers from  $S$  with the same residue  $\pmod{a_3},$  and each pair has an absolute difference of more than  $a_3t.$  Take a pair  $a_1u_1+a_2u_2$  and  $a_1v_1+a_2v_2$  from  $S$  with the same residue, so   $$ a_1(u_1-v_1) + a_2(u_2-v_2) = sa_3 $$  for some  $2s > s > t,$  and obviously  $u_1-v_1, u_2-v_2$  must both be positive. Take another pair  $a_1u_1'+a_2u_2'$  and  $a_1v_1'+a_2v_2'$  from  $S$  with another shared residue where   $$ a_1(u_1'-v_1') + a_2(u_2'-v_2') = s'a_3 $$  for some  $2s> s' > t,$  and obviously  $u_1'-v_1', u_2'-v_2'$  must both be positive as well. If we do not have  $u_1-v_1 = u_1'-v_1'$  and  $u_2-v_2=u_2'-v_2'$  we could take the difference  $sa_3-s'a_3$  and be done. 

So  $u_1-v_1$  is some constant  $c_1$  and  $u_2-v_2$  is some constant  $c_2$  across all pairs of integers from  $S$  with the same residue  $\pmod{a_3}.$  Also,  $c_1+c_2 \ge t+2$  in order to force  $c_1+c_2 > s > t.$  But we can only have at most   $$ (t-c_1+1)(t-c_2+1) \le \frac{(2t-c_1-c_2+2)^2}{4} \le \frac{t^2}{4} \le \frac{1}{4} \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{a_3} \right)^2 = \frac{1}{3}a_3 $$  same residue pairs, which is not enough. Contradiction.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$  be a map such that the image of every compact set is compact, and the image of every connected set is connected. Prove that  $f$  is continuous.
solution_md:
Solved with **mira74, AIME12345**:

Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $f$  is not continuous. Then we can find some  $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$  and  $\varepsilon > 0$  such that for all  $\delta > 0$ , there exists a  $y$  such that  $|x-y| \leq \delta$  and  $|f(x) - f(y)| > \varepsilon$ .

For all positive integers  $n$ , we consider the set of all  $y$  with  $|x-y|\leq \frac{1}{n}$  and  $|f(x)-f(y)| > \varepsilon$ ; let this set be  $S_n$ . We claim that for some  $n$ ,  $f(S_n)$  is finite. If this was not the case, for all  $n$ , we could pick some  $y_n$  with  $|x-y_n| \leq \frac{1}{n}$  and  $|f(x)-f(y_n)| > \varepsilon$  such that  $f(y_n) \not\in \{f(y_1),f(y_2),\ldots,f(y_{n-1})\}$ .

Now, take some convergent subsequence  $\{f(y_{n_k})\}_{n_k \in \mathbb{N}}$  of  $\{f(y_{n})\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ , and suppose it converges to  $Y$ . Since \[\{x,y_{n_1},y_{n_2},\ldots\}\] only has the limit point  $x$ , and it is bounded, it must be compact. Thus, the set \[\{f(x),f(y_{n_1}),f(y_{n_2}),\ldots \}\] is compact and hence contains  $Y$ . Since  $|f(y_{n_i})-f(x)|>\varepsilon$  for all  $i$ ,  $Y \neq f(x)$ , so we must have  $f(y_{n_i})=Y$  for some  $i$ . This  $i$  is unique since  $a \rightarrow f(y_a)$  is injective by definition. Now, we have that the compact set
\[\{x,y_{n_1},y_{n_2},\ldots\}\setminus\{y_{n_i}\}\] maps to the noncompact set \[\{f(x),f(y_{n_1}),f(y_{n_2}),\ldots \}\setminus\{f(y_{n_i})\},\] which is a contradiction, as desired. 

We found that for some fixed  $x$  and  $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a  $\delta > 0$  and finite set  $S$  such that if  $|x-y| \leq \delta$ , then  $|f(x)-f(y)| \leq \varepsilon$  or  $f(y) \in S$ . Now, the closed ball with center  $\delta$  around  $x$  maps to the union of  $S$  with some subset of the ball with radius  $\varepsilon$  centered at  $f(x)$ , but unless  $S$  is empty, this is disconnected.  $\square$

Arguing by contradiction, suppose there exists a point  $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ , and  $f$  is not continuous at  $x_0$ . Let  $y_0=f(x_0)$ . 

It means there exists  $\varepsilon_0>0$ , such that  we can find points  $x$  as close to  $x_0$  as we want, with   $f(x)\not\in B_{\varepsilon_0}(y_0)$ . Denote:
\[Y_{k,\ell} = \{x\in \mathbb{R}^n : \|x-x_0\|\leq 1/k, \|f(x)-y_0 \|\in (\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0+1/\ell]  \}\].
There are two possibilities:

Let's consider the two cases:

2) In that case the image of  $B_{1/k}(x_0)$  is not connected since there exist points in that ball that go outside  $B_{\varepsilon_0}(y_0)$ ; the point  $x_0$  goes inside the latter ball, and no point goes in a ring around it.

stem_md: Find the units of  $R=\mathbb Z[t][\sqrt{t^2-1}]$ .
solution_md:
That's an interesting problem, it's like a Pell's equation for  $\mathbb{Z}[t]$  instead of  $\mathbb{Z}$  (see the identity  $(*)$  below). 

Let  $$ R:=\mathbb{Z}[t][\sqrt{t^2-1}]=\mathbb{Z}[t]+\sqrt{t^2-1}\mathbb{Z}[t]. $$  I can show that  $\pm T_n(t) \pm \sqrt{t^2-1}U_{n-1}(t), \ n \ge 0,$  where  $T_n,U_n$  are the Chebyshev polynomials and  $U_{-1}(t)=0$ , are units of  $R$  and I think they are in fact all the units of  $R$  (that needs a proof!). 

To see that, let  $p(t)+\sqrt{t^2-1}q(t), \ \ p(t),q(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t],$  be a unit of  $R.$  So there exist polynomials  $u(t),v(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t]$  such that   $$ (p(t)+\sqrt{t^2-1}q(t))(u(t)+\sqrt{t^2-1}v(t))=1 $$  and hence   $$ (p(t)-\sqrt{t^2-1}q(t))(u(t)-\sqrt{t^2-1}v(t))=1. $$  Multiplying the above identities together gives  $(p^2(t)-(t^2-1)q^2(t))(u^2(t)-(t^2-1)v^2(t))=1$  and so   $$ p^2(t)-(t^2-1)q^2(t)=\pm 1. $$   
But we can't have  $p^2(t)-(t^2-1)q^2(t)=-1$  because then we'll get  $p^2(1)=-1,$  which is not possible. So   $$ p^2(t)-(t^2-1)q^2(t)=1. \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (*) $$  Conversely, if  $(*)$  holds, then  $(p(t)+\sqrt{t^2-1}q(t))(p(t)-\sqrt{t^2-1}q(t))=1$  and so  $p(t)+\sqrt{t^2-1}q(t)$  is a unit of  $R.$  Now it is known, and fairly easy to prove, that for any integer  $n \ge 0,$  the polynomials   $$ p(t)=\pm T_n(t), \ \ \ \ q(t)=\pm U_{n-1}(t) $$   
satisfy  $(*).$  Hence  $\pm T_n(t) \pm \sqrt{t^2-1}U_{n-1}(t)$  is a unit of  $R$  for all  $n \ge 0$  and I believe they're all the units of  $R.$  I think we can prove that by probably modifying the proof for Pell's equation over  $\mathbb{Z}.$  I might think about it later.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Hungary Contests/Miklós Schweitzer/2001 Miklós Schweitzer/1381930.json

First, get two more variables  $ z,w $  as I said.  $ f(x)+f(y)+f(z)+f(w)=f\left( \frac{x+y}{2}\right) + f\left( \frac{z+w}{2}\right)+ f\left(\frac{2xy}{x+y} \right)+ f\left(\frac{2zw}{z+w} \right)=f\left ( \frac{x+y+z+w}{4} \right )+f\left (\frac{xyz+yzw+zwx+wxy}{(x+y)(z+w)}  \right )+f\left ( \frac{(x+y)(z+w)}{x+y+z+w} \right )+f\left ( \frac{4xyzw}{xyz+yzw+zwx+wxy} \right ) $ And now, we switch  $ y,z $  here.  $ f\left (\frac{xyz+yzw+zwx+wxy}{(x+z)(y+w)}  \right )+f\left ( \frac{(x+z)(y+w)}{x+y+z+w} \right )=f\left (\frac{xyz+yzw+zwx+wxy}{(x+y)(z+w)}  \right )+f\left ( \frac{(x+y)(z+w)}{x+y+z+w} \right ) $ And it looks dirty, so we plug in  $ y=w=\sqrt{xz} $ .
Hence, if we say  $ t=\frac{2(x+z)}{(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{z})^{2}},s=\sqrt{xz} $ , then  $ f\left ( ts \right )+f\left ( \frac{s}{t} \right )=2f(s) $ .
Plus,  $ t $  gets all real number between  $ 1 $  and  $ 2 $ . So, it's easy from now. :)

stem_md: Let  $I\subset \mathbb R$  be a non-empty open interval,  $\varepsilon\geq 0$  and  $f\colon I\rightarrow\mathbb R$  a function satisfying the  $$ f(tx+(1-t)y)\leq tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)+\varepsilon t(1-t)|x-y| $$  inequality for all  $x,y\in I$  and  $t\in [0,1]$ . Prove that there exists a convex  $g\colon I\rightarrow\mathbb R$  function, such that the function  $l :=f-g$  has the  $\varepsilon$ -Lipschitz property, that is  $$ |l(x)-l(y)|\leq \varepsilon|x-y|\text{     for all }x,y\in I $$
solution_md:
Let  $g(x)$  be the convex hull of  $f(x), x\in I$ . That is:  $$ g(x) := \sup\{h(x) \mid h \text{ is a convex function }, \forall t\in I\,,\, h(t)\leq f(t)\}.   $$   
Then  $g(x),x\in I$  is convex and  $g(x)\leq f(x)$  for all  $x\in I$ . Let  $\ell(x)=f(x)-g(x)$ . It follows  $\ell(x)\geq 0$ . If  $g(x)>0$  on some interval  $I'\subset I$  then  $g$  is a straight line on  $I'$ . Indeed, if not, we can straighten a bit  $g$  which contradicts with it being the convex hull.

Now, arguing by contradiction suppose  $\ell(x)$  doesn't satisfy  $\varepsilon$ -Lipschitz property, that is for some  $x_1<x_2\in I$ , it holds:  $$ |\ell(x_1)-\ell(x_2)| > \varepsilon |x_1-x_2|.  $$  If there exists  $c\in(x_1,x_2)$  for which  $\ell(c)=0$  we can consider  $(x_1,c)$  or  $(c,x_2)$ . For one of them the Lipschitz property of  $\ell$  also fails. Thereby, WLOG we can suppose  $\ell(x)$  is positive inside  $(x_1,x_2)$ . 
Let  $a, b\in I, a\leq x_1<x_2\leq b$  satisfy  $\ell(a)=\ell(b)=0$  and  $\ell$  is positive inside  $(a,b)$ . As said above, it means  $g(x)$  is a straight line through the points  $(a,f(a));(b,f(b))$ . Hence  $\ell(x)=f-g$  also satisfies the problem statement condition on  $(a,b)$ :  $$ (*)\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\ell(tx+(1-t)y)\leq \ell(x)+(1-t)\ell(y)+\varepsilon t(1-t)|x-y|\,,\,\forall x,y\in(a,b) $$  Suppose WLOG  $\ell(x_1)<\ell(x_2)$ , otherwise, we could flip the interval  $I$ , exchanging its ends. The idea is to construct points  $x_3,x_4,\dots$  with  $x_1<x_2<x_3<x_4<\dots$  and a constant step  $x_{i+1}-x_i=x_2-x_1$ . Using  $(*)$  we'll see consecutively that  $\ell(x_i),i=3,4,\dots$  couldn't drop below  $\ell(x_1)$  and particularly it cannot vanish, but on the other hand  $\ell(b)=0$ .

More details: Let  $\Delta x=x_2-x_1$ . Then  $\ell(x_2)-\ell(x_1)>\varepsilon\Delta x$ . Applying  $(*)$  to  $x_1,x_2,x_3$ , yields  $\ell(x_3)-\ell(x_1)\geq (1-1/4)\varepsilon\Delta x$ . Applying  $(*)$  to  $(x_1,x_n,x_{n+1})$  gives us:   $$ \ell(x_{n+1})\geq \ell(x_n)-\frac{1}{n^2}\varepsilon\Delta x $$  The above estimate also holds for  $x\in (x_n,x_{n+1})$ . Hence, for any  $x\in (x_n,x_{n+1}]$ , we have:
\[\ell(x)-\ell(x_1)\geq \varepsilon\Delta x\left(1-\frac{1}{2^2}-\dots-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\]
It yields  $\ell(x)-\ell(x_1)>0$  for any  $x>x_1$ , a contradiction, since  $\ell(b)=0$ .

stem_md: Let  $H$  be a complex Hilbert space. The bounded linear operator  $A$  is called *positive* if  $\langle Ax, x\rangle \geq 0$  for all  $x\in H$ . Let  $\sqrt A$  be the positive square root of  $A$ , i.e. the uniquely determined positive operator satisfying  $(\sqrt{A})^2=A$ . On the set of positive operators we introduce the  $$ A\circ B=\sqrt A B\sqrt B $$  operation. Prove that for a given pair  $A, B$  of positive operators the identity  $$ (A\circ B)\circ C=A\circ (B\circ C) $$  holds for all positive operator  $C$  if and only if  $AB=BA$ .
solution_md:
We keep the definition proposed by dominicleejun:  $A\circ B=\sqrt A B\sqrt A$ .
Note that the eigenspaces of  $A$  and  $\sqrt{A}$  (resp.  $B$  and  $\sqrt{B}$ ) are the same.
1.  If  $AB=BA$ , then  $A\circ B=AB$  because  $\sqrt{A}B=B\sqrt{A}$ . We deduce that  $(A\circ B)\circ C=\sqrt{AB}C\sqrt{AB}$ .
On the other hand,  $A\circ(B\circ C)=\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B}C\sqrt{B}\sqrt{A}$ . The equality -for every  $C$ - comes from  $\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B}=\sqrt{B}\sqrt{A}=\sqrt{AB}$ .
2. If, for every  $C$ ,   $(A\circ B)\circ C=A\circ (B\circ C)$ , then, for every  $C\geq 0$ ,  $\sqrt{\sqrt{A}B\sqrt{A}}C\sqrt{\sqrt{A}B\sqrt{A}}=\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B}C\sqrt{B}\sqrt{A}$ , that is, the functions  $X\in S^+\rightarrow PXP$  and  $X\in S^+\rightarrow QXQ^T$  are equal.
 That implies (I think so, but it would be necessary to detail)  $P\otimes P=Q\otimes Q$   (the above  $2$  functions defined on whole  $L(H)$  remain equal).
If  $P=0$ , then  $\sqrt{A}B\sqrt{A}=0=\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B}(\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B})^T$  is symmetric  $\geq 0$ ; then  $\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B}=\sqrt{B}\sqrt{A}=0$  and  $AB=BA$ .
If  $P\not= 0$ , then there is  $a\not=0$  s.t.  $P=aQ,Q=aP$ ; thus   $Q$  is symmetric and  $\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B}=\sqrt{B}\sqrt{A}$  and  $AB=BA$ .

stem_md: Let  $G$  be a simple  $k$  edge-connected graph on  $n$  vertices and let  $u$  and  $v$  be different vertices of  $G$ . Prove that there are  $k$  edge-disjoint paths from  $u$  to  $v$  each having at most  $\frac{20n}{k}$  edges.
solution_md:
Yes you are absolutely right about that. The original poster also told me, and here I'm copying my reply to his private message. 

The constant  $3e^2$  is larger than  $20$ , but pretty close. To deal the final blow, let's fist reconsider the argument for  $km \leq 3n + 2s$ . We have the chain  $C = v_0 v_1 \dots v_m$ . Consider the **multi-set**  $T = N(v_0) \cup N(v_1) \cup \dots \cup N(v_m)$ , which counts the vertices adjacent to some  $v_j$  as well as the multiplicities.  $|T| = k(m+1)$ . Now each  $v_j$  appears two times in  $T$  as being adjacent to  $v_{j-1}$  and  $v_{j+1}$ . Except for these, a vertex  $v_j$  could appear in  $T$  only if it belongs to a removed edge of the form  $v_iv_j$ , and as you pointed out such an edge is counted twice. For a vertex  $w$  not on the chain,  $w$  could appear in  $T$  as part of a removed edge  $v_iw$ , which is counted once. Otherwise  $w$  is adjacent to at most  $3$  vertices on the chain, or the chain can be shortened. Combining these observations, we obtain   $$ k(m+1) \leq 2(m+1) + 2s_1 + s_2 + 2(n-m-1) + q, $$  where  $s_1$  is the number of removed edges  $v_iv_j$ ,  $s_2$  is the number of removed edges  $v_iw$ , and  $q$  is the number of those  $w$  adjacent to  $3$  vertices on the chain after previous edges have been removed. We deduce by simple algebra that 
\begin{align}
k(m+1) \leq 2n + 2s + q - (s_2 + 2s_3),
\end{align}
where  $s_3$  is the number of removed edges that are of the form  $ww'$ . Note that  $s = s_1 + s_2 + s_3$ . 

Obviously  $q \leq n$ , so we recover our previous result. To be more refined, we show either  $q$  is small, or  $s_2 + 2s_3$  is large. So define  $Q = \{w: w\notin C, w \text{ is adjacent to 3 vertices on } C \text{ after previous edges are removed}\}$ . Each  $w$  in  $Q$  must be adjacent to three consecutive vertices  $v_{i-1}, v_{i}, v_{i+1}$ , for otherwise the chain can again be shortened. Now w.l.o.g. assume one third of such  $w$  correspond to indices  $i$  that are divisible by  $3$ ; call them the set  $W$ . If  $w'$  is adjacent to  $v_{j-1}, v_{j}, v_{j+1}$  with  $j \geq i + 3$ , then after previous edges are removed  $w$  and  $w'$  cannot be adjacent, otherwise the path  $v_{i-1} w w' v_{j+1}$  shortens  $v_{i-1} v_{i} \dots v_{j+1}$ , which has length at least  $5$ . The same argument shows there cannot be any vertex adjacent to both  $w$  and  $w'$ , after previous edges are removed. Therefore by considering the multi-set  $\cup_{w \in W} N(w)$ , we can obtain  
\[
k \cdot \frac{q}{3} \leq n + s_2 + 2s_3.
\]
This is because each removed edge of the form  $w w' ~(w,w' \in W)$  is counted twice, and their number is at most  $s_3$ . Each removed edge of the form  $w u ~(w\in W, u\notin W)$  is counted once, and their number is at most  $s_2$ . 

Plugging the above estimate back into (1), it is not hard to conclude that  $k(m+1) \leq 2n + 2s + \frac{3n}{k} \leq 2.15n + 2s$  (since we could assume  $k > 20$ ). This then reduces the final constant to  $2.15e^2 < 20$ .
